anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.name: Anterior belly of digastric muscle
anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.summary: Anterior belly of the digastric, running from the chin to the hyoid via a fibrous sling. It elevates the hyoid during swallowing and assists in opening the mouth.
anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.origin: Digastric fossa on the lower border of the mandible close to the symphysis menti.
anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.insertion: Intermediate tendon of digastric, anchored to the body and greater horn of the hyoid by a fibrous sling.
anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.action: Elevates the hyoid and floor of mouth during swallowing; assists depression of the mandible when the hyoid is fixed.
anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.innervation: Mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (mandibular division of trigeminal, V3).
anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.blood_supply: Submental branch of the facial artery and mylohyoid branch of the inferior alveolar artery.
anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.relations: Lies superficial to the mylohyoid and forms the lateral wall of the submental triangle; the submental vessels run on the mylohyoid between it and the mandible; the mylohyoid nerve descends with it.

injector_notes.relevance: Boundary of the submental region; injectors treating submental fullness with deoxycholic acid or energy devices work in the fat plane superficial to this muscle and the mylohyoid.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not a routine neurotoxin target.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep or posterior submental injections risk diffusion to suprahyoid muscles causing transient dysphagia, and spread toward the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve can cause lower lip asymmetry.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.name: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle
ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.summary: Continuation of the oblique arytenoid fibres into the aryepiglottic fold. It acts as a sphincter of the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.
ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.origin: Muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage (as continuation of the oblique arytenoid).
ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.insertion: Lateral margin of the epiglottis via the aryepiglottic fold.
ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.action: Narrows and closes the laryngeal inlet and approximates the aryepiglottic folds during swallowing.
ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.innervation: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus, CN X).
ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.blood_supply: Laryngeal branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries.
ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.relations: Lies within the aryepiglottic fold, lateral to the laryngeal vestibule; the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels enter the larynx nearby through the thyrohyoid membrane.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; part of laryngeal anatomy relevant to neck surgery and voice procedures.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable for aesthetic toxin use.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep neck injections near the thyroid cartilage can reach laryngeal muscles and cause dysphonia or dysphagia.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.name: Ascending part of trapezius muscle
ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.summary: Lower (ascending) fibres of the trapezius sweeping up from the lower thoracic spine to the scapula. Together with the other parts it stabilizes and rotates the scapula during arm elevation.
ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.origin: Spinous processes of T4 to T12 and the supraspinous ligament.
ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.insertion: Medial end and tubercle of the spine of the scapula.
ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.action: Depresses the medial scapula and, with the other trapezius parts, upwardly rotates the scapula.
ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) with proprioceptive fibres from C3-C4.
ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.blood_supply: Transverse cervical artery and dorsal scapular artery, with intercostal perforators.
ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.relations: Lies superficial in the lower posterior neck and upper back over the rhomboids and erector spinae; the spinal accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle toward its deep surface at the anterior border of the upper trapezius.

injector_notes.relevance: Occasionally included in off-label trapezius contouring (trap tox) protocols targeting upper shoulder bulk, though the lower fibres contribute little to shoulder line aesthetics.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Off-label toxin treatment for trapezius hypertrophy or chronic myofascial pain; placement principle is intramuscular injection into the thickest palpable portion of the muscle, avoiding the midline spine.
injector_notes.cautions: Wide diffusion over the posterior triangle can weaken scapular stabilizers and cause shoulder fatigue; keep injections intramuscular and avoid deep injections toward the thoracic cage.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)

bucinator.name: Buccinator muscle
bucinator.summary: Thin muscular wall of the cheek between the maxilla and mandible. It keeps the cheek pressed against the teeth during chewing and is used in blowing and sucking.
bucinator.origin: Alveolar processes of the maxilla and mandible opposite the molar teeth, and the anterior edge of the pterygomandibular raphe.
bucinator.insertion: Modiolus and fibres of the orbicularis oris at the angle of the mouth.
bucinator.action: Compresses the cheek against the teeth and gums, aids mastication and expulsion of air; assists lip closure.
bucinator.innervation: Buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
bucinator.blood_supply: Buccal branch of the maxillary artery and branches of the facial and infraorbital arteries.
bucinator.relations: The buccal fat pad lies on its superficial surface in the cheek; the parotid duct pierces it opposite the upper second molar; buccal branches of the facial nerve and the transverse facial vessels cross superficial to it; the buccal nerve (V3) supplies sensation to its deep surface.

injector_notes.relevance: Important backdrop for mid-face filler and masseter toxin; injectors must know its relation to the parotid duct and buccal fat pad. Not a routine toxin target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Rarely targeted; experimental toxin use for cheek biting or facial synkinesis has been described but is not routine practice.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion from masseter or perioral toxin into the buccinator causes cheek laxity, food trapping and asymmetric smile; deep cheek filler must avoid the parotid duct and facial vessels crossing the anterior border of the masseter.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)

corrugator-supercilii.name: Corrugator supercilii muscle
corrugator-supercilii.summary: Small brow muscle deep to the frontalis that pulls the eyebrows medially and downward. Its contraction produces the vertical glabellar frown lines.
corrugator-supercilii.origin: Medial end of the superciliary arch of the frontal bone.
corrugator-supercilii.insertion: Deep surface of the skin of the medial eyebrow, blending with frontalis and orbicularis oculi.
corrugator-supercilii.action: Draws the eyebrow medially and downward, producing vertical wrinkles of the glabella.
corrugator-supercilii.innervation: Temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
corrugator-supercilii.blood_supply: Supratrochlear and supraorbital branches of the ophthalmic artery.
corrugator-supercilii.relations: Lies deep to the depressor supercilii, frontalis and orbicularis oculi at the medial brow; the supratrochlear nerve and vessels pass through or just medial to it, and the supraorbital neurovascular bundle exits at the supraorbital notch roughly at the midpupillary line.

injector_notes.relevance: Primary target of glabellar complex neurotoxin treatment; weakening it smooths vertical frown lines and can subtly elevate the medial brow.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Glabellar frown lines; the principle is deep intramuscular placement at the medial brow, directed laterally and upward away from the orbit, keeping clear of the supraorbital rim.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion through the orbital septum to the levator palpebrae superioris causes upper lid ptosis; intravascular injection near the supratrochlear vessels is a reported filler danger zone because of anastomoses with the ophthalmic artery.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

deep-part-of-masseter.name: Deep part of masseter
deep-part-of-masseter.summary: Deeper, vertically oriented portion of the masseter arising from the deep surface of the zygomatic arch. It is a strong elevator of the mandible.
deep-part-of-masseter.origin: Inferior border and deep (medial) surface of the posterior part of the zygomatic arch.
deep-part-of-masseter.insertion: Upper part of the lateral surface of the ramus and coronoid process of the mandible.
deep-part-of-masseter.action: Elevates the mandible; contributes to clenching.
deep-part-of-masseter.innervation: Masseteric nerve (anterior division of V3), reaching it via the mandibular notch.
deep-part-of-masseter.blood_supply: Masseteric branch of the maxillary artery and transverse facial artery branches.
deep-part-of-masseter.relations: Covered by the superficial part of the masseter and the parotid gland posterolaterally; the masseteric nerve and vessels pass through the mandibular notch to reach its deep surface; the temporomandibular joint lies just posterosuperior.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to masseteric hypertrophy treatment; some protocols target the deeper belly near the zygomatic origin for better contouring of the upper masseter.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Masseter toxin for bruxism or lower face slimming is placed intramuscularly; the principle is to stay in the lower, thicker portion of the muscle and posterior to its anterior border, whether superficial or deep bellies are treated.
injector_notes.cautions: Injection too close to the zygomatic arch or too anterior risks diffusion to the risorius, buccinator or zygomaticus muscles causing smile asymmetry; the parotid duct and transverse facial vessels cross the muscle surface about one fingerbreadth below the arch.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)

depressor-anguli-oris.name: Depressor Anguli Oris (Downturned Mouth Corners)
depressor-anguli-oris.summary: Weakening DAO releases the downward pull on the mouth corner and allows zygomaticus major and levator anguli oris to lift it. Place one point per side in the DAO belly, roughly at the intersection of the marionette line and a point well lateral to the modiolus and above the mandibular border. Stay lateral to avoid the depressor labii inferioris (weakness causes asymmetric lower lip and speech or eating problems), stay above the mandibular border to avoid the marginal mandibular nerve, and respect the facial artery as it crosses toward the mouth corner. No doses given.
depressor-anguli-oris.plane: Intramuscular into the DAO belly, posterolateral to the mouth corner and above the mandibular border
depressor-anguli-oris.danger: Marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve, Facial artery, Inferior labial artery
depressor-anguli-oris.common_complications: Lower lip asymmetry from spread to depressor labii inferioris; dysarthria or drooling with overtreatment; bruising along facial or inferior labial artery; paradoxical marionette deepening if placed too medial

injector_notes.relevance: Injection zone — a study overlay showing where this treatment is placed and which structures make it risky.
injector_notes.cautions: Lower lip asymmetry from spread to depressor labii inferioris; dysarthria or drooling with overtreatment; bruising along facial or inferior labial artery; paradoxical marionette deepening if placed too medial

depressor-labii-inferioris.name: Depressor labii inferioris muscle
depressor-labii-inferioris.summary: Quadrangular muscle between the mandible and the lower lip that depresses and everts the lower lip. It is important in showing the lower teeth during a full smile.
depressor-labii-inferioris.origin: Oblique line of the mandible between the symphysis menti and the mental foramen.
depressor-labii-inferioris.insertion: Skin and mucosa of the lower lip, blending with orbicularis oris.
depressor-labii-inferioris.action: Depresses the lower lip and draws it slightly laterally and downward, everting the vermilion.
depressor-labii-inferioris.innervation: Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
depressor-labii-inferioris.blood_supply: Inferior labial branch of the facial artery and mental branches of the inferior alveolar artery.
depressor-labii-inferioris.relations: Medial edge overlaps the mentalis; its lateral border is covered by the depressor anguli oris; the mental nerve and vessels emerge from the mental foramen deep to its lateral part, and the inferior labial artery runs between the muscle and the mucosa.

injector_notes.relevance: Targeted with toxin on the hyperactive side to correct asymmetric lower lip movement and selected gummy or full-smile cases.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Asymmetric smile correction (weakening the overactive side) and selected lower lip eversion patterns; the principle is conservative injection into the lateral belly, staying clear of the midline mentalis and the orbicularis oris.
injector_notes.cautions: Spread to the mentalis or orbicularis oris causes lower lip incompetence, drooling, slurred speech and asymmetric smile; injections near the mental foramen risk the mental neurovascular bundle.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

depressor-septi-nasi.name: Depressor septi nasi muscle
depressor-septi-nasi.summary: Slender muscle between the maxilla and the nasal septum that pulls the nasal tip downward and narrows the nostril. It is active in smiling and speaking in some individuals.
depressor-septi-nasi.origin: Incisive fossa of the maxilla above the central and lateral incisors.
depressor-septi-nasi.insertion: Mobile part of the nasal septum and the posterior aspect of the ala of the nose.
depressor-septi-nasi.action: Pulls the nasal septum and tip downward and constricts the nares; contributes to upper lip shortening on smiling.
depressor-septi-nasi.innervation: Buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
depressor-septi-nasi.blood_supply: Superior labial branch of the facial artery.
depressor-septi-nasi.relations: Lies deep to the mucosa of the upper lip at the base of the columella, just above the orbicularis oris; the superior labial vessels and the nasopalatine structures of the incisive canal lie medially.

injector_notes.relevance: Toxin target for patients whose nasal tip drops on smiling (dynamic tip ptosis) and for shortening of the upper lip during animation.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Dynamic nasal tip depression and bunny line adjunct treatment; the principle is a small, superficial injection at the base of the columella, midline, staying below the septum and above the orbicularis oris.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion into the orbicularis oris causes upper lip flattening, lengthening of the lip and impaired animation; treat conservatively and avoid injection near the superior labial vessels.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.name: Descending part of trapezius muscle
descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.summary: Upper fibres of the trapezius from the skull and cervical ligament to the clavicle. They elevate the scapula and form the contour of the side of the neck.
descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.origin: Medial third of the superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, and the nuchal ligament of the cervical spine.
descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.insertion: Posterior surface of the lateral third of the clavicle.
descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.action: Elevates the scapula and assists upward rotation; acting with the head fixed it extends and laterally flexes the neck.
descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) with proprioceptive fibres from C3-C4.
descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.blood_supply: Transverse cervical artery and branches of the occipital artery.
descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.relations: Forms the superficial muscle of the posterior neck triangle; the spinal accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle from the sternocleidomastoid to its anterior border, and the greater occipital nerve and occipital artery emerge deep and medial to its upper attachment.

injector_notes.relevance: Target of off-label trapezius toxin (trap tox or shoulder slimming) for hypertrophy-related shoulder contour and myofascial pain.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Off-label toxin treatment of upper trapezius bulk; the principle is multiple intramuscular points spread over the palpable thickened upper belly, staying superficial and lateral to the midline.
injector_notes.cautions: Large treatment area means high total exposure and risk of shoulder weakness, fatigue and difficulty carrying loads; deep injections risk the levator scapulae and, medially, structures of the posterior triangle including the accessory nerve.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)

external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.name: External part of thyro-arytenoid muscle
external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.summary: Main body of the thyroarytenoid lying alongside the vocal fold. It adducts, shortens and relaxes the vocal fold and shapes phonation.
external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.origin: Lower half of the angle of the thyroid cartilage and the cricothyroid ligament.
external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.insertion: Anterolateral surface of the arytenoid cartilage.
external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.action: Adducts and shortens the vocal folds and adjusts their tension during phonation; the medial fibres (vocalis) fine-tune pitch.
external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.innervation: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus, CN X).
external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.blood_supply: Laryngeal branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries.
external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.relations: Lies deep to the thyroid cartilage lamina, lateral to the vocal ligament and laryngeal ventricle; the superior laryngeal vessels and internal laryngeal nerve run above it after piercing the thyrohyoid membrane.

injector_notes.relevance: Not an aesthetic target; it is the therapeutic target of EMG-guided botulinum toxin injections for adductor spasmodic dysphonia performed by laryngologists.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Laryngeal toxin for spasmodic dysphonia is delivered through the cricothyroid membrane under EMG guidance into the thyroarytenoid; this is a specialist medical procedure, not aesthetic practice.
injector_notes.cautions: Overdose or diffusion causes breathy voice, weak cough and aspiration; aesthetic injectors must avoid deep anterior neck injections near the larynx.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

frontalis-muscle.name: Frontalis muscle
frontalis-muscle.summary: Anterior belly of the occipitofrontalis and the only elevator of the eyebrows. Its contraction produces the horizontal forehead lines.
frontalis-muscle.origin: Galea aponeurotica (epicranial aponeurosis) near the coronal suture.
frontalis-muscle.insertion: Skin and subcutaneous tissue of the eyebrows and root of the nose, interdigitating with orbicularis oculi, corrugator and procerus.
frontalis-muscle.action: Elevates the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead transversely; assists in expressions of surprise.
frontalis-muscle.innervation: Temporal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
frontalis-muscle.blood_supply: Supratrochlear and supraorbital branches of the ophthalmic artery and frontal branch of the superficial temporal artery.
frontalis-muscle.relations: Lies directly under the forehead skin with no bony attachment below; the supraorbital and supratrochlear neurovascular bundles pass from the orbit through or deep to its lower border; the frontal branch of the superficial temporal artery runs on its lateral surface.

injector_notes.relevance: Core toxin target for horizontal forehead lines; because it is the sole brow elevator, treatment must be balanced against the brow depressors.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Horizontal forehead rhytids; the principle is superficial microinjections in the upper two thirds of the muscle with conservative treatment of the lateral fibres to preserve brow elevation and avoid brow heaviness.
injector_notes.cautions: Over-treatment or low injection produces brow ptosis and a heavy or frozen look; treating the glabella without the frontalis can cause compensatory lateral brow lift (Mephisto or Spock brow); filler in this plane is a vascular danger zone via supratrochlear and supraorbital anastomoses to the ophthalmic artery.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

genioglossus-muscle.name: Genioglossus muscle
genioglossus-muscle.summary: Large extrinsic tongue muscle fanning from the chin into the tongue. It protrudes the tongue and keeps the airway open during sleep.
genioglossus-muscle.origin: Superior mental spine (genial tubercle) on the inner surface of the mandibular symphysis.
genioglossus-muscle.insertion: Fans into the body of the tongue from root to tip; lowest fibres attach to the body of the hyoid.
genioglossus-muscle.action: Protrudes and depresses the tongue; posterior fibres pull the tongue forward to maintain the airway.
genioglossus-muscle.blood_supply: Sublingual branch of the lingual artery.
genioglossus-muscle.relations: Lies in the floor of the mouth above the geniohyoid and mylohyoid; the lingual artery and hypoglossal nerve run lateral to it, and the submandibular duct and lingual nerve lie anterolateral between it and the hyoglossus.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; relevant as deep anatomy of the submental and floor-of-mouth region.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics; experimental toxin use for tongue thrust or obstructive sleep apnea is investigational only.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep submental injections could theoretically spread to tongue musculature and affect speech or swallowing; stay in the subcutaneous plane.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

geniohyoid-muscle.name: Geniohyoid muscle
geniohyoid-muscle.summary: Slender suprahyoid muscle between the chin and the hyoid, lying on the mylohyoid. It elevates the hyoid and helps open the mouth.
geniohyoid-muscle.origin: Inferior mental spine on the inner surface of the mandibular symphysis.
geniohyoid-muscle.insertion: Anterior surface of the body of the hyoid bone.
geniohyoid-muscle.action: Elevates and protracts the hyoid during swallowing; depresses the mandible when the hyoid is fixed.
geniohyoid-muscle.innervation: Fibres of C1 carried with the hypoglossal nerve.
geniohyoid-muscle.blood_supply: Sublingual branch of the lingual artery.
geniohyoid-muscle.relations: Lies on the superior surface of the mylohyoid, medial to the anterior belly of the digastric below; the sublingual gland and submandibular duct lie lateral to it.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; part of the suprahyoid complex relevant to submental treatments.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable for routine aesthetic toxin use.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep submental injections that reach the suprahyoid muscles can cause transient dysphagia; remain superficial to the mylohyoid plane.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

hyoglossus-muscle.name: Hyoglossus muscle
hyoglossus-muscle.summary: Flat extrinsic tongue muscle running vertically from the hyoid into the side of the tongue. It depresses and retracts the tongue.
hyoglossus-muscle.origin: Body and greater horn of the hyoid bone.
hyoglossus-muscle.insertion: Side and inferior aspect of the tongue, blending with the styloglossus and intrinsic tongue muscles.
hyoglossus-muscle.blood_supply: Deep lingual and dorsal lingual branches of the lingual artery.
hyoglossus-muscle.relations: Key surgical landmark of the submandibular region: the lingual artery passes deep to its posterior border, while the hypoglossal nerve, submandibular duct and lingual nerve run on its lateral surface; it overlies the middle pharyngeal constrictor.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; defines the plane of the lingual artery in the submandibular region.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable for routine aesthetic toxin use.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep injections in the submandibular triangle risk the lingual vessels and hypoglossal nerve in the plane of this muscle.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.name: Inferior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.summary: Lower head of the lateral pterygoid, the main protruder and opener of the jaw. It pulls the condyle and disc forward during mouth opening.
inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.origin: Lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate.
inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.insertion: Pterygoid fovea on the neck of the mandibular condyle, with fibres to the TMJ capsule and articular disc.
inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.action: Protrudes the mandible and pulls the condyle and disc anteriorly; acting alternately with the opposite side it produces side-to-side grinding movements.
inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.innervation: Lateral pterygoid nerve from the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3).
inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.blood_supply: Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery.
inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.relations: The maxillary artery runs superficial or deep to it within the infratemporal fossa; the buccal nerve and anterior deep temporal nerves emerge between its two heads; the maxillary nerve lies above and the lingual and inferior alveolar nerves below it.

injector_notes.relevance: Advanced target of EMG-guided toxin for lateral pterygoid hyperactivity in TMJ disorders and selected bruxism cases; not an aesthetic target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Toxin for TMJ dysfunction is placed under EMG or imaging guidance via an intraoral or subzygomatic approach into the muscle belly; this is specialist practice.
injector_notes.cautions: The maxillary artery and its branches surround the muscle; blind injection risks hematoma and diffusion to the pharyngeal muscles causing dysphagia or dysarthria.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)

inferior-oblique-muscle.name: Inferior oblique muscle
inferior-oblique-muscle.summary: Short extraocular muscle from the orbital floor passing back under the eyeball. It elevates the eye when the eye is adducted.
inferior-oblique-muscle.origin: Orbital surface of the maxilla just lateral to the nasolacrimal groove.
inferior-oblique-muscle.insertion: Posterolateral part of the sclera, deep to the lateral rectus.
inferior-oblique-muscle.action: Elevates, abducts and laterally rotates (excyclotorts) the eyeball; principal elevator in adduction.
inferior-oblique-muscle.innervation: Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
inferior-oblique-muscle.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery and the infraorbital artery.
inferior-oblique-muscle.relations: Passes between the orbital floor and the inferior rectus; lies in the inferolateral orbit near the infraorbital canal; separated from the lower lid by the orbital septum and Lockwood ligament.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; relevant because toxin injected at the lower lid can rarely diffuse to it and cause vertical diplopia.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep periorbital toxin injections at the inferolateral lid have been associated with transient diplopia from spread to the inferior oblique or inferior rectus; keep lower lid injections superficial and preseptal.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.name: Inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle
inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.summary: Lowest of the three pharyngeal constrictors, including the cricopharyngeus which acts as the upper esophageal sphincter. It propels the bolus from pharynx to esophagus.
inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.origin: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage (thyropharyngeus) and the side of the cricoid cartilage (cricopharyngeus).
inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.insertion: Median pharyngeal raphe, blending with the opposite muscle.
inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.action: Constricts the lower pharynx sequentially during swallowing; the cricopharyngeus maintains tonic closure of the pharyngoesophageal junction and relaxes to admit the bolus.
inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.innervation: Pharyngeal plexus (vagus CN X) with contributions from the recurrent and external laryngeal nerves.
inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.blood_supply: Ascending pharyngeal artery and inferior thyroid artery branches.
inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.relations: Lies behind the larynx and upper esophagus; the recurrent laryngeal nerve and inferior laryngeal vessels ascend in the tracheoesophageal groove deep to its lateral border; the potential weak area between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus (Killian dehiscence) is the site of Zenker diverticulum; the carotid sheath lies lateral.

injector_notes.relevance: Not an aesthetic target; cricopharyngeal toxin injection is an established ENT treatment for cricopharyngeal spasm and dysphagia under endoscopic or EMG guidance.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Specialist toxin treatment of the cricopharyngeus for upper esophageal sphincter dysfunction; not part of aesthetic practice.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion risks include dysphonia and aspiration; aesthetic neck injections must stay far from this deep plane.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

inferior-rectus-muscle.name: Inferior rectus muscle
inferior-rectus-muscle.summary: Extraocular muscle running along the orbital floor to the underside of the eyeball. It primarily depresses the eye.
inferior-rectus-muscle.origin: Common tendinous ring at the orbital apex.
inferior-rectus-muscle.insertion: Anteroinferior surface of the sclera behind the corneoscleral junction.
inferior-rectus-muscle.action: Depresses the eyeball; secondarily adducts and excyclotorts it.
inferior-rectus-muscle.innervation: Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
inferior-rectus-muscle.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery and the infraorbital artery.
inferior-rectus-muscle.relations: Lies between the eyeball and the orbital floor, close to the infraorbital nerve in the orbital floor; the inferior oblique crosses beneath it; its fascial sheath connects to the lower lid retractors, which is why toxin spread can alter lid position.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; relevant to lower lid toxin complications.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics; ophthalmologists use toxin in extraocular muscles for strabismus.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep injections at the lower orbital rim can diffuse to the inferior rectus causing transient vertical diplopia; keep periorbital toxin superficial.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.name: Intermediate tendon of digastric muscle
intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.summary: Fibrous tendon joining the two bellies of the digastric, tethered to the hyoid by a fascial sling. It transmits the pull of both bellies to the hyoid.
intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.origin: Fibrous continuation of the posterior belly at the hyoid region.
intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.insertion: Fibrous continuation of the anterior belly; the tendon itself is bound to the body and greater horn of the hyoid by a fibrous sling, sometimes perforated by the stylohyoid.
intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.action: Acts as the fulcrum through which the digastric bellies elevate or stabilize the hyoid.
intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.innervation: Not applicable to the tendon; the bellies are innervated by the facial nerve (posterior belly) and mylohyoid nerve (anterior belly).
intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.blood_supply: Small branches of the submental and occipital arteries.
intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.relations: Lies above the hyoid at the junction of the submandibular and submental regions, crossing near the intermediate tendon of the omohyoid and the carotid triangle contents more deeply.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; a palpable landmark in the suprahyoid region.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable.
injector_notes.cautions: None specific to aesthetic practice; deep injections above the hyoid risk the suprahyoid muscles and lingual vessels.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

interspinales-colli-muscles.name: Interspinales colli muscles
interspinales-colli-muscles.summary: Small paired muscles linking the spinous processes of adjacent cervical vertebrae. They assist extension and stabilize the cervical spine.
interspinales-colli-muscles.origin: Superior aspect of the spinous process of each cervical vertebra from C3 to T1.
interspinales-colli-muscles.insertion: Inferior aspect of the spinous process of the vertebra above (C2 to C7).
interspinales-colli-muscles.action: Assist extension of the cervical spine and provide segmental proprioceptive stabilization.
interspinales-colli-muscles.innervation: Dorsal rami of the cervical spinal nerves.
interspinales-colli-muscles.blood_supply: Deep cervical artery and segmental branches of the vertebral artery.
interspinales-colli-muscles.relations: Lie deep in the posterior neck between the spinous processes, deep to the semispinalis and multifidus; the cervical facet joints and their medial branch nerves lie anterolateral.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; relevant to pain physicians performing cervical medial branch blocks.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep paraspinal injections in the cervical region risk the vertebral artery and epidural space; not within aesthetic scope.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.name: Lateral crico-arytenoid muscle
lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.summary: Intrinsic laryngeal muscle from the cricoid arch to the arytenoid. It adducts the vocal folds for phonation and airway protection.
lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.origin: Upper border of the arch of the cricoid cartilage.
lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.insertion: Muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage.
lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.action: Rotates the arytenoid medially to adduct the vocal folds.
lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.innervation: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus CN X).
lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.blood_supply: Laryngeal branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries.
lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.relations: Lies on the lateral aspect of the larynx deep to the thyroid cartilage lamina, anterior to the posterior cricoarytenoid; the recurrent laryngeal nerve enters the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint near it.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; part of the laryngeal framework that deep neck injections must avoid.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion of toxin into laryngeal adductors from anterior neck injections causes dysphonia; keep platysmal and submental treatments superficial.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

lateral-rectus-muscle.name: Lateral rectus muscle
lateral-rectus-muscle.summary: Extraocular muscle on the lateral side of the globe. It abducts the eye and is the muscle paralyzed in sixth nerve palsy.
lateral-rectus-muscle.origin: Common tendinous ring at the orbital apex, by two heads flanking the superior orbital fissure.
lateral-rectus-muscle.insertion: Lateral surface of the sclera behind the corneoscleral junction.
lateral-rectus-muscle.innervation: Abducens nerve (CN VI), entering its ocular surface.
lateral-rectus-muscle.blood_supply: Lacrimal artery and muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
lateral-rectus-muscle.relations: Runs along the lateral orbital wall with the lacrimal artery and nerve above; the abducens nerve crosses the orbital apex within the annulus to reach it; the ciliary ganglion lies between it and the optic nerve.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; relevant to diplopia risk from deep lateral orbital injections.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics; specialist strabismus treatment only.
injector_notes.cautions: Crow's feet toxin placed too deep or too posterior can theoretically track along the lateral orbital wall; transient diplopia after lateral canthal injections has been reported rarely.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

levator-anguli-oris.name: Levator anguli oris muscle
levator-anguli-oris.summary: Deep muscle of the upper lip that elevates the corner of the mouth. It contributes to the nasolabial fold and the smile.
levator-anguli-oris.origin: Canine fossa of the maxilla, just below the infraorbital foramen.
levator-anguli-oris.insertion: Modiolus and skin at the angle of the mouth.
levator-anguli-oris.action: Elevates the angle of the mouth, as in smiling, and helps define the nasolabial fold.
levator-anguli-oris.innervation: Zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
levator-anguli-oris.blood_supply: Infraorbital artery and superior labial branch of the facial artery.
levator-anguli-oris.relations: Lies deep to the levator labii superioris and zygomaticus minor; the infraorbital nerve and vessels emerge just above its origin; the facial vein and buccal fat pad lie lateral to it.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine direct toxin target; must be understood when treating the gummy smile complex and injecting mid-face filler near the canine fossa.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Occasionally included in gummy smile or asymmetric smile protocols as part of the lip elevator complex; the principle is to target the more superficial levator labii superioris alaeque nasi and levator labii superioris rather than this deep muscle.
injector_notes.cautions: Toxin diffusion here weakens the smile and elevates risk of lip asymmetry; filler at the canine fossa must respect the infraorbital neurovascular bundle just superior.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

levator-labii-superioris.name: Levator labii superioris muscle
levator-labii-superioris.summary: Broad lip elevator from the lower orbital margin to the upper lip. It raises and everts the upper lip and deepens the nasolabial fold.
levator-labii-superioris.origin: Maxilla and zygomatic bone along the inferior orbital margin, above the infraorbital foramen.
levator-labii-superioris.insertion: Skin and orbicularis oris of the lateral half of the upper lip.
levator-labii-superioris.action: Elevates and everts the upper lip; contributes to the nasolabial fold.
levator-labii-superioris.innervation: Zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
levator-labii-superioris.blood_supply: Infraorbital artery and superior labial and angular branches of the facial artery.
levator-labii-superioris.relations: Lies deep to the orbicularis oculi at the orbital margin and superficial to the levator anguli oris; the infraorbital nerve emerges beneath its medial border; the facial artery ascends toward the angular artery between it and the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi medially.

injector_notes.relevance: Part of the gummy smile toxin target complex and relevant to mid-face filler and nasolabial fold treatment.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Gummy smile (excessive gingival display) protocols target the lip elevator complex at the nasofacial junction; the principle is conservative injection where the elevators converge at the upper nasolabial fold, avoiding the orbicularis oris.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion to the orbicularis oris causes upper lip ptosis, elongation of the lip and impaired articulation; over-treatment produces a flat or asymmetric smile; the angular and infraorbital vessels traverse the field.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

levator-nasolabialis.name: Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi muscle
levator-nasolabialis.summary: Slip running from the frontal process of the maxilla to the nose and upper lip along the nasolabial fold. It elevates the upper lip and flares the nostril and is a key gummy smile muscle.
levator-nasolabialis.origin: Upper part of the frontal process of the maxilla, beside the nose.
levator-nasolabialis.insertion: Divides into a slip to the alar cartilage and skin of the nose and a slip to the upper lip within the nasolabial fold.
levator-nasolabialis.action: Elevates the upper lip and elevates and everts the ala of the nose; deepens the nasolabial fold and contributes to bunny lines at the nasal sidewall.
levator-nasolabialis.innervation: Zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
levator-nasolabialis.blood_supply: Angular artery (terminal branch of the facial artery) and infraorbital branches.
levator-nasolabialis.relations: Lies along the nasal sidewall and medial nasolabial fold; the angular artery and vein run just medial and deep to it toward the inner canthus; the levator labii superioris is directly lateral and the orbicularis oculi above.

injector_notes.relevance: Primary toxin target for gummy smile and for dynamic bunny lines at the nasal root and sidewall.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Gummy smile and bunny lines; the principle is superficial injection at the nasofacial groove over the upper nasolabial fold where this muscle is most superficial, kept small in volume to limit spread.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion medially into the orbicularis oris or laterally into the levator labii superioris unbalances the smile; the angular vessels are a filler danger zone at the medial end of this muscle with anastomoses to the ophthalmic system.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

levator-palpebrae-superioris.name: Levator palpebrae superioris muscle
levator-palpebrae-superioris.summary: Muscle of the upper orbit that elevates the upper eyelid. Its accidental weakening by toxin diffusion is the cause of post-treatment ptosis.
levator-palpebrae-superioris.origin: Inferior surface of the lesser wing of the sphenoid, above and anterior to the optic canal.
levator-palpebrae-superioris.insertion: Skin of the upper eyelid and the anterior surface of the superior tarsal plate via a wide aponeurosis; a smooth muscle component (superior tarsal or Muller muscle) attaches to the upper edge of the tarsus.
levator-palpebrae-superioris.action: Elevates the upper eyelid and maintains the palpebral fissure.
levator-palpebrae-superioris.innervation: Superior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III); the smooth muscle part is supplied by sympathetic fibres.
levator-palpebrae-superioris.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
levator-palpebrae-superioris.relations: Lies directly above the superior rectus, sharing a fascial sheath, just below the orbital roof; the frontal nerve and supraorbital vessels run above it in the upper orbit; its aponeurosis fuses with the orbital septum at the lid crease.

injector_notes.relevance: Not injected directly; it is the structure to protect in every brow, forehead and glabella toxin treatment because spread to it causes upper lid ptosis.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Toxin placed low near the supraorbital rim or injected with pressure toward the orbit can diffuse to the levator and produce ptosis lasting weeks; direct injections downward at the orbital rim and massage immediately after glabellar treatment should be avoided.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

levator-scapulae.name: Levator scapulae muscle
levator-scapulae.summary: Strap-like muscle from the upper cervical transverse processes to the superior scapular angle. It elevates the scapula and is a common site of neck myofascial pain.
levator-scapulae.origin: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C1 to C4.
levator-scapulae.insertion: Medial border of the scapula above the spine, including the superior angle.
levator-scapulae.action: Elevates the scapula and tilts the glenoid downward; with the scapula fixed it laterally flexes and rotates the neck.
levator-scapulae.innervation: Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) with branches from C3 and C4.
levator-scapulae.blood_supply: Dorsal scapular artery and transverse cervical artery.
levator-scapulae.relations: Lies deep to the sternocleidomastoid above and the trapezius below in the posterior triangle; the spinal accessory nerve crosses its surface, and the dorsal scapular nerve and artery run deep to it; the scalenus medius and the brachial plexus lie anterior.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine aesthetic target; relevant to trapezius toxin treatments because deep diffusion can weaken it and to trigger point injections for neck pain.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Occasionally treated with toxin for chronic myofascial neck pain by pain specialists; the principle is EMG or palpation-guided intramuscular placement away from the posterior triangle neurovascular structures.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep injections risk the accessory nerve on its surface and the dorsal scapular neurovascular bundle; combined trapezius and levator weakness impairs scapular control.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

longissimus-capitis-muscle.name: Longissimus capitis muscle
longissimus-capitis-muscle.summary: Intermediate-layer erector spinae muscle running from the upper thoracic and lower cervical transverse processes to the mastoid region. It extends and rotates the head.
longissimus-capitis-muscle.origin: Transverse processes of T1 to T5 and articular processes of C4 to C7.
longissimus-capitis-muscle.insertion: Posterior margin of the mastoid process, deep to the splenius capitis and sternocleidomastoid.
longissimus-capitis-muscle.action: Bilaterally extends the head; unilaterally laterally flexes and rotates the head to the same side.
longissimus-capitis-muscle.innervation: Dorsal rami of the cervical spinal nerves.
longissimus-capitis-muscle.blood_supply: Occipital artery, deep cervical artery and vertebral artery branches.
longissimus-capitis-muscle.relations: Lies between the splenius capitis superficially and the semispinalis capitis medially; the occipital artery crosses near its insertion; the greater occipital nerve pierces the semispinalis just medial to it.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; part of the deep suboccipital anatomy relevant to occipital nerve blocks for headache.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable; cervicogenic headache toxin protocols target more superficial muscles.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep injections in the suboccipital region risk the vertebral artery in the suboccipital triangle and the occipital vessels at the mastoid.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

longissimus-colli-muscle.name: Longissimus colli muscle
longissimus-colli-muscle.summary: Cervical part of the longissimus, connecting thoracic and cervical transverse processes. It extends and laterally flexes the neck.
longissimus-colli-muscle.origin: Transverse processes of the upper thoracic vertebrae (about T1 to T5).
longissimus-colli-muscle.insertion: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C2 to C6.
longissimus-colli-muscle.action: Extends and laterally flexes the cervical spine; assists ipsilateral rotation.
longissimus-colli-muscle.innervation: Dorsal rami of the lower cervical spinal nerves.
longissimus-colli-muscle.blood_supply: Deep cervical artery and branches of the transverse cervical and vertebral arteries.
longissimus-colli-muscle.relations: Lies on the posterior aspect of the cervical transverse processes deep to the splenius cervicis and levator scapulae; the cervical dorsal rami cross it; the vertebral artery runs anterior to the transverse processes it spans.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep posterior cervical injections risk the vertebral artery and nerve roots; outside aesthetic scope.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

longus-capitis-muscle.name: Longus capitis muscle
longus-capitis-muscle.summary: Prevertebral muscle from the cervical transverse processes to the skull base. It flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.
longus-capitis-muscle.origin: Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3 to C6.
longus-capitis-muscle.insertion: Inferior surface of the basilar part of the occipital bone.
longus-capitis-muscle.action: Flexes the head and upper cervical spine; assists rotation to the same side.
longus-capitis-muscle.innervation: Ventral rami of C1 to C3.
longus-capitis-muscle.blood_supply: Ascending pharyngeal artery and muscular branches of the vertebral artery.
longus-capitis-muscle.relations: Lies on the anterior aspect of the upper cervical spine behind the pharynx and retropharyngeal space; the cervical sympathetic trunk runs on its anterior surface within the prevertebral fascia; the internal carotid artery and jugular vein are anterolateral.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable.
injector_notes.cautions: The sympathetic trunk on its surface is at risk in deep anterior neck procedures; deep injections here are outside aesthetic practice.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

longus-colli-muscle.name: Longus colli muscle
longus-colli-muscle.summary: Long prevertebral muscle on the front of the cervical and upper thoracic vertebral bodies. It flexes the neck and is a deep neck flexor important in posture.
longus-colli-muscle.origin: Bodies of C5 to T3 vertebrae and anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3 to C5.
longus-colli-muscle.insertion: Anterior arch of the atlas, bodies of C2 to C4, and transverse processes of C5 and C6.
longus-colli-muscle.action: Flexes the neck and assists rotation and lateral flexion to the same side.
longus-colli-muscle.innervation: Ventral rami of C2 to C6.
longus-colli-muscle.blood_supply: Inferior thyroid, vertebral and ascending pharyngeal arterial branches.
longus-colli-muscle.relations: Lies behind the pharynx and esophagus, covered by prevertebral fascia; the sympathetic trunk lies on its anterolateral surface, and the carotid sheath is lateral; the recurrent laryngeal nerve and inferior thyroid artery cross anterior to its lower part.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; relevant to understanding the deep anterior neck plane that must never be entered by aesthetic injectables.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep anterior neck injections can injure the sympathetic trunk (Horner syndrome), the recurrent laryngeal nerve or the esophagus; stay within the subcutaneous plane in the anterior neck.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

medial-pterygoid-muscle.name: Medial pterygoid muscle
medial-pterygoid-muscle.summary: Thick muscle on the inner surface of the mandibular ramus, mirror image of the masseter. It elevates and protrudes the jaw and is a cause of trismus when irritated.
medial-pterygoid-muscle.origin: Deep head from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and pyramidal process of the palatine bone; superficial head from the maxillary tuberosity.
medial-pterygoid-muscle.insertion: Medial surface of the ramus and angle of the mandible, above and behind the mylohyoid groove.
medial-pterygoid-muscle.action: Elevates the mandible and assists protrusion; acting alternately it produces side-to-side movements.
medial-pterygoid-muscle.innervation: Medial pterygoid nerve from the mandibular division (V3).
medial-pterygoid-muscle.blood_supply: Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery.
medial-pterygoid-muscle.relations: The lingual and inferior alveolar nerves descend between it and the ramus laterally; the tensor veli palatini, auditory tube and otic ganglion lie medial; the maxillary artery crosses its lower border; the inferior alveolar nerve block is given in the space between its upper part and the ramus.

injector_notes.relevance: Advanced target for toxin in trismus, bruxism with medial pterygoid involvement and selected TMJ disorders; encountered in intraoral approaches to the infratemporal fossa.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Toxin for trismus or jaw clenching is placed intraorally or with EMG guidance into the muscle belly; specialist practice only.
injector_notes.cautions: The inferior alveolar and lingual nerves and maxillary vessels surround the muscle; diffusion to pharyngeal muscles causes dysphagia and dysarthria; risk of deep hematoma.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)

medial-rectus-muscle.name: Medial rectus muscle
medial-rectus-muscle.summary: Extraocular muscle on the medial side of the globe and the strongest of the recti. It adducts the eye.
medial-rectus-muscle.origin: Common tendinous ring at the orbital apex.
medial-rectus-muscle.insertion: Medial surface of the sclera behind the corneoscleral junction.
medial-rectus-muscle.innervation: Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
medial-rectus-muscle.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
medial-rectus-muscle.relations: Lies close to the medial orbital wall (lamina papyracea of the ethmoid) with only periorbital fat between; the nasolacrimal sac and angular vessels are anterior and medial at the canthus; relevant to medial orbital filler danger zones.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; relevant to rare diplopia after medial periorbital injections and to the medial canthal vascular danger zone.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics; specialist strabismus treatment only.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep injections near the medial canthus risk the angular vessels and, rarely, diffusion to medial orbital structures; tear trough filler must respect the angular artery and vein.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

mentalis-muscle.name: Mentalis muscle
mentalis-muscle.summary: Paired muscle at the chin tip that elevates and protrudes the lower lip and wrinkles the chin skin. Hyperactivity produces chin dimpling (peau d'orange).
mentalis-muscle.origin: Incisive fossa of the mandible below the incisor teeth.
mentalis-muscle.action: Raises and protrudes the lower lip (pouting) and wrinkles the skin of the chin.
mentalis-muscle.innervation: Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
mentalis-muscle.blood_supply: Inferior labial branch of the facial artery and mental branches of the inferior alveolar artery.
mentalis-muscle.relations: Lies at the tip of the chin deep to the skin, overlapped laterally by the depressor labii inferioris; the mental nerve and vessels emerge from the mental foramen superior and lateral to it; the inferior labial arteries run medial and superior.

injector_notes.relevance: Common toxin target for chin dimpling and cobblestone chin; also treated to elongate and project the chin in combination with filler.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Chin dimpling (peau d'orange) and hyperactive mentalis; the principle is injection deep into the muscle belly low on the chin near its insertion, avoiding the lip and the depressor labii inferioris laterally.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion upward into the orbicularis oris or laterally into the depressor labii inferioris causes lower lip asymmetry, drooling and speech problems; over-treatment causes lower lip incompetence and difficulty with straws or articulation.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

middle-pharyngeal-constrictor.name: Middle pharyngeal constrictor muscle
middle-pharyngeal-constrictor.summary: Fan-shaped middle constrictor arising from the hyoid horns. It constricts the mid pharynx during swallowing.
middle-pharyngeal-constrictor.origin: Greater and lesser horns of the hyoid bone and the stylohyoid ligament.
middle-pharyngeal-constrictor.insertion: Median pharyngeal raphe, overlapping the inferior constrictor below and overlapped by the superior constrictor above.
middle-pharyngeal-constrictor.action: Constricts the pharyngeal wall sequentially during swallowing to propel the bolus downward.
middle-pharyngeal-constrictor.blood_supply: Ascending pharyngeal artery and tonsillar branches of the facial artery.
middle-pharyngeal-constrictor.relations: Lies behind the oropharynx; the glossopharyngeal nerve and stylopharyngeus pass into the pharynx through the gap between it and the superior constrictor; the internal carotid artery lies lateral in the carotid sheath, and the hyoglossus is anterior.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep injections in the lateral neck near the hyoid can approach this muscle and the carotid sheath; dysphagia after neck toxin usually reflects diffusion toward the constrictors.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

multifidus-colli-muscle.name: Multifidus colli muscle
multifidus-colli-muscle.summary: Deep segmental muscle of the cervical spine spanning two to four vertebrae per fascicle. It stabilizes the cervical spine segmentally.
multifidus-colli-muscle.origin: Articular processes of C4 to C7.
multifidus-colli-muscle.insertion: Spinous processes of vertebrae two to four segments above, from C2 to C5.
multifidus-colli-muscle.action: Stabilizes the cervical vertebrae; assists extension and contralateral rotation.
multifidus-colli-muscle.innervation: Medial branches of the dorsal rami of the cervical spinal nerves.
multifidus-colli-muscle.blood_supply: Deep cervical artery and segmental branches of the vertebral artery.
multifidus-colli-muscle.relations: Lies deep to the semispinalis cervicis, directly on the cervical laminae and facet capsules; the medial branch nerves that supply the facet joints cross its surface, making it the landmark for medial branch blocks.

injector_notes.relevance: Not an aesthetic target; landmark muscle for cervical medial branch blocks and radiofrequency treatment of facet joint pain.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep cervical paraspinal injections risk epidural or intra-arterial vertebral artery injection; strictly interventional pain territory.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

mylohyoid-muscle.name: Mylohyoid muscle
mylohyoid-muscle.summary: Sheet forming the muscular floor of the mouth between the two sides of the mandible. It supports the tongue and elevates the hyoid and floor of mouth in swallowing.
mylohyoid-muscle.origin: Mylohyoid line on the inner surface of the mandible.
mylohyoid-muscle.insertion: Anterior fibres into the median mylohyoid raphe; posterior fibres into the body of the hyoid bone.
mylohyoid-muscle.action: Elevates the floor of the mouth and tongue during swallowing and the first stage of speech; helps depress the mandible.
mylohyoid-muscle.innervation: Mylohyoid nerve from the inferior alveolar nerve (V3).
mylohyoid-muscle.blood_supply: Submental branch of the facial artery and mylohyoid branch of the inferior alveolar artery.
mylohyoid-muscle.relations: Forms the diaphragm of the floor of mouth: the sublingual gland, submandibular duct, lingual and hypoglossal nerves lie above it; the submandibular gland wraps around its posterior free border; the submental vessels and anterior belly of digastric lie below it.

injector_notes.relevance: Defines the treatment plane for submental fat reduction: injectables such as deoxycholic acid are placed in the fat superficial to the mylohyoid; deeper placement risks glandular and muscular injury.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not a routine neurotoxin target.
injector_notes.cautions: Submental injections placed too deep or posterior can involve the submandibular gland, the suprahyoid muscles (transient dysphagia) and, near the mandibular border, the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

nasalis-muscle.name: Nasalis muscle
nasalis-muscle.summary: Muscle of the external nose with transverse and alar parts. It compresses and flares the nostrils and contributes to bunny lines at the nasal sidewall.
nasalis-muscle.origin: Transverse part from the maxilla above and lateral to the canine tooth; alar part from the maxilla above the lateral incisor.
nasalis-muscle.insertion: Transverse part into the aponeurosis over the nasal dorsum meeting the opposite muscle; alar part into the posterior part of the greater alar cartilage.
nasalis-muscle.action: Transverse part compresses the nasal aperture; alar part flares the nostril; together they wrinkle the skin over the nasal bridge.
nasalis-muscle.innervation: Buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
nasalis-muscle.blood_supply: Angular and lateral nasal branches of the facial artery and infraorbital branches.
nasalis-muscle.relations: Lies over the nasal cartilages and lateral nasal sidewall beneath thin skin; the angular artery and vein ascend along the nasofacial junction medial to it; the external nasal nerve (anterior ethmoidal) emerges between the nasal bone and cartilage.

injector_notes.relevance: Toxin target for bunny lines (transverse wrinkles over the nasal dorsum and sidewall) and for excessive nostril flare.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Bunny lines and nasal flare; the principle is superficial injection over the upper lateral nasal sidewall, away from the medial canthus and the lip elevators.
injector_notes.cautions: The angular vessels cross the medial treatment field and are a filler danger zone with ophthalmic anastomoses; diffusion into the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi or orbicularis oris alters the smile and upper lip.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.name: Oblique part of cricothyroid muscle
oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.summary: Oblique fascicles of the cricothyroid, the only tensor of the vocal folds. It tilts the thyroid cartilage forward to lengthen and tense the folds.
oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.origin: Anterolateral surface of the cricoid arch.
oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.insertion: Inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage (pars obliqua).
oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.action: Tilts the thyroid cartilage forward and downward on the cricoid, stretching and tensing the vocal folds for higher pitch.
oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.innervation: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus CN X).
oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.blood_supply: Cricothyroid branch of the superior thyroid artery.
oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.relations: Lies on the anterolateral larynx, separated from the midline by the cricothyroid membrane; the external laryngeal nerve descends on the inferior constrictor with the superior thyroid vessels to reach it; the cricothyroid artery crosses the membrane between the two muscles.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; landmark muscle for laryngeal EMG and for the external laryngeal nerve in thyroid surgery.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Anterior neck toxin placed deep toward the larynx can affect voice; the cricothyroid membrane approach is a medical procedure only.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

obliquus-inferior-capitis-muscle.name: Obliquus inferior capitis muscle
obliquus-inferior-capitis-muscle.summary: Suboccipital muscle between the axis and the atlas, the main rotator of the head at the atlanto-axial joint. It bounds the suboccipital triangle containing the vertebral artery.
obliquus-inferior-capitis-muscle.origin: Apex of the spinous process of the axis (C2).
obliquus-inferior-capitis-muscle.insertion: Posteroinferior aspect of the transverse process of the atlas (C1).
obliquus-inferior-capitis-muscle.action: Rotates the head to the same side at the atlanto-axial joint.
obliquus-inferior-capitis-muscle.blood_supply: Vertebral artery (third part) and deep cervical branches.
obliquus-inferior-capitis-muscle.relations: Forms the inferolateral boundary of the suboccipital triangle, within which the third part of the vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve lie on the posterior arch of the atlas; the greater occipital nerve (C2 dorsal ramus) curves up over it.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; key landmark warning for anyone injecting or dry needling the upper posterior neck because of the vertebral artery.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Injection or needling within the suboccipital triangle risks catastrophic vertebral artery injury; upper cervical procedures require imaging guidance.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

obliquus-superior-capitis-muscle.name: Obliquus superior capitis muscle
obliquus-superior-capitis-muscle.summary: Suboccipital muscle from the atlas transverse process to the occipital bone. It extends and laterally flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.
obliquus-superior-capitis-muscle.origin: Superior surface of the transverse process of the atlas (C1).
obliquus-superior-capitis-muscle.insertion: Occipital bone between the superior and inferior nuchal lines, lateral to the semispinalis capitis.
obliquus-superior-capitis-muscle.action: Extends the head and bends it laterally at the atlanto-occipital joint.
obliquus-superior-capitis-muscle.blood_supply: Vertebral artery and occipital artery branches.
obliquus-superior-capitis-muscle.relations: Forms the superolateral boundary of the suboccipital triangle; the vertebral artery passes medial and deep to it after exiting the atlas transverse foramen; the occipital artery runs superficial to its upper attachment.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; vertebral artery landmark for deep upper cervical work.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: As with the whole suboccipital region, blind deep injection risks vertebral artery puncture; outside aesthetic scope.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

occipitalis-muscle.name: Occipitalis muscle
occipitalis-muscle.summary: Posterior belly of the occipitofrontalis over the back of the skull. It retracts the scalp and works with the frontalis through the galea aponeurotica.
occipitalis-muscle.origin: Lateral two thirds of the superior nuchal line and the mastoid part of the temporal bone.
occipitalis-muscle.insertion: Galea aponeurotica at the back of the skull.
occipitalis-muscle.action: Pulls the scalp backward; fixes the galea so the frontalis can elevate the brows.
occipitalis-muscle.innervation: Posterior auricular branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
occipitalis-muscle.relations: Lies on the occipital bone beneath the scalp; the occipital artery and greater occipital nerve pierce the fascia at its medial border to reach the scalp, and the lesser occipital and third occipital nerves lie nearby; this is the classic field for greater occipital nerve blocks.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine aesthetic target; included in some migraine toxin protocols as injection sites over the occipital region and relevant to occipital nerve blocks for cervicogenic headache.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Chronic migraine protocols place fixed toxin sites over the occipitalis and surrounding muscles; the principle is superficial intramuscular injection at standardized points, a medical rather than aesthetic indication.
injector_notes.cautions: Keep injections superficial to avoid the occipital vessels and greater occipital nerve; deep injection near the midline risks the suboccipital region and vertebral artery higher up.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)

omohyoid-muscle.name: Omohyoid muscle
omohyoid-muscle.summary: Narrow infrahyoid muscle with two bellies from the scapula to the hyoid. It depresses the hyoid and is a key surgical landmark of the lateral neck.
omohyoid-muscle.origin: Superior border of the scapula near the suprascapular notch (inferior belly).
omohyoid-muscle.insertion: Lower border of the body of the hyoid (superior belly), the two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon bound to the clavicle by fascia.
omohyoid-muscle.action: Depresses and fixes the hyoid; tenses the deep cervical fascia.
omohyoid-muscle.blood_supply: Suprascapular and inferior thyroid arteries and branches of the transverse cervical artery.
omohyoid-muscle.relations: Crosses the posterior triangle superficial to the brachial plexus and suprascapular vessels; its superior belly crosses the carotid sheath (internal jugular vein, common carotid artery, vagus) at the level of the cricoid and lies deep to the sternocleidomastoid.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; a landmark for the carotid sheath and internal jugular vein in the lateral neck.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Its course marks the deeper neurovascular plane of the neck; keep aesthetic injections subcutaneous and well superficial to the omohyoid.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

orbicularis-oris-muscle.name: Orbicularis oris muscle
orbicularis-oris-muscle.summary: Sphincter muscle of the mouth encircling the lips. It closes and protrudes the lips and is essential for speech, eating and expression.
orbicularis-oris-muscle.origin: Intrinsic fibres from the perioral skin, modiolus and alveolar bone of the incisor region; extrinsic fibres from the many muscles converging on the modiolus.
orbicularis-oris-muscle.insertion: Mucosa and skin of the lips, fibres encircling the mouth and decussating at the angles.
orbicularis-oris-muscle.action: Closes the lips, protrudes them (kissing, whistling) and shapes them in speech; the pars peripheralis compresses and the pars marginalis everts the vermilion.
orbicularis-oris-muscle.innervation: Buccal and marginal mandibular branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
orbicularis-oris-muscle.blood_supply: Superior and inferior labial branches of the facial artery, which run between the muscle and the mucosa.
orbicularis-oris-muscle.relations: Lies directly beneath the vermilion and perioral skin; the labial arteries course in the submucosal plane at the wet-dry junction; the modiolus at each mouth corner is the convergence hub with zygomaticus major, risorius, buccinator, depressor and levator anguli oris; the facial artery gives labial branches near the mouth corners.

injector_notes.relevance: Targeted with microdroplet toxin for perioral (smoker) lines, lip flip eversion of the vermilion, and gummy smile adjuncts; filler augments the lip body along the same plane.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Perioral rhytids and lip flip; the principle is very conservative, superficial microinjections at the vermilion border spaced around the lip, sparing the philtral columns and modiolus, treating few points per session.
injector_notes.cautions: Over-treatment or diffusion causes oral incompetence, slurred speech, drooling, asymmetric smile and inability to use a straw or whistle; lip filler must respect the labial arteries in the submucosal plane; intravascular injection is a classic complication.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.name: Orbital part of orbicularis oculi
orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.summary: Outer portion of the orbicularis oculi sweeping around the orbital rim onto the brow and temple. Its contraction squints the eye and produces crow's feet.
orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.origin: Medial orbital margin, medial palpebral ligament and frontal process of the maxilla.
orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.insertion: Fibres form concentric loops around the orbital margin, inserting into the skin of the brow, temple and cheek and the lateral palpebral raphe.
orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.action: Forceful closure of the eyelids (squinting); depresses the lateral brow and produces lateral canthal (crow's feet) wrinkles.
orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.innervation: Temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.blood_supply: Superficial temporal, zygomaticofacial and transverse facial branches of the external carotid system and palpebral branches of the ophthalmic artery.
orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.relations: Lies superficially over the orbital rim and zygomatic bone; the zygomatic branches of the facial nerve cross deep to its lower border toward the zygomaticus muscles; the temporal branch of the facial nerve crosses the zygomatic arch below its upper edge; the sentinel vein and zygomaticotemporal vessels lie deep in the lateral orbit region.

injector_notes.relevance: The target of crow's feet toxin treatment at the lateral orbital rim; also shapes lateral brow position.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Lateral canthal lines; the principle is superficial injections lateral to the orbital rim (about a fingerbreadth from the bony rim), fanned over the wrinkle pattern, keeping volume low inferiorly over the zygoma to protect the smile muscles.
injector_notes.cautions: Inferior diffusion weakens the zygomaticus major causing smile asymmetry and upper lip droop; medial and deep diffusion causes lower lid laxity, diplopia or epiphora; bruising is common over the periorbital vessels.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

palatopharyngeus-muscle.name: Palatopharyngeus muscle
palatopharyngeus-muscle.summary: Longitudinal muscle of the soft palate and pharynx forming the posterior faucial pillar. It elevates the pharynx and larynx and helps close off the nasopharynx.
palatopharyngeus-muscle.origin: Posterior part of the soft palate (palatine aponeurosis).
palatopharyngeus-muscle.insertion: Posterior border of the thyroid cartilage and the pharyngeal wall, blending with the stylopharyngeus.
palatopharyngeus-muscle.action: Elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing; approximates the posterior faucial pillars and tenses the soft palate.
palatopharyngeus-muscle.blood_supply: Ascending palatine branch of the facial artery and tonsillar and pharyngeal branches.
palatopharyngeus-muscle.relations: Forms the posterior pillar of the fauces behind the palatine tonsil, which sits between it and the palatoglossus; the tonsillar branch of the facial artery and the glossopharyngeal nerve lie in the tonsillar bed medial to it.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: None for aesthetic practice; relevant only to oropharyngeal surgery.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.name: Palpebral part of orbicularis oculi
palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.summary: Portion of the orbicularis oculi within the eyelids. It closes the eye gently in blinking and pumps tears through the lacrimal drainage system.
palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.origin: Medial palpebral ligament and the adjacent frontal process of the maxilla (with a lacrimal part from the posterior lacrimal crest).
palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.insertion: Lateral palpebral raphe at the outer canthus; the pretarsal fibres anchor to the tarsal plates.
palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.action: Gently closes the eyelids as in blinking and sleep; assists tear drainage via the lacrimal pump.
palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.innervation: Temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.blood_supply: Medial and lateral palpebral arteries forming the palpebral arcades, from the ophthalmic and lacrimal systems.
palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.relations: Lies within the eyelids superficial to the orbital septum and tarsal plates; the angular artery and vein lie at the medial canthus deep to its origin; the levator palpebrae superioris aponeurosis and Muller muscle lie deep to the upper pretarsal fibres; the inferior oblique and inferior rectus lie deep in the lower lid region.

injector_notes.relevance: Targeted cautiously with microdroplet toxin for lower eyelid lines and the hypertrophic pretarsal roll (jelly roll), and to widen the palpebral aperture subtly.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Lower lid fine lines and pretarsal bulge; the principle is very superficial microinjections in the pretarsal or preseptal muscle, only in patients with good lid snap-back, avoiding the lid margin and the infraorbital area.
