injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion to the inferior oblique or inferior rectus causes transient diplopia; over-weakening causes lower lid laxity, ectropion, dry eye and epiphora; avoid patients with poor lid tone or previous lid surgery; medial injections risk the angular vessels and lacrimal drainage.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

platysma.name: Platysma muscle
platysma.summary: Broad thin sheet of muscle in the superficial neck fascia from the chest to the lower face. It tenses the neck skin, forms vertical neck bands with age, and acts as a lower face depressor.
platysma.origin: Superficial fascia over the upper pectoralis major and deltoid.
platysma.insertion: Lower border of the mandible, skin of the lower face and the modiolus via the depressor anguli oris and risorius region.
platysma.action: Tenses the skin of the neck, pulls down the lower lip and mouth corners, and assists in forced depression of the mandible.
platysma.innervation: Cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
platysma.blood_supply: Submental branch of the facial artery and suprascapular and transverse cervical branches.
platysma.relations: Lies in the superficial cervical fascia directly under the skin; the external jugular vein, great auricular nerve and transverse cervical nerve run deep to it over the sternocleidomastoid; the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve crosses the mandibular border deep to its upper edge; the cervical branch of CN VII enters its deep surface near the hyoid; the carotid sheath lies deep.

injector_notes.relevance: Major toxin target for vertical platysmal bands, neck laxity patterns and jawline definition (Nefertiti-type lift) by releasing its downward pull on the lower face.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Platysmal bands and jawline depressor release; the principle is superficial microinjections directly into visible bands grasped between fingers, and a row of injections along the mandibular border and upper neck, keeping well above the deeper neck structures.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion to the underlying strap muscles, pharyngeal muscles or larynx causes dysphagia, dysphonia and weak neck flexion, especially in thin or elderly necks; injections too high at the jawline risk the depressor labii inferioris and marginal mandibular nerve with smile asymmetry; avoid the external jugular vein.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.name: Posterior belly of digastric muscle
posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.summary: Posterior belly of the digastric from the mastoid notch to the hyoid tendon. It elevates the hyoid and is a key landmark of the carotid triangle and skull base neurovascular structures.
posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.origin: Mastoid (digastric) notch on the medial side of the mastoid process.
posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.insertion: Intermediate tendon of digastric at the hyoid via the fibrous sling.
posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.action: Elevates the hyoid during swallowing; helps open the mouth when the hyoid is fixed.
posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.innervation: Digastric branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.relations: The stylohyoid runs alongside it from the styloid process; deep to it at the skull base lie the internal jugular vein, internal and external carotid arteries and the last four cranial nerves; the facial nerve exits the stylomastoid foramen just lateral to its upper end; the spinal accessory nerve crosses the internal jugular vein on its deep surface; it separates the carotid triangle below from the submandibular region above.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; a crucial landmark for the deep neurovascular structures of the upper neck that injectors must avoid.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep injections in the submandibular and upper neck region near this muscle endanger the facial nerve trunk, the carotid sheath contents and the accessory nerve.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.name: Posterior crico-arytenoid muscle
posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.summary: Intrinsic laryngeal muscle on the back of the cricoid lamina and the only abductor of the vocal folds. It opens the glottis for breathing.
posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.origin: Posterior surface of the lamina of the cricoid cartilage.
posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.insertion: Muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage.
posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.action: Rotates the arytenoid laterally to abduct the vocal folds and open the airway.
posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.innervation: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus CN X).
posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.blood_supply: Laryngeal branches of the inferior thyroid artery.
posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.relations: Lies on the posterior cricoid, covered posteriorly by the inferior constrictor and related to the esophagus behind; the recurrent laryngeal nerves ascend in the tracheoesophageal grooves to reach it.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; key clinical relevance is bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy causing airway obstruction.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep posterior neck injections are outside aesthetic practice; thyroid surgery risks the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplying this muscle.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

procerus-muscle.name: Procerus muscle
procerus-muscle.summary: Small muscle over the nasal root between the eyebrows. It depresses the medial brows and produces the transverse wrinkle at the nasal root.
procerus-muscle.origin: Lower part of the nasal bone and the upper lateral nasal cartilage.
procerus-muscle.insertion: Skin between the eyebrows over the glabella.
procerus-muscle.action: Draws the medial eyebrows downward, creating a transverse crease at the root of the nose, as in frowning or concentration.
procerus-muscle.innervation: Buccal (and lower zygomatic) branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
procerus-muscle.blood_supply: Angular branches of the facial artery and supratrochlear branches of the ophthalmic artery.
procerus-muscle.relations: Lies over the glabella and nasal root beneath the skin, continuous above with the frontalis; the supratrochlear vessels emerge just lateral to it at the orbital rim; the angular vessels ascend along the nasofacial junction lateral to it; the glabella is the highest-risk zone for filler-related vision loss due to supratrochlear and dorsal nasal anastomoses with the ophthalmic artery.

injector_notes.relevance: Standard part of glabellar complex toxin treatment for the horizontal nasal root line.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Transverse glabellar line; the principle is a midline injection into the muscle belly over the nasal root, kept superficial and combined with corrugator treatment for balanced glabellar relaxation.
injector_notes.cautions: The glabella is a classic filler danger zone for vascular occlusion and blindness via dorsal nasal and supratrochlear anastomoses; toxin diffusion laterally can reach the corrugator or orbicularis and alter brow position.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.name: Rectus capitis anterior muscle
rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.summary: Short prevertebral muscle between the atlas and the skull base. It flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.
rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.origin: Anterior surface of the lateral mass of the atlas (C1).
rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.insertion: Basilar part of the occipital bone in front of the occipital condyle.
rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.action: Flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.
rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.innervation: Ventral rami of C1 and C2.
rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.relations: Lies deep in the upper neck behind the pharynx, medial to the internal carotid artery and jugular vein; the hypoglossal nerve and the superior cervical sympathetic ganglion lie anterior.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep upper neck injections near this muscle endanger the internal carotid artery, jugular vein and lower cranial nerves.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

rectus-lateralis-capitis-muscle.name: Rectus capitis lateralis muscle
rectus-lateralis-capitis-muscle.summary: Short muscle from the atlas transverse process to the jugular process of the occipital bone. It laterally flexes the head.
rectus-lateralis-capitis-muscle.origin: Upper surface of the transverse process of the atlas (C1).
rectus-lateralis-capitis-muscle.insertion: Jugular process of the occipital bone.
rectus-lateralis-capitis-muscle.action: Laterally flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.
rectus-lateralis-capitis-muscle.relations: Lies immediately behind the internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen, with the vertebral artery medial and the accessory, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves anterior at the skull base.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable.
injector_notes.cautions: Marks the danger zone of the jugular foramen and vertebral artery; avoid deep injections in this region.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

rectus-posterior-major-capitis-muscle.name: Rectus capitis posterior major muscle
rectus-posterior-major-capitis-muscle.summary: Suboccipital muscle from the spinous process of the axis to the occipital bone. It extends and rotates the head and forms the medial wall of the suboccipital triangle.
rectus-posterior-major-capitis-muscle.insertion: Lateral part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone.
rectus-posterior-major-capitis-muscle.action: Extends the head and rotates it to the same side.
rectus-posterior-major-capitis-muscle.blood_supply: Vertebral artery (third part) and deep cervical artery branches.
rectus-posterior-major-capitis-muscle.relations: Forms the superomedial boundary of the suboccipital triangle with the obliquus inferior below and obliquus superior above; the third part of the vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve lie in the triangle on its floor; the greater occipital nerve winds around the lower border of the obliquus inferior just medial.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; the suboccipital triangle it bounds contains the vertebral artery, the critical structure in upper cervical injections and dry needling.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Blind injection or needling in the suboccipital triangle risks vertebral artery puncture with potentially fatal consequences; image guidance is mandatory for deep work here.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

rectus-posterior-minor-capitis-muscle.name: Rectus capitis posterior minor muscle
rectus-posterior-minor-capitis-muscle.summary: Small suboccipital muscle from the atlas to the occipital bone near the midline. It extends the head and is linked to the dura by a connective tissue bridge implicated in cervicogenic headache.
rectus-posterior-minor-capitis-muscle.origin: Posterior tubercle of the posterior arch of the atlas (C1).
rectus-posterior-minor-capitis-muscle.insertion: Medial part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone.
rectus-posterior-minor-capitis-muscle.action: Extends the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.
rectus-posterior-minor-capitis-muscle.blood_supply: Vertebral artery and deep cervical branches.
rectus-posterior-minor-capitis-muscle.relations: Lies medial to the rectus capitis posterior major under the semispinalis capitis; its deep surface is attached to the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane, which connects via the myodural bridge to the spinal dura; the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve pass lateral to it over the posterior arch of the atlas.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; of interest in cervicogenic headache mechanisms rather than aesthetics.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep midline upper cervical injections risk the vertebral artery and the dura at the atlanto-occipital interval.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

risorius-muscle.name: Risorius muscle
risorius-muscle.summary: Slender, variable muscle of the cheek pulling the mouth corner sideways. It produces a grinning expression and dimples in some people.
risorius-muscle.origin: Fascia over the parotid gland and masseter.
risorius-muscle.insertion: Modiolus and skin at the angle of the mouth.
risorius-muscle.action: Retracts the angle of the mouth laterally, as in grinning.
risorius-muscle.innervation: Buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
risorius-muscle.blood_supply: Transverse facial artery and branches of the facial artery.
risorius-muscle.relations: Lies horizontally in the cheek superficial to the masseteric fascia; the parotid duct, buccal branches of the facial nerve and the transverse facial vessels run near its upper border; the facial artery and vein cross the mandible below its anterior end.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine direct target; its inadvertent weakening by masseter toxin diffusion is a classic cause of smile asymmetry after jaw slimming.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not routinely targeted; the principle in masseter treatment is to keep injections low, deep and behind a line from the earlobe to the mouth corner so that diffusion to the risorius is minimized.
injector_notes.cautions: Toxin spread to the risorius or zygomaticus major produces asymmetric or altered smile; filler near the modiolus must respect the facial vessels.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

scalenus-anterior-muscle.name: Scalenus anterior muscle
scalenus-anterior-muscle.summary: Anterior scalene from the cervical transverse processes to the first rib. It is the key landmark of the root of the neck, separating the subclavian vein in front from the subclavian artery and brachial plexus behind.
scalenus-anterior-muscle.origin: Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3 to C6.
scalenus-anterior-muscle.insertion: Scalene tubercle on the inner border of the first rib.
scalenus-anterior-muscle.action: Elevates the first rib during inspiration; flexes, laterally flexes and rotates the neck.
scalenus-anterior-muscle.innervation: Ventral rami of C4 to C6.
scalenus-anterior-muscle.blood_supply: Ascending cervical branch of the inferior thyroid artery.
scalenus-anterior-muscle.relations: The phrenic nerve descends vertically on its anterior surface under the prevertebral fascia; the subclavian vein passes anterior to its insertion, while the subclavian artery and brachial plexus trunks pass posterior to it in the interscalene triangle; the carotid sheath, vagus nerve and sympathetic trunk lie medial; the pleural apex is deep.

injector_notes.relevance: Not an aesthetic target; central to interscalene brachial plexus blocks and to understanding thoracic outlet syndrome.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Investigational toxin treatment of the scalenes for neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome is performed with image guidance by specialists.
injector_notes.cautions: Injection here risks phrenic nerve palsy, pneumothorax, and injury to the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus; strictly outside aesthetic practice.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

scalenus-medius-muscle.name: Scalenus medius muscle
scalenus-medius-muscle.summary: Middle and largest scalene behind the brachial plexus. It elevates the first rib and laterally flexes the neck.
scalenus-medius-muscle.origin: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C2 to C7.
scalenus-medius-muscle.insertion: Upper surface of the first rib behind the subclavian groove.
scalenus-medius-muscle.action: Elevates the first rib; laterally flexes the neck.
scalenus-medius-muscle.innervation: Ventral rami of C3 to C8.
scalenus-medius-muscle.blood_supply: Ascending cervical and dorsal scapular arteries.
scalenus-medius-muscle.relations: The brachial plexus and subclavian artery emerge between it and the scalenus anterior; the dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves pierce its substance; the levator scapulae lies posterior and the pleural apex medial.

injector_notes.relevance: Not an aesthetic target; part of the interscalene region for regional anesthesia.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Investigational image-guided toxin for thoracic outlet syndrome by specialists only.
injector_notes.cautions: Close relation to the brachial plexus and long thoracic nerve; injection risks nerve injury and pneumothorax.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

scalenus-posterior-muscle.name: Scalenus posterior muscle
scalenus-posterior-muscle.summary: Posterior scalene from the lower cervical transverse processes to the second rib. It is an accessory muscle of inspiration.
scalenus-posterior-muscle.origin: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C4 to C6.
scalenus-posterior-muscle.insertion: Outer surface of the second rib behind the tuberosity for serratus anterior.
scalenus-posterior-muscle.action: Elevates the second rib; assists lateral neck flexion.
scalenus-posterior-muscle.innervation: Ventral rami of C6 to C8.
scalenus-posterior-muscle.blood_supply: Ascending cervical artery and deep branch of the transverse cervical artery.
scalenus-posterior-muscle.relations: Lies deep to the levator scapulae and the posterior triangle contents; the brachial plexus and subclavian artery are anterolateral and the pleural apex medial.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep lateral neck injections risk the brachial plexus and pleural apex; outside aesthetic scope.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

semispinalis-colli-muscle.name: Semispinalis colli muscle
semispinalis-colli-muscle.summary: Deep posterior neck muscle running from the upper thoracic transverse processes to the cervical spinous processes. It extends the neck and forms the bulk of the deep posterior cervical musculature.
semispinalis-colli-muscle.origin: Transverse processes of T1 to T6.
semispinalis-colli-muscle.insertion: Spinous processes of C2 to C5.
semispinalis-colli-muscle.action: Extends the cervical spine and rotates it to the opposite side.
semispinalis-colli-muscle.innervation: Dorsal rami of the cervical spinal nerves (medial branches).
semispinalis-colli-muscle.blood_supply: Deep cervical artery and branches of the occipital and vertebral arteries.
semispinalis-colli-muscle.relations: Lies deep to the splenius and trapezius and superficial to the multifidus; the greater occipital nerve pierces its upper continuation (semispinalis capitis) to reach the scalp; the cervical facet medial branch nerves cross deep to it; the vertebral artery runs anterolateral at the transverse processes.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; part of the muscle field for migraine and cervicogenic headache injections in the suboccipital region.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Chronic migraine protocols place toxin sites over the cervical paraspinal muscles; the principle is superficial intramuscular injection avoiding the midline deep structures and the vertebral artery territory.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep injections risk the vertebral artery and cervical nerve roots; excessive weakening of neck extensors causes head drop and neck fatigue.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)

spinalis-capitis-muscle.name: Spinalis capitis muscle
spinalis-capitis-muscle.summary: Medial slip of the erector spinae complex from the lower cervical and upper thoracic spines to the occiput, often blended with the semispinalis capitis. It extends the head.
spinalis-capitis-muscle.origin: Spinous processes of C7 to T1 and the lower nuchal ligament.
spinalis-capitis-muscle.insertion: Occipital bone near the midline, blending with the medial part of the semispinalis capitis.
spinalis-capitis-muscle.innervation: Dorsal rami of the cervical spinal nerves.
spinalis-capitis-muscle.relations: Lies in the midline of the upper posterior neck deep to the trapezius and splenius, medial to the semispinalis capitis; the third occipital nerve crosses near it; the greater occipital nerve ascends lateral to it.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Midline deep posterior neck injections risk the cervical epidural space and vertebral artery; avoid in aesthetic practice.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

spinalis-colli-muscle.name: Spinalis colli muscle
spinalis-colli-muscle.summary: Most medial part of the erector spinae in the neck, linking adjacent spinous processes. It assists cervical extension.
spinalis-colli-muscle.origin: Spinous processes of T1 to T2 (often including C7).
spinalis-colli-muscle.insertion: Spinous processes of C2 to C4.
spinalis-colli-muscle.action: Assists extension of the cervical spine.
spinalis-colli-muscle.innervation: Dorsal rami of the lower cervical spinal nerves.
spinalis-colli-muscle.relations: Lies on the cervical spinous processes deep to the semispinalis and trapezius, adjacent to the interspinales; the cervical facet joints and their medial branch nerves lie lateral.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep midline cervical injections are outside aesthetic practice and risk neural and vascular injury.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

splenius-capitis-muscle.name: Splenius capitis muscle
splenius-capitis-muscle.summary: Broad strap muscle from the lower cervical and upper thoracic spines to the mastoid and occiput. It extends and rotates the head and forms part of the posterior neck contour.
splenius-capitis-muscle.origin: Lower half of the nuchal ligament and the spinous processes of C7 to T3 or T4.
splenius-capitis-muscle.insertion: Mastoid process and the lateral part of the superior nuchal line, deep to the sternocleidomastoid.
splenius-capitis-muscle.action: Bilaterally extends the head and neck; unilaterally rotates and laterally flexes the head to the same side.
splenius-capitis-muscle.innervation: Dorsal rami of the middle cervical spinal nerves (C2 to C5).
splenius-capitis-muscle.blood_supply: Occipital artery and deep cervical artery.
splenius-capitis-muscle.relations: Lies deep to the trapezius above and the sternocleidomastoid at its insertion; the semispinalis capitis and longissimus capitis lie deep; the occipital artery crosses its insertion near the mastoid; the spinal accessory nerve and the posterior triangle contents are anterolateral; the greater occipital nerve emerges medial to its lower border.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine aesthetic target; included in some chronic migraine toxin protocols and trigger point treatments for neck pain.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Migraine or myofascial protocols inject the splenius region superficially; the principle is palpation-guided intramuscular placement lateral to the midline, avoiding the occipital vessels and the suboccipital triangle.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep or high injections risk the vertebral artery at the suboccipital level and the occipital artery at the mastoid; over-treatment weakens neck extension.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)

splenius-colli-muscle.name: Splenius colli muscle
splenius-colli-muscle.summary: Lower part of the splenius connecting the upper thoracic spines to the upper cervical transverse processes. It extends and rotates the neck.
splenius-colli-muscle.origin: Spinous processes of T3 to T6.
splenius-colli-muscle.insertion: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C1 to C3.
splenius-colli-muscle.action: Extends the neck and rotates it to the same side.
splenius-colli-muscle.innervation: Dorsal rami of the lower cervical spinal nerves.
splenius-colli-muscle.blood_supply: Deep cervical artery and transverse cervical artery branches.
splenius-colli-muscle.relations: Lies deep to the trapezius and levator scapulae in the lower posterior neck; the dorsal scapular vessels and nerve cross its region; the vertebral artery ascends anterior to the transverse processes it attaches to.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep lower posterior neck injections risk the dorsal scapular neurovascular bundle and the vertebral artery superiorly.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

sternocleidomastoid-muscle.name: Sternocleidomastoid muscle
sternocleidomastoid-muscle.summary: Prominent superficial muscle of the lateral neck from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid. It rotates the head to the opposite side and flexes the neck, and it covers the great vessels of the neck.
sternocleidomastoid-muscle.origin: Sternal head from the anterior manubrium; clavicular head from the medial third of the clavicle.
sternocleidomastoid-muscle.insertion: Mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line.
sternocleidomastoid-muscle.action: Unilaterally rotates the face to the opposite side and laterally flexes the neck to the same side; bilaterally flexes the neck and assists in forced inspiration.
sternocleidomastoid-muscle.innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) with proprioceptive fibres from C2 to C3.
sternocleidomastoid-muscle.blood_supply: Branches of the superior thyroid, occipital and suprascapular arteries.
sternocleidomastoid-muscle.relations: The external jugular vein crosses its superficial surface toward the clavicle; the great auricular and transverse cervical nerves and the lesser occipital nerve emerge at its posterior border (nerve point of the neck); the carotid sheath with the common carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus nerve lies deep; the spinal accessory nerve enters its deep surface in the upper third; the cervical branch of the facial nerve lies near its lower anterior edge; the parotid gland overlaps its upper anterior border.

injector_notes.relevance: Toxin target for cervical dystonia (spasmodic torticollis) and occasionally for hypertrophy; a key landmark that jawline and neck injectors must identify before treating the platysma or jaw contour.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Cervical dystonia and SCM hypertrophy; the principle is palpation- or EMG-guided injection into the muscle belly of the affected side, in the middle third, staying within the muscle and away from its deep surface over the carotid sheath.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep injection risks the carotid sheath and the accessory nerve; bilateral or excessive treatment causes dysphagia (from diffusion to strap and pharyngeal muscles), weak neck flexion and voice change; the external jugular vein and great auricular nerve lie on its surface and cause bleeding or numbness if hit.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

sternohyoid-muscle.name: Sternohyoid muscle
sternohyoid-muscle.summary: Superficial strap muscle of the anterior neck from the sternum to the hyoid. It depresses the hyoid after swallowing.
sternohyoid-muscle.origin: Posterior surface of the manubrium and the medial end of the clavicle.
sternohyoid-muscle.insertion: Lower border of the body of the hyoid bone.
sternohyoid-muscle.action: Depresses the hyoid after it has been elevated in swallowing.
sternohyoid-muscle.relations: Lies under the platysma in the anterior neck, lateral to the midline; it overlies the sternothyroid, thyroid gland and trachea; the anterior jugular vein runs in the suprasternal space between it and the deep fascia; the cervical branch of the facial nerve lies above near the hyoid.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; relevant because platysma toxin in the anterior neck can diffuse to the strap muscles and cause dysphagia.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Keep anterior neck toxin injections superficial within the platysma; diffusion to sternohyoid and the other strap muscles weakens hyoid control and swallowing.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

sternothyroid-muscle.name: Sternothyroid muscle
sternothyroid-muscle.summary: Strap muscle deep to the sternohyoid running from the sternum to the thyroid cartilage. It depresses the larynx and hyoid.
sternothyroid-muscle.origin: Posterior surface of the manubrium below the sternohyoid origin.
sternothyroid-muscle.insertion: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage.
sternothyroid-muscle.action: Depresses the larynx and hyoid after swallowing and phonation.
sternothyroid-muscle.relations: Lies directly on the thyroid gland and trachea; the recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove deep and medial to it; the inferior thyroid artery crosses deep to its upper part; the omohyoid crosses it obliquely.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; part of the deep anterior neck anatomy overlying the thyroid gland.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep anterior neck injections risk the thyroid, trachea and recurrent laryngeal nerve; aesthetic injections in this region should remain subcutaneous.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.name: Straight part of cricothyroid muscle
straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.summary: Vertical fascicles of the cricothyroid muscle (pars recta) at the front of the larynx. Together with the oblique part it tenses the vocal folds for pitch control.
straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.origin: Anterolateral surface of the arch of the cricoid cartilage.
straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.insertion: Inferior border of the lamina of the thyroid cartilage (pars recta).
straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.action: Pulls the thyroid cartilage forward and down on the cricoid, lengthening and tensing the vocal folds.
straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.innervation: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus CN X).
straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.blood_supply: Cricothyroid branch of the superior thyroid artery.
straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.relations: Lies on the anterolateral larynx beside the cricothyroid membrane, which is crossed by the small cricothyroid artery; the external laryngeal nerve approaches it on the surface of the inferior constrictor alongside the superior thyroid vessels.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; landmark for the cricothyroid membrane used in emergency airway access and laryngeal EMG.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Any deep injection at the anterior larynx risks the airway and voice; strictly outside aesthetic practice.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

stylohyoid-muscle.name: Stylohyoid muscle
stylohyoid-muscle.summary: Slender muscle from the styloid process to the hyoid, running with the posterior belly of the digastric. It elevates and retracts the hyoid.
stylohyoid-muscle.origin: Posterolateral surface of the styloid process of the temporal bone.
stylohyoid-muscle.insertion: Body of the hyoid at its junction with the greater horn, the tendon splitting to pass around the digastric tendon.
stylohyoid-muscle.action: Elevates and retracts the hyoid, assisting swallowing.
stylohyoid-muscle.innervation: Stylohyoid branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
stylohyoid-muscle.relations: Runs with the posterior belly of the digastric at the skull base; the external carotid artery crosses deep to it; an elongated styloid process or ossified stylohyoid ligament here causes Eagle syndrome with throat pain on swallowing; the glossopharyngeal nerve and carotid sheath lie medial.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; landmark of the deep upper neck.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep injections near the styloid region risk the carotid arteries and the glossopharyngeal and facial nerves.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

stylopharyngeus-muscle.name: Stylopharyngeus muscle
stylopharyngeus-muscle.summary: Longitudinal pharyngeal muscle from the styloid process into the pharyngeal wall, and the only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. It elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing.
stylopharyngeus-muscle.origin: Medial surface of the styloid process of the temporal bone.
stylopharyngeus-muscle.insertion: Posterior border of the thyroid cartilage and the pharyngeal wall, blending with the palatopharyngeus.
stylopharyngeus-muscle.action: Elevates and widens the pharynx and elevates the larynx during swallowing.
stylopharyngeus-muscle.blood_supply: Ascending pharyngeal artery and tonsillar branches of the facial artery.
stylopharyngeus-muscle.relations: Enters the pharynx through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors; the glossopharyngeal nerve curves around its lateral and posterior surface, a classic surgical landmark; the internal and external carotid arteries lie lateral and the stylohyoid ligament anterolateral.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep parapharyngeal injections risk the carotid arteries and cranial nerves IX to XII; outside aesthetic scope.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

superficial-part-of-masseter.name: Superficial part of masseter
superficial-part-of-masseter.summary: Largest and most superficial portion of the masseter from the zygomatic arch to the mandibular angle. It is the main chewing muscle and the target of masseter toxin for bruxism and lower face slimming.
superficial-part-of-masseter.origin: Inferior border of the anterior two thirds of the zygomatic arch and the maxillary process of the zygomatic bone.
superficial-part-of-masseter.insertion: Lateral surface of the angle and lower ramus of the mandible (masseteric tuberosity).
superficial-part-of-masseter.action: Powerfully elevates the mandible and assists protrusion; active in clenching.
superficial-part-of-masseter.innervation: Masseteric nerve (anterior division of V3), entering via the mandibular notch.
superficial-part-of-masseter.blood_supply: Masseteric branch of the maxillary artery, transverse facial artery (superficial temporal) and branches of the facial artery.
superficial-part-of-masseter.relations: The parotid gland overlies its posterior part; the parotid duct crosses its surface horizontally about one to two fingerbreadths below the zygomatic arch together with the buccal branches of the facial nerve and the transverse facial vessels; the facial artery and vein cross the mandibular border at its anterior edge; the risorius and platysma lie superficial and anterior; the zygomaticus major arises above its anterior border.

injector_notes.relevance: One of the most common toxin targets in the lower face: masseteric hypertrophy, bruxism, TMJ-related pain and square jaw slimming.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Masseteric hypertrophy and bruxism; the principle is multiple intramuscular injections into the lower, thicker part of the muscle below the line from tragus to mouth corner, posterior to the anterior border, and deep enough to stay in muscle rather than the parotid or subcutaneous plane.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion anteriorly to the risorius or zygomaticus major causes asymmetric smile; injection too high near the zygomatic arch causes hollowing and can reach the deep belly; injury to the parotid duct causes sialocele; the facial vessels at the anterior border and the buccal branches of the facial nerve on the muscle surface must be respected; over-treatment causes chewing fatigue and paradoxical bulging of untreated fibres.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.name: Superior head of lateral pterygoid muscle
superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.summary: Upper head of the lateral pterygoid inserting into the TMJ disc. It stabilizes the disc during closing and is implicated in disc displacement disorders.
superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.origin: Infratemporal surface and infratemporal crest of the greater wing of the sphenoid.
superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.insertion: Anterior margin of the articular disc and capsule of the temporomandibular joint.
superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.action: Pulls the articular disc forward and stabilizes it during closing and protrusion of the mandible.
superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.innervation: Branches of the mandibular nerve (V3), often via the buccal nerve or a direct lateral pterygoid branch.
superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.blood_supply: Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery.
superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.relations: Lies deep in the infratemporal fossa above the inferior head, with the maxillary artery crossing between or over the two heads; the buccal nerve emerges between the heads; the TMJ lies directly posterior.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; occasionally included in specialist EMG-guided treatment of TMJ disc disorders.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Investigational toxin treatment for lateral pterygoid hyperactivity under imaging or EMG guidance; specialist practice only.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep infratemporal injections risk the maxillary artery, pterygoid plexus and diffusion to pharyngeal muscles; not for aesthetic injectors.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)

superior-oblique-muscle.name: Superior oblique muscle
superior-oblique-muscle.summary: Extraocular muscle passing through the trochlear pulley at the superomedial orbit to the back of the globe. It depresses the eye in adduction and intorts it, and is supplied by the trochlear nerve.
superior-oblique-muscle.origin: Body of the sphenoid above and medial to the optic canal.
superior-oblique-muscle.insertion: Posterolateral part of the superior sclera, behind the equator, after the tendon turns through the trochlea.
superior-oblique-muscle.action: Depresses, abducts and internally rotates (incyclotorts) the eyeball; principal depressor in adduction.
superior-oblique-muscle.innervation: Trochlear nerve (CN IV), entering its orbital surface.
superior-oblique-muscle.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery.
superior-oblique-muscle.relations: Runs along the superomedial orbital wall with the trochlear nerve above it; its tendon passes through the trochlea at the superomedial orbital rim near the supratrochlear nerve and vessels; the superior rectus and levator palpebrae lie lateral and the ethmoid sinuses medial.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; relevant to rare complications of deep superomedial orbital injections.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics; specialist strabismus treatment only.
injector_notes.cautions: Trochlear region injections and aggressive massage after glabellar filler or toxin risk injury near the superior oblique pulley; Brown-type vertical diplopia is a theoretical complication.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

superior-pharyngeal-constrictor.name: Superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle
superior-pharyngeal-constrictor.summary: Uppermost pharyngeal constrictor from the pterygoid region, mandible and tongue to the pharyngeal raphe. It initiates pharyngeal contraction in swallowing and forms Passavant ridge.
superior-pharyngeal-constrictor.origin: Pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe, posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible and the side of the tongue.
superior-pharyngeal-constrictor.insertion: Median pharyngeal raphe, ascending to the pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone.
superior-pharyngeal-constrictor.action: Constricts the upper pharynx during swallowing; its upper fibres form the ridge that meets the elevated soft palate to close the nasopharynx.
superior-pharyngeal-constrictor.blood_supply: Ascending pharyngeal artery, tonsillar branch of the facial artery and dorsal lingual branches.
superior-pharyngeal-constrictor.relations: Anteriorly it is continuous with the buccinator at the pterygomandibular raphe; the auditory tube and levator veli palatini enter the pharynx through the gap above it (sinus of Morgagni); the stylopharyngeus and glossopharyngeal nerve pass through the gap between it and the middle constrictor; the internal carotid artery lies lateral.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Its gap with the middle constrictor transmits the glossopharyngeal nerve; deep injections in this region are outside aesthetic practice.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

superior-rectus-muscle.name: Superior rectus muscle
superior-rectus-muscle.summary: Extraocular muscle on the top of the globe, the main elevator of the eye. It shares a fascial sheath with the levator palpebrae superioris above it.
superior-rectus-muscle.origin: Common tendinous ring at the orbital apex.
superior-rectus-muscle.insertion: Anterosuperior surface of the sclera behind the corneoscleral junction.
superior-rectus-muscle.action: Elevates the eyeball; secondarily adducts and incyclotorts it.
superior-rectus-muscle.innervation: Superior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).
superior-rectus-muscle.blood_supply: Muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery and the lacrimal artery.
superior-rectus-muscle.relations: Lies directly below the levator palpebrae superioris, the two sharing fascial connections so that toxin or surgery affecting one can influence the other; the frontal nerve and supraorbital vessels run above the levator; the superior ophthalmic vein and nasociliary nerve cross above it.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; its fascial link to the levator explains some cases of lid ptosis after periorbital toxin.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep injections over the orbital roof region risk diffusion toward the superior rectus and levator complex causing ptosis or vertical diplopia.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

temporalis-muscle.name: Temporalis muscle
temporalis-muscle.summary: Large fan-shaped muscle filling the temporal fossa and inserting on the coronoid process. It elevates and retracts the mandible and is active in clenching and grinding.
temporalis-muscle.origin: Temporal fossa of the parietal and frontal bones and the deep surface of the temporal fascia.
temporalis-muscle.insertion: Apex and medial surface of the coronoid process and the anterior border of the ramus of the mandible.
temporalis-muscle.action: Anterior fibres elevate the mandible; posterior horizontal fibres retract it; active in clenching and side-to-side grinding.
temporalis-muscle.innervation: Deep temporal nerves from the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3).
temporalis-muscle.blood_supply: Anterior and posterior deep temporal arteries from the maxillary artery and the middle temporal artery from the superficial temporal artery.
temporalis-muscle.relations: The temporal fascia and temporoparietalis cover it; the superficial temporal artery and vein and the auriculotemporal nerve run on the fascia above; the zygomatic arch crosses its tendon below; the deep temporal nerves and vessels ascend between the muscle and the skull; the buccal fat pad and the masseter are anteroinferior; the temporal fat pads create the layered planes used in temple filler.

injector_notes.relevance: Toxin target in some bruxism and TMJ protocols; the temple region is also a major filler site where knowledge of its layered planes and the middle temporal vein is essential for safety.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Bruxism and TMJ dysfunction protocols sometimes treat the anterior temporalis; the principle is intramuscular injection into the palpably contracting belly high in the temporal fossa, sparing the anterior fibres over the hairline region and avoiding the superficial temporal vessels.
injector_notes.cautions: Temple filler is a recognized vascular danger zone: the deep temporal arteries within the muscle, the middle temporal vein and anastomoses with the orbital circulation can transmit emboli; toxin diffusion downward can weaken the masseter and alter the bite; over-treatment causes temple hollowing and chewing fatigue.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

temporoparietalis-muscle.name: Temporoparietalis muscle
temporoparietalis-muscle.summary: Thin muscle of the side of the head between the ear and the galea. It tenses the scalp fascia and slightly elevates the auricle.
temporoparietalis-muscle.origin: Auricular muscles and fascia around the external ear.
temporoparietalis-muscle.action: Tenses the galea and elevates the auricle slightly; vestigial ear-wiggling function in some people.
temporoparietalis-muscle.innervation: Temporal and posterior auricular branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
temporoparietalis-muscle.relations: Lies in the temple within the superficial musculoaponeurotic layer; the superficial temporal vessels and the auriculotemporal nerve run on or within it; the temporal branch of the facial nerve crosses the zygomatic arch and runs under its anterior edge toward the frontalis; it overlies the deep temporal fascia and temporal fat pads.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine target; it is the SMAS-equivalent layer of the temple used as a plane reference for temple filler and thread procedures, and the temporal branch of the facial nerve runs at its anterior border.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Filler placed in the wrong plane in the temple risks the superficial temporal vessels and the temporal branch of the facial nerve anteriorly, causing alopecia, weakness of brow elevation or vascular occlusion.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.name: Thyro-epiglottic part of thyro-arytenoid muscle
thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.summary: Fibres of the thyroarytenoid extending into the aryepiglottic fold to the epiglottis. They help widen the laryngeal inlet during inspiration.
thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.origin: Angle of the thyroid cartilage (as a continuation of the thyroarytenoid).
thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.insertion: Lateral margin of the epiglottis within the aryepiglottic fold.
thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.action: Assists in opening the laryngeal inlet and positioning the epiglottis during breathing and swallowing.
thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.innervation: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus CN X).
thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.blood_supply: Laryngeal branches of the superior and inferior thyroid arteries.
thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.relations: Lies within the aryepiglottic fold alongside the aryepiglottic part of the oblique arytenoid; the superior laryngeal vessels and internal laryngeal nerve enter the larynx nearby through the thyrohyoid membrane.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Deep injections near the thyrohyoid membrane endanger the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels and can affect voice and airway protection.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

thyrohyoid-muscle.name: Thyrohyoid muscle
thyrohyoid-muscle.summary: Short strap muscle between the thyroid cartilage and the hyoid. It depresses the hyoid or raises the larynx when the hyoid is fixed.
thyrohyoid-muscle.origin: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage.
thyrohyoid-muscle.insertion: Lower border of the body and greater horn of the hyoid bone.
thyrohyoid-muscle.action: Depresses the hyoid; raises the larynx toward the hyoid during swallowing when the hyoid is fixed.
thyrohyoid-muscle.innervation: Fibres of C1 carried with the hypoglossal nerve.
thyrohyoid-muscle.relations: Covers the thyrohyoid membrane; the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal vessels pierce that membrane just lateral and deep to it, making it the landmark for superior laryngeal nerve blocks; the superior thyroid vessels run at its lower border.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target; landmark for the superior laryngeal nerve and the thyrohyoid membrane.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: Injections at the thyrohyoid interval risk the internal laryngeal nerve (loss of supraglottic sensation and aspiration) and the superior laryngeal vessels.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Moore, Clinically Oriented Anatomy 8e

transverse-arytenoid-muscle.name: Transverse arytenoid muscle
transverse-arytenoid-muscle.summary: Single unpaired muscle bridging the backs of the two arytenoid cartilages. It draws the arytenoids together to close the back of the glottis.
transverse-arytenoid-muscle.origin: Posterior surface and lateral border of one arytenoid cartilage.
transverse-arytenoid-muscle.insertion: Posterior surface and lateral border of the opposite arytenoid cartilage.
transverse-arytenoid-muscle.action: Approximates the arytenoid cartilages, closing the posterior part of the rima glottidis during phonation.
transverse-arytenoid-muscle.innervation: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of vagus CN X).
transverse-arytenoid-muscle.blood_supply: Laryngeal branches of the inferior thyroid artery.
transverse-arytenoid-muscle.relations: Lies in the interarytenoid region posterior to the vocal folds, covered by the posterior laryngeal mucosa and the aryepiglottic folds; the esophagus and the cricopharyngeus lie posterior.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine injection target.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Not applicable in aesthetics.
injector_notes.cautions: No aesthetic relevance; deep laryngeal procedures are ENT territory.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e

transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.name: Transverse part of trapezius muscle
transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.summary: Middle fibres of the trapezius running horizontally from the lower cervical and upper thoracic spines to the shoulder girdle. They retract the scapula.
transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.origin: Spinous processes of C7 to T3 and the supraspinous ligament.
transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.insertion: Medial margin of the acromion and the superior crest of the spine of the scapula.
transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.action: Retracts the scapula toward the midline and, with the other parts, assists upward rotation.
transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) with proprioceptive fibres from C3 to C4.
transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.relations: Lies superficial across the lower neck and upper back over the supraspinatus, rhomboids and splenius; the spinal accessory nerve runs on its deep surface after crossing the posterior triangle.

injector_notes.relevance: Occasionally included in off-label trapezius contouring protocols; mainly relevant as part of the trapezius mass treated for shoulder line slimming.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Off-label trapezius toxin for contour or myofascial pain; the principle is intramuscular injection into the thickened belly, spread over multiple points, avoiding deep injection toward the rib cage.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffuse treatment of the whole trapezius risks generalized shoulder weakness and scapular instability; deep injections risk the pleura and suprascapular region.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)

zygomaticus-major-muscle.name: Zygomaticus major muscle
zygomaticus-major-muscle.summary: Main smiling muscle running from the cheekbone to the mouth corner. It elevates and draws the angle of the mouth laterally and is the key muscle of a natural smile.
zygomaticus-major-muscle.origin: Zygomatic bone just lateral to the zygomaticomaxillary suture.
zygomaticus-major-muscle.insertion: Modiolus at the angle of the mouth, blending with the orbicularis oris.
zygomaticus-major-muscle.action: Elevates the angle of the mouth and draws it laterally, as in smiling.
zygomaticus-major-muscle.innervation: Zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
zygomaticus-major-muscle.blood_supply: Transverse facial artery and branches of the facial artery.
zygomaticus-major-muscle.relations: Runs diagonally across the cheek; the zygomatic branch of the facial nerve crosses deep to its origin; the parotid duct and the facial vessels pass inferomedial to it; the masseter lies below its posterior part; the levator anguli oris and the buccal fat pad lie deep to its insertion at the modiolus.

injector_notes.relevance: Not a routine direct target, but crucial to protect: accidental weakening by crow's feet or masseter toxin diffusion is a classic cause of smile asymmetry and upper lip droop; occasionally treated on the hyperactive side for asymmetric smile.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Selected asymmetric smile or synkinesis cases treat the overactive zygomaticus major; the principle is a tiny, precisely placed injection into the muscle belly under animation testing, performed only by experienced injectors.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion from lateral canthal or masseter injections weakens this muscle and flattens the smile for weeks; injections near its insertion risk the modiolus complex and the facial vessels.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

zygomaticus-minor-muscle.name: Zygomaticus minor muscle
zygomaticus-minor-muscle.summary: Slender muscle from the cheekbone to the upper lip medial to the zygomaticus major. It elevates the upper lip and deepens the nasolabial fold.
zygomaticus-minor-muscle.origin: Zygomatic bone medial to the origin of the zygomaticus major.
zygomaticus-minor-muscle.insertion: Upper lip at the nasolabial fold, blending with the orbicularis oris and the levator labii superioris.
zygomaticus-minor-muscle.action: Elevates the upper lip and contributes to nasolabial fold definition and expressions of disdain.
zygomaticus-minor-muscle.innervation: Zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII).
zygomaticus-minor-muscle.blood_supply: Angular and superior labial branches of the facial artery and infraorbital branches.
zygomaticus-minor-muscle.relations: Lies between the zygomaticus major laterally and the levator labii superioris medially, deep to the orbicularis oculi at its origin; the angular vessels ascend medial to it along the nasofacial junction; the infraorbital nerve emerges deep and medial to its belly.

injector_notes.relevance: Occasionally included as an adjunct target in gummy smile treatment and relevant to mid-face filler planes near the nasolabial fold.
injector_notes.toxin_targets: Adjunct in gummy smile protocols targeting the lip elevators; the principle is conservative injection where the elevator complex converges at the upper nasolabial fold, keeping clear of the orbicularis oris.
injector_notes.cautions: Diffusion into the orbicularis oris or levator labii superioris causes upper lip ptosis and asymmetric smile; the angular artery and vein at the medial end of this muscle are a filler danger zone.

refs: Standring, Gray's Anatomy 42e
Carruthers & Carruthers, Botulinum Toxin (Procedures in Cosmetic Dermatology)
Cotofana S et al., facial anatomy for injectors (PRS / ASJ)

common-carotid-artery.name: Common carotid artery
common-carotid-artery.summary: Paired great artery of the neck supplying head and neck structures via its terminal bifurcation into internal and external carotid arteries.
common-carotid-artery.course: Right arises from brachiocephalic trunk behind the right sternoclavicular joint, left directly from the aortic arch; ascends within the carotid sheath, deep to sternocleidomastoid and anterior to the prevertebral fascia and longus colli, medial to the internal jugular vein, from the thoracic inlet to the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3-C4), where it bifurcates into internal and external carotid arteries; palpable at the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid at the level of the cricoid.
common-carotid-artery.branches: No branches in the neck before the bifurcation into internal carotid artery and external carotid artery; carotid sinus and carotid body located at the bifurcation.
common-carotid-artery.relations: Lateral to trachea, oesophagus, recurrent laryngeal nerve, thyroid and larynx; medial and slightly deep to the internal jugular vein with the vagus nerve posterolateral between them within the carotid sheath; crossed superficially by the omohyoid, sternocleidomastoid and, near the bifurcation, by the hypoglossal nerve and superior root of the ansa cervicalis.

injector_notes.relevance: Primary source of all extracranial facial arterial supply relevant to injectors; landmark for deep neck anatomy when treating the neck.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Not a direct injection target, but deep or blind needle placement in the anterior neck (submental, hyoid, thyroid region) can theoretically reach the carotid sheath; carotid puncture causes expanding haematoma and airway compromise.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Keep all anterior neck injections superficial (intradermal or subcutaneous for platysma) and know that the carotid pulse at the anterior SCM border marks the deep limit; never inject at or deep to the palpable carotid pulse.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

internal-carotid-artery-cervical-part.name: Internal carotid artery (cervical part)
internal-carotid-artery-cervical-part.summary: Terminal branch of the common carotid artery that ascends to the skull base without giving any branches in the neck, supplying brain, orbit and forehead via the ophthalmic artery.
internal-carotid-artery-cervical-part.course: Arises at the carotid bifurcation at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3-C4), posterolateral to the external carotid artery at origin; ascends vertically within the carotid sheath, deep to sternocleidomastoid, posterior belly of digastric and parotid gland, anterior to the longus capitis and cervical sympathetic trunk, to the carotid canal at the skull base.
internal-carotid-artery-cervical-part.branches: No branches in the cervical part; intracranially gives the ophthalmic artery, which gives rise to the supraorbital, supratrochlear and dorsal nasal arteries of the face.
internal-carotid-artery-cervical-part.relations: Internal jugular vein lies lateral, vagus nerve posterior between the two within the sheath; glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory and hypoglossal nerves cross its upper part; external carotid artery lies anteromedial at origin.

injector_notes.relevance: Origin of the ophthalmic artery system whose facial terminal branches (supraorbital, supratrochlear, dorsal nasal) are the vessels implicated in filler-related blindness.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Indirect: intravascular filler in any ophthalmic anastomosis (glabella, nose, forehead, temple) can embolise retrograde into the ophthalmic artery and then anterograde into the central retinal artery, causing irreversible blindness.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Not encountered by injectors directly; safe practice is to minimise intravascular risk in its distal anastomotic territories by using small aliquots, aspiration where feasible, slow retrograde injection and cannulas in high-risk zones.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.
Beleznay K et al. Update on Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Recent Review of the World Literature. Aesthet Surg J 2019;39(6):662-674.

external-carotid-artery.name: External carotid artery
external-carotid-artery.summary: Terminal branch of the common carotid artery supplying the face, scalp, oral and nasal cavities and most neck structures; parent vessel of nearly every named facial artery relevant to injectors.
external-carotid-artery.course: Arises at the carotid bifurcation at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3-C4), anteromedial to the internal carotid artery; ascends in the carotid triangle deep to sternocleidomastoid, then passes deep to the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, grooves the parotid gland, and within the parotid divides behind the neck of the mandible into its terminal branches, the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries, at the level of the earlobe.
external-carotid-artery.branches: Superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, maxillary and superficial temporal arteries (mnemonic covering its eight branches in order).
external-carotid-artery.relations: Hypoglossal nerve and the facial and lingual veins cross it superficially; internal carotid artery lies posterolateral above; styloid process and stylopharyngeus separate it from the internal carotid artery superiorly; retromandibular vein and facial nerve trunk lie superficial within the parotid.

injector_notes.relevance: Parent trunk of the facial, superficial temporal and maxillary arterial trees that define all facial filler danger zones.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Not directly at risk from aesthetic injections, but understanding its branching pattern explains why seemingly distant sites (lip, chin) share the same embolic risk network via the facial artery.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Not directly injectable territory; knowledge supports overall safe depth selection in parotid and preauricular regions where its terminal bifurcation lies deep within the gland.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

superior-thyroid-artery.name: Superior thyroid artery
superior-thyroid-artery.summary: First anterior branch of the external carotid artery, descending to supply the thyroid gland, larynx and adjacent infrahyoid muscles.
superior-thyroid-artery.course: Arises from the anterior aspect of the external carotid artery just below the greater horn of the hyoid, deep to sternocleidomastoid; descends obliquely forwards along the inferior constrictor to the apex of the thyroid lobe, passing superficial to the external laryngeal nerve near its termination.
superior-thyroid-artery.branches: Infrahyoid, sternocleidomastoid, superior laryngeal (pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the internal laryngeal nerve), cricothyroid and glandular branches to the thyroid.
superior-thyroid-artery.relations: Deep to omohyoid, sternohyoid and sternothyroid superiorly; the external laryngeal nerve runs medial to its upper part and crosses it near the thyroid pole.

injector_notes.relevance: Minor direct relevance; part of anterior neck vascular anatomy beneath the strap muscles.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep anterior neck injections (off-label) over the thyroid cartilage and upper trachea risk puncture and haematoma.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Aesthetic neck treatments should remain in the subcutaneous or intradermal plane over the platysma, well superficial to the strap muscles that cover this vessel.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

lingual-artery.name: Lingual artery
lingual-artery.summary: Second anterior branch of the external carotid artery, supplying the tongue, floor of mouth and sublingual gland.
lingual-artery.course: Arises from the external carotid artery at the tip of the greater horn of the hyoid; loops upward then forwards, deep to the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid, passes deep to hyoglossus (where it is crossed superficially by the hypoglossal nerve), then runs forward on the genioglossus in the floor of the mouth to the tip of the tongue.
lingual-artery.branches: Suprahyoid, dorsal lingual, sublingual and deep lingual arteries.
lingual-artery.relations: Hypoglossal nerve crosses superficial to it at the hyoglossus; the submandibular duct and lingual nerve lie above it in the floor of the mouth; internal jugular vein tributaries accompany its branches.

injector_notes.relevance: Important for intraoral and submental approaches; bleeding from its branches can compromise the airway in the floor of mouth.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep submental and intraoral floor-of-mouth injections risk haematoma of the floor of mouth, a recognised cause of airway obstruction.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Submental contouring and chin treatments should stay subcutaneous over the mylohyoid and mentalis, never deep through the floor-of-mouth musculature.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

facial-artery.name: Facial artery
facial-artery.summary: Principal artery of the face; tortuous anterior branch of the external carotid artery crossing the face from the lower border of the mandible to the medial canthus, where it continues as the angular artery.
facial-artery.course: Arises in the carotid triangle just above the lingual artery; ascends deep to the posterior belly of digastric, stylohyoid and the submandibular gland (grooving it), hooks over the lower border of the mandible at the anterior edge of masseter (antegonial notch, where its pulse is palpable), deep to platysma and risorius; then ascends obliquely across the cheek, deep to zygomaticus major and levator labii superioris at first, becoming more superficial as it approaches the nose, passing about 1 cm lateral to the oral commissure (deep to the modiolus muscles), along the nasolabial fold to the alar base and up to the medial canthus, where it terminates as the angular artery anastomosing with the dorsal nasal branch of the ophthalmic artery.
facial-artery.branches: Ascending palatine, tonsillar, glandular (submandibular), submental, inferior labial, superior labial, lateral nasal and muscular branches; terminates as the angular artery.
facial-artery.relations: At the mandibular border it lies deep to platysma, superficial to the mandible, with the anterior facial vein posterior to it and the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve crossing above; on the cheek it lies deep to the levator muscles but subcutaneous segments are common along the nasolabial fold; the facial vein follows a straighter, more posterior course.

injector_notes.relevance: One of the most important vessels in filler safety: its branches (labial, lateral nasal, angular) supply the lip, nasolabial fold and nose, all high-volume injection sites.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Nasolabial fold, nasal ala and medial canthus: the artery is frequently subcutaneous in the nasolabial fold, and its angular termination anastomoses with ophthalmic branches, so intravascular filler here can embolise retrograde to the ophthalmic artery causing blindness, or cause local skin and alar necrosis. Lips: the labial branches run deep to orbicularis oris, so superficial filler placed intramuscularly or deep risks intravascular injection and lip necrosis.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Nasolabial fold: inject deep (supraperiosteal) or very superficial dermal, avoiding the mid-subcutaneous plane where the artery often runs. Nose/alar base: use small boluses, supraperiosteal or subcutaneous midline placement, avoid lateral deep injections. Lips: stay in the submucosal or subdermal plane, avoiding the deep plane between orbicularis oris and mucosa where the labial arteries run.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.
Cotofana S et al. Injection-anatomy literature on the facial artery course and depth relative to fat compartments and mimetic muscles.

submental-artery.name: Submental artery
submental-artery.summary: Largest cervical branch of the facial artery, running forward under the chin to supply the submental region and chin pad.
submental-artery.course: Arises from the facial artery as it grooves the submandibular gland; runs forwards on the superficial surface of the mylohyoid, deep to the anterior belly of digastric near its termination, between the mandible and mylohyoid, to reach the chin where it anastomoses with the mental and inferior labial arteries.
submental-artery.branches: Cutaneous branches to the submental skin and chin; small branches to mylohyoid, anterior digastric and the submandibular gland.
submental-artery.relations: Superficial to mylohyoid, deep to the mandible margin and anterior belly of digastric; accompanied by the submental vein; the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve passes above the mandibular border nearby.

injector_notes.relevance: Supplies the chin and submental skin; relevant to chin filler and submental treatments including deoxycholic acid injections.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Submental injections placed too deep (through platysma/mylohyoid) risk bleeding and haematoma; anastomoses with mental and labial systems mean emboli could propagate along the chin pad.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Keep submental injections in the pre-platysmal fat (subcutaneous plane) between skin and platysma; for chin filler use supraperiosteal midline placement or superficial subcutaneous, avoiding deep lateral injections near the mandibular border where the artery runs.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

inferior-labial-artery.name: Inferior labial artery
inferior-labial-artery.summary: Branch of the facial artery supplying the lower lip, running horizontally within the lip deep to orbicularis oris.
inferior-labial-artery.course: Arises from the facial artery near the angle of the mouth, deep to depressor anguli oris; pierces and then runs horizontally forward between orbicularis oris and the labial mucosa, near the wet-dry vermilion border, anastomosing with its contralateral fellow and with the mental artery.
inferior-labial-artery.branches: Branches to the lower lip mucosa, vermilion, orbicularis oris and chin pad anastomoses.
inferior-labial-artery.relations: Deep to orbicularis oris, superficial to the labial mucosa; the facial artery lies lateral to the commissure; accompanied by labial veins draining to the facial vein.

injector_notes.relevance: Directly relevant to lower lip augmentation, one of the most common filler procedures.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Intravascular injection causes lower lip and chin skin necrosis; emboli can theoretically track retrograde to the facial artery. Deep fanning across the lip raises vessel-hit risk.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Inject in the submucosal or subdermal plane; the artery usually sits deep to orbicularis oris at the wet-dry junction, so superficial placement (subdermal vermilion border, small submucosal boluses) with the lip everted and small aliquots reduces intravascular risk.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
Cotofana S et al. Injection-anatomy literature on the perioral region and labial artery depth.

superior-labial-artery.name: Superior labial artery
superior-labial-artery.summary: Branch of the facial artery supplying the upper lip, running horizontally deep to orbicularis oris and giving the columellar branch to the nasal base.
superior-labial-artery.course: Arises from the facial artery lateral to the oral commissure, larger and more tortuous than the inferior labial; runs medially between orbicularis oris and the labial mucosa near the wet-dry junction of the upper lip, anastomosing with the contralateral artery; near the philtrum it gives the septal and columellar branches ascending toward the nasal tip.
superior-labial-artery.branches: Alar and septal branches and the columellar artery ascending in the columella toward the nasal tip.
superior-labial-artery.relations: Deep to orbicularis oris, superficial to mucosa; superior labial vein drains to the facial vein; the infraorbital nerve's superior labial branches descend over it.

injector_notes.relevance: Directly relevant to upper lip filler and lip flip techniques; its columellar branch links the lip to the nasal tip vascular network.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Upper lip intravascular injection risks lip and columellar necrosis; because the columellar artery connects to the angular-dorsal nasal-ophthalmic network, emboli from upper lip injections have a theoretical route toward the ophthalmic circulation.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Place upper lip filler submucosally or subdermally with small aliquots; avoid deep injections along the wet-dry junction where the artery runs; lip flip toxin should be intradermal/superficial intramuscular at the vermilion border only.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.

lateral-nasal-artery.name: Lateral nasal artery
lateral-nasal-artery.summary: Branch of the facial (or angular) artery supplying the ala and dorsum of the nose, part of the rich nasal anastomotic network.
lateral-nasal-artery.course: Arises from the facial artery as it passes the nasal ala; runs along the naso-facial groove and over the lateral nasal cartilage, superficial to the alar muscles and deep to or within the subcutaneous layer of the nasal sidewall, anastomosing with the dorsal nasal, infraorbital and contralateral branches.
lateral-nasal-artery.branches: Alar branches and dorsal nasal sidewall branches; anastomotic arcades across the nasal dorsum.
lateral-nasal-artery.relations: Lies superficial on the lateral nasal wall near the alar groove; close to the external nasal nerve branches deep to nasalis; the angular artery continues superiorly from it toward the medial canthus.

injector_notes.relevance: Key vessel for non-surgical rhinoplasty and alar base injections.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Nasal ala and sidewall: intravascular filler can cause alar and tip necrosis and can embolise via the dorsal nasal-angular anastomosis to the ophthalmic artery causing blindness; the nose is among the highest-risk filler regions.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Keep nasal filler midline, supraperiosteal or supraperichondrial, in small boluses with aspiration and slow injection; avoid the lateral sidewall and alar groove where this artery is superficial.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.

angular-artery.name: Angular artery
angular-artery.summary: Terminal branch of the facial artery at the medial canthus; the critical link between the facial and ophthalmic arterial systems.
angular-artery.course: Continuation of the facial artery from the alar base upward along the side of the nose, superficial to the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, within or deep to the subcutaneous tissue of the naso-facial junction, to the medial canthus where it anastomoses with the dorsal nasal and infraorbital branches of the ophthalmic system.
angular-artery.branches: Lateral nasal branches and terminal twigs anastomosing with the dorsal nasal artery (ophthalmic), infraorbital artery and contralateral angular artery.
angular-artery.relations: Accompanied by the angular vein (more medial/superficial); overlies the medial part of the orbicularis oculi at the canthus; lies roughly along a line from the alar base to the medial canthus.

injector_notes.relevance: The single most cited vessel in filler-induced blindness because it directly bridges the external carotid (facial) and internal carotid (ophthalmic) systems.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Naso-facial groove, nasal dorsum, glabella and medial canthus: intravascular filler injected with sufficient pressure can travel retrograde through the angular artery into the dorsal nasal and ophthalmic arteries, then anterograde into the central retinal artery, causing irreversible blindness; also causes nasal skin necrosis.
injector_notes.depth_tips: In the naso-orbital region use minimal volumes, supraperiosteal placement on bone, slow low-pressure retrograde injection, and consider cannula from a distant entry; avoid direct bolus into the naso-facial groove where the artery is superficial.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
