Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.
Beleznay K et al. Update on Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Recent Review of the World Literature. Aesthet Surg J 2019;39(6):662-674.

occipital-artery.name: Occipital artery
occipital-artery.summary: Posterior branch of the external carotid artery supplying the occipital scalp, posterior neck muscles and posterior meninges.
occipital-artery.course: Arises from the posterior aspect of the external carotid artery opposite the facial artery; passes deep to the posterior belly of digastric (crossed by the hypoglossal nerve), grooves the mastoid process on the occipital artery groove, then ascends between the mastoid attachments of sternocleidomastoid and splenius capitis, pierces the deep fascia at the superior nuchal line between the trapezius and SCM attachments, and ramifies in the occipital scalp superficial to the galea.
occipital-artery.branches: Sternocleidomastoid, mastoid, auricular, meningeal, descending and terminal occipital (scalp) branches.
occipital-artery.relations: At its scalp emergence it lies with the greater occipital nerve (nerve usually medial to the artery) about 2-3 cm lateral to the external occipital protuberance; crosses the internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus, accessory and hypoglossal nerves deep in the neck.

injector_notes.relevance: Landmark for the greater occipital nerve in occipital neuralgia treatment; supplies the occipital scalp where scalp filler/hair treatments are performed.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Occipital scalp injections risk vessel injury with brisk bleeding; artery palpation helps locate the adjacent greater occipital nerve for blocks.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Occipital scalp injections should stay in the subcutaneous plane above the galea with pressure available; for nerve blocks inject adjacent to the palpable artery at the superior nuchal line rather than into it.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

posterior-auricular-artery.name: Posterior auricular artery
posterior-auricular-artery.summary: Posterior branch of the external carotid artery supplying the auricle, scalp behind the ear and the facial nerve within the temporal bone.
posterior-auricular-artery.course: Arises from the posterior aspect of the external carotid artery above the occipital artery at the upper border of the posterior belly of digastric; ascends between the parotid gland and styloid process to the groove between the auricle and mastoid process, deep to the auricularis posterior, dividing into auricular and occipital branches on the scalp behind the ear.
posterior-auricular-artery.branches: Stylomastoid artery (entering the stylomastoid foramen to supply the facial nerve), auricular and occipital branches.
posterior-auricular-artery.relations: Facial nerve trunk lies anterior at the stylomastoid foramen; the posterior auricular vein and great auricular nerve run superficially over the mastoid and SCM nearby; parotid gland is anterior.

injector_notes.relevance: Minor direct relevance; part of periauricular anatomy for ear and postauricular procedures.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Postauricular injections (ear correction, occipital scalp) risk bleeding; proximity to the stylomastoid foramen is a reminder that the facial nerve trunk lies deep and medial here.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Keep periauricular injections subcutaneous; avoid deep injection into the mastoid-external auditory canal groove.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

maxillary-artery.name: Maxillary artery
maxillary-artery.summary: Larger terminal branch of the external carotid artery supplying the deep face, infratemporal fossa, jaws, teeth, meninges and, via its terminal branches, the cheek, lower eyelid and nose.
maxillary-artery.course: Arises behind the neck of the mandible within the parotid gland; passes forward deep to the mandibular neck (first/mandibular part), then across the infratemporal fossa superficial or deep to the lateral pterygoid (second/pterygoid part), and through the pterygomaxillary fissure into the pterygopalatine fossa (third/pterygopalatine part), giving branches along each segment.
maxillary-artery.branches: First part: deep auricular, anterior tympanic, middle meningeal, accessory meningeal, inferior alveolar. Second part: deep temporal, pterygoid, masseteric, buccal. Third part: posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, descending palatine, artery of the pterygoid canal, pharyngeal, sphenopalatine.
maxillary-artery.relations: Auriculotemporal nerve roots encircle the middle meningeal artery; the maxillary nerve lies above in the pterygopalatine fossa; the buccal nerve and artery descend together on buccinator; the sphenopalatine artery's posterior lateral nasal branches anastomose with the facial system on the nasal dorsum.

injector_notes.relevance: Parent of the infraorbital, mental, buccal and sphenopalatine systems encountered in midface and jawline injections; deep temple injections approach its deep temporal branches.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep preauricular and infratemporal injections (rare in aesthetics) risk major haemorrhage; its terminal branches define the infraorbital and mental foramen danger zones.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Stay out of the infratemporal fossa entirely; midface filler should be supraperiosteal on the maxilla or subcutaneous, never deep toward the pterygopalatine fossa or behind the mandibular ramus.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

infraorbital-artery.name: Infraorbital artery
infraorbital-artery.summary: Branch of the third part of the maxillary artery that traverses the inferior orbital fissure and infraorbital canal to emerge onto the face, supplying the lower eyelid, cheek, upper lip and nasal sidewall.
infraorbital-artery.course: Arises in the pterygopalatine fossa, enters the orbit via the inferior orbital fissure, runs forward in the infraorbital groove and canal in the orbital floor, and emerges through the infraorbital foramen (about 6-10 mm below the infraorbital rim in the mid-pupillary line), deep to levator labii superioris, dividing into its terminal branches.
infraorbital-artery.branches: Anterior superior alveolar branches within the canal; on the face: inferior palpebral, nasal and superior labial branches anastomosing with the facial, angular, transverse facial and buccal arteries and the dorsal nasal branch of the ophthalmic artery.
infraorbital-artery.relations: Emerges with the infraorbital nerve (artery typically medial/superomedial to the nerve) and vein; deep to levator labii superioris, superficial to the maxilla at the foramen; close to the nasolacrimal duct medially.

injector_notes.relevance: Central to midface, tear trough and cheek filler safety; foramen location guides both avoidance and nerve blocks.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Infraorbital/tear trough region (a Scheuer facial danger zone): intravascular injection can cause cheek and lid necrosis and, via anastomoses with the dorsal nasal and ophthalmic system, retrograde embolisation causing blindness; vessel and nerve injury also cause prolonged pain and dysaesthesia.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Tear trough and midface filler: inject supraperiosteal (on bone) or subcutaneous below the orbital rim, approaching from below or lateral to the foramen; avoid direct needle passes through the foramen zone (about 1 cm below the rim on the pupil line); small aliquots, aspiration, cannula preferred.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.

mental-artery.name: Mental artery
mental-artery.summary: Terminal branch of the inferior alveolar artery that exits the mental foramen to supply the chin and lower lip.
mental-artery.course: Branch of the inferior alveolar artery within the mandibular canal; emerges through the mental foramen (typically below the second premolar, midway up the mandibular body) with the mental nerve, running superficially onto the chin, deep to depressor anguli oris, anastomosing with the inferior labial and submental arteries.
mental-artery.branches: Chin and lower lip branches; anastomoses with submental and inferior labial arteries.
mental-artery.relations: Accompanies the mental nerve at the foramen; depressor anguli oris overlies it; the inferior labial artery approaches from the commissure.

injector_notes.relevance: Directly relevant to chin and jawline augmentation and mentalis toxin treatment.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Chin: intravascular filler at or near the mental foramen can cause chin pad and lower lip necrosis, and emboli can track into the labial-facial system; nerve-vessel injury at the foramen causes lower lip numbness and bleeding.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Chin filler: place supraperiosteal in the midline and paramedian or subcutaneously, avoiding deep lateral injections at the level of the mental foramen (second premolar line); fan from a midline entry rather than direct foramen passes.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

buccal-artery.name: Buccal artery
buccal-artery.summary: Branch of the second part of the maxillary artery running with the buccal nerve to supply the cheek and buccinator.
buccal-artery.course: Arises in the infratemporal fossa, descends obliquely forward between the medial pterygoid and the ramus/temporalis tendon onto the surface of buccinator, deep to the masseter and ramus, accompanying the buccal nerve (V3), to anastomose with the facial and infraorbital arteries on the cheek.
buccal-artery.branches: Branches to buccinator, buccal mucosa and cheek skin; anastomoses with facial and infraorbital arteries.
buccal-artery.relations: Runs with the buccal nerve (sensory, V3) on the lateral surface of buccinator, deep to the parotid duct region and masseter; the buccal branch of the facial nerve (motor) crosses the cheek more superficially.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to deep cheek and buccal space procedures and buccal fat pad surgery.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep cheek filler or buccal fat region injections risk bleeding and, via facial-inferior ophthalmic anastomoses, a small theoretical embolic risk; injury causes cheek haematoma.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Cheek augmentation should be supraperiosteal on the zygoma/maxilla or subcutaneous; avoid deep injections into the buccal space and through buccinator.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

superficial-temporal-artery.name: Superficial temporal artery
superficial-temporal-artery.summary: Smaller terminal branch of the external carotid artery supplying the temple, scalp, parotid and lateral face; palpable over the zygomatic arch root in front of the tragus.
superficial-temporal-artery.course: Arises behind the neck of the mandible within the parotid gland; ascends over the posterior root of the zygomatic arch, emerging from the parotid, running upward in the temporoparietal fascia (superficial temporal fascia) about 1 cm anterior to the tragus, and divides into frontal and parietal branches roughly 2-5 cm above the zygomatic arch.
superficial-temporal-artery.branches: Parotid, transverse facial, anterior auricular, zygomatico-orbital, middle temporal and terminal frontal and parietal branches.
superficial-temporal-artery.relations: Auriculotemporal nerve runs just posterior to it; superficial temporal vein runs with it; the temporal branch of the facial nerve crosses the zygomatic arch anteroinferiorly; the temporoparietal fascia containing the artery overlies the deep temporal fascia.

injector_notes.relevance: Central to temple filler safety and scalp injections; its palpation in front of the tragus maps the main trunk.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Temple: intravascular filler in the artery or its frontal branch can embolise, and anastomoses with the supraorbital and lacrimal systems create a route toward the ophthalmic circulation; temple and forehead blindness cases are reported. Vessel injury also causes pulsatile bleeding and haematoma.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Temple filler: inject either supraperiosteal on the temporal bone (deep to muscle, below the vessels) or very superficially in the subcutaneous layer, avoiding the intermediate temporoparietal fascia plane where the artery and frontal branch run; palpate and mark the pulse before injecting.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.

transverse-facial-artery.name: Transverse facial artery
transverse-facial-artery.summary: Branch of the superficial temporal artery crossing the cheek horizontally below the zygomatic arch, supplying the parotid region, masseter and lateral face.
transverse-facial-artery.course: Arises from the superficial temporal artery within the parotid; runs forward across the cheek between the zygomatic arch and the parotid duct, on the surface of the masseter and deep to the parotid fascia/platysma, accompanied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve and the parotid duct, anastomosing with the facial, infraorbital and buccal arteries.
transverse-facial-artery.branches: Parotid, masseteric and cutaneous branches to the lateral cheek.
transverse-facial-artery.relations: Lies with the parotid duct (below) and buccal branch of facial nerve (above/around), on masseter, roughly one finger-breadth below the zygomatic arch; transverse facial vein accompanies it.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to cheek filler and masseter toxin injections.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Masseter toxin: deep diffusion near the duct/vessels can rarely affect the zygomaticus/buccal branch region causing asymmetric smile; cheek filler placed intramuscularly risks intravascular injection and cheek necrosis.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Masseter toxin: inject into the lower posterior masseter belly, staying within muscle below the duct line. Cheek filler: supraperiosteal or subcutaneous, avoiding the horizontal band just below the zygomatic arch.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

frontal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-a.name: Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery
frontal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-a.summary: Anterior terminal branch of the superficial temporal artery supplying the temple, forehead and anterior scalp, anastomosing with the supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries.
frontal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-a.course: Arises from the superficial temporal artery above the zygomatic arch; runs obliquely forward and upward across the temple within the temporoparietal fascia, over the frontal process of the zygomatic bone toward the forehead, superficial to the temporalis and frontalis, anastomosing with the supraorbital, supratrochlear and lacrimal systems near the brow.
frontal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-a.branches: Temple and forehead cutaneous branches; anastomoses with supraorbital, supratrochlear and zygomatico-orbital arteries.
frontal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-a.relations: Runs in the same fascial plane as the temporal branch of the facial nerve (nerve deep/inferior within the temporoparietal fascia); the middle temporal vein (sentinel vein) crosses nearby deeper; superficial temporal vein runs parallel.

injector_notes.relevance: Major consideration for temple and hairline filler and for forehead volumisation via the temple.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Temple and lateral forehead: intravascular injection can embolise through supraorbital/supratrochlear anastomoses toward the ophthalmic artery causing blindness; injury causes prominent bleeding in this vascular plane.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Temple filler: supraperiosteal deep placement (one-up-one-over technique on bone) or superficial subcutaneous; avoid the temporoparietal fascia plane where this artery and the frontal branch run; cannula from a hairline entry reduces vessel encounters.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.

parietal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-.name: Parietal branch of superficial temporal artery
parietal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-.summary: Posterior terminal branch of the superficial temporal artery supplying the parietal scalp.
parietal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-.course: Arises above the zygomatic arch posterior to the frontal branch; curves upward and backward over the parietal region within the superficial fascia of the scalp, anastomosing with the posterior auricular and occipital arteries and the contralateral vessels.
parietal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-.branches: Parietal scalp branches; anastomoses with posterior auricular, occipital and contralateral superficial temporal branches.
parietal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-.relations: Runs with the superficial temporal vein; auriculotemporal nerve lies anteroinferior near the root; the galea aponeurotica and occipitofrontalis lie deep.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to scalp procedures and hair restoration rather than facial injectables.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Scalp injections risk brisk bleeding due to the dense connective tissue trapping open vessels; embolic risk is minimal but scalp necrosis reported with large volumes.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Scalp injections should stay in the subcutaneous plane with compression available; avoid deep subgaleal boluses over vessel courses.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

middle-temporal-artery.name: Middle temporal artery
middle-temporal-artery.summary: Branch of the superficial temporal artery that pierces the deep temporal fascia to supply the temporalis muscle and temple region.
middle-temporal-artery.course: Arises from the superficial temporal artery just above the zygomatic arch; pierces the deep temporal fascia near the posterior end of the arch and runs upward on or within the temporalis, giving branches to the muscle and anastomosing with the deep temporal arteries from the maxillary artery.
middle-temporal-artery.branches: Branches to temporalis; anastomoses with anterior and posterior deep temporal arteries.
middle-temporal-artery.relations: Travels with the middle temporal vein (sentinel vein), which pierces the deep temporal fascia near the lateral orbital rim; lies deep to the temporoparietal fascia and superficial to/within temporalis.

injector_notes.relevance: Part of the vascular anatomy of the temporal danger zone; its companion vein (the sentinel vein) is the key surface landmark for safe temple injections.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Temporal fossa: bleeding when piercing the deep temporal fascia during supraperiosteal temple filler; contributes to the vascular network linking to orbital anastomoses.
injector_notes.depth_tips: When placing supraperiosteal temple filler, enter perpendicular down to bone with aspiration; the sentinel vein zone (roughly at the lateral orbital rim/temporal fusion line) should be avoided or traversed with caution to prevent deep haematoma.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
Cotofana S et al. Injection-anatomy literature on the temporal fossa and sentinel vein.

zygomatico-orbital-artery.name: Zygomatico-orbital artery
zygomatico-orbital-artery.summary: Branch of the superficial temporal (occasionally lacrimal) artery running along the upper border of the zygomatic arch to the lateral orbit.
zygomatico-orbital-artery.course: Arises from the superficial temporal artery near the arch; runs forward along the superior border of the zygomatic arch within the superficial temporal fat pad/fascial layers to the lateral orbital margin, supplying orbicularis oculi and anastomosing with the lacrimal and transverse facial arteries.
zygomatico-orbital-artery.branches: Branches to orbicularis oculi and lateral periorbital skin; anastomoses with lacrimal and palpebral branches of the ophthalmic system.
zygomatico-orbital-artery.relations: Lies near the temporal branch of the facial nerve as it crosses the arch; the sentinel vein and zygomaticotemporal nerve are nearby in the temporal region.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to lateral brow, temple and lateral periorbital (crow's feet area) injections.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Lateral orbital rim/temporal junction: intravascular filler has a potential lacrimal-ophthalmic anastomotic route; vessel injury causes periorbital bruising.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Periorbital and lateral brow injections should be intradermal or superficial subcutaneous; temple filler should be supraperiosteal on bone away from the arch border; small aliquots.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

supraorbital-artery.name: Supraorbital artery
supraorbital-artery.summary: Branch of the ophthalmic artery that exits the orbit through the supraorbital notch or foramen to supply the forehead and anterior scalp; an ophthalmic-external carotid anastomotic vessel.
supraorbital-artery.course: Arises from the ophthalmic artery in the orbit; passes forward to the supraorbital margin, exits through the supraorbital notch/foramen (at the junction of the medial third and lateral two-thirds of the brow, roughly on the medial limbus/pupil line, about 25 mm from midline) with the supraorbital nerve, and ascends on the forehead, dividing into a superficial branch (through/over frontalis to the scalp) and a deep branch (between bone and frontalis up toward the vertex), anastomosing with the supratrochlear and superficial temporal systems.
supraorbital-artery.branches: Superficial and deep forehead branches; anastomoses with supratrochlear, angular-dorsal nasal and frontal branch of the superficial temporal arteries.
supraorbital-artery.relations: Exits with the supraorbital nerve (nerve usually lateral or through the same notch); superficial branch pierces frontalis; deep branch runs supraperiosteal deep to frontalis to the vertex; corrugator supercilii lies medial.

injector_notes.relevance: Key vessel for forehead filler and brow procedures; defines the supraorbital neurovascular bundle for blocks.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Forehead and brow: intravascular filler can embolise retrograde into the ophthalmic artery causing blindness; forehead skin necrosis also occurs. The glabellar-forehead complex is a leading blindness site in the literature.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Forehead filler: small aliquots in the subcutaneous plane or supraperiosteal midline, avoiding the supraorbital bundle zone (pupil line at the brow); aspirate, inject slowly with low pressure; toxin for frontalis should stay intramuscular above 2 cm from the brow to avoid ptosis.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.

supratrochlear-artery.name: Supratrochlear artery
supratrochlear-artery.summary: Terminal branch of the ophthalmic artery exiting the superomedial orbit to supply the medial forehead and glabella; the principal vessel of the glabellar danger zone.
supratrochlear-artery.course: Arises from the ophthalmic artery, exits the orbit between the trochlea and the supraorbital foramen (about 1.7-2.2 cm from the midline at the medial brow) with the supratrochlear nerve, pierces corrugator supercilii and frontalis, and ascends vertically up the paramedian forehead in the subcutaneous/intramuscular plane toward the hairline, anastomosing with the supraorbital, angular/dorsal nasal and contralateral vessels.
supratrochlear-artery.branches: Forehead branches; rich anastomoses with the dorsal nasal artery (ophthalmic), angular artery (facial), supraorbital and frontal branch of the superficial temporal artery.
supratrochlear-artery.relations: Accompanies the supratrochlear nerve; pierces corrugator and frontalis as it ascends; the angular artery meets the dorsal nasal system just below it at the medial canthus.

injector_notes.relevance: The glabella is the highest-volume toxin site and a common filler site; this artery makes it one of the top blindness-risk zones.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Glabella and medial forehead (Scheuer danger zone 1): intravascular filler embolises directly retrograde into the ophthalmic artery, then to the central retinal artery, causing blindness; numerous published blindness cases involve glabellar injection. Also glabellar skin necrosis.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Glabellar filler is best avoided or performed by experts with deep supraperiosteal placement on bone, tiny aliquots, strong aspiration, slow low-pressure injection; toxin for glabellar lines is intramuscular into corrugator/procerus and carries no blindness risk but medial diffusion can cause lid ptosis via levator palpebrae.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.
Beleznay K et al. Update on Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Recent Review of the World Literature. Aesthet Surg J 2019;39(6):662-674.

dorsal-nasal-artery.name: Dorsal nasal artery
dorsal-nasal-artery.summary: Terminal branch of the ophthalmic artery that leaves the orbit at the medial canthus and runs down the nasal dorsum; the direct ophthalmic-side link in nasal filler embolism.
dorsal-nasal-artery.course: Arises as a terminal branch of the ophthalmic artery; exits the orbit above the medial canthal tendon with the infratrochlear nerve, descends along the nasal root and dorsum in the subcutaneous plane over the nasal bones and upper lateral cartilages, anastomosing with the angular and lateral nasal branches of the facial artery and the external nasal region.
dorsal-nasal-artery.branches: Nasal root and dorsum branches; anastomoses with angular, lateral nasal and supratrochlear arteries; contributes to nasal tip supply via lateral nasal arcades.
dorsal-nasal-artery.relations: Lies superficial on the nasal dorsum over the nasal bones; the angular artery meets it at the medial canthus; infratrochlear nerve exits beside it above the medial canthal tendon.

injector_notes.relevance: Central vessel in non-surgical rhinoplasty risk assessment.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Nasal dorsum and radix: intravascular filler can flow retrograde into the ophthalmic artery causing blindness; the nasal skin envelope also has limited collateral reserve, so occlusion causes dorsal skin necrosis. Nose and glabella account for a large share of blindness cases.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Nasal filler: midline only, supraperiosteal/supraperichondrial plane, minimal volumes, aspirate and inject slowly; avoid lateral dorsal injections where the artery and its anastomoses run; consider cannula from the tip with extreme caution.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.

columellar-artery.name: Columellar artery
columellar-artery.summary: Ascending branch of the superior labial artery supplying the columella and contributing to nasal tip perfusion.
columellar-artery.course: Arises from the superior labial artery near the philtrum; ascends in the columella between the skin and the medial crura of the lower lateral cartilages toward the nasal tip, anastomosing with the lateral nasal and dorsal nasal systems at the tip.
columellar-artery.branches: Columellar and septal twigs; tip anastomoses with lateral nasal and dorsal nasal branches.
columellar-artery.relations: Runs within the columella superficial to the medial crura; the superior labial artery lies within the upper lip deep to orbicularis oris; the external nasal nerve supplies the overlying skin.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to nasal tip filler and columellar support injections.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Nasal tip/columella: intravascular injection or overfilling causes tip and columellar necrosis, and the tip network connects toward the angular-dorsal nasal-ophthalmic route.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Tip and columellar filler: minimal volumes in the subcutaneous/deep subcutaneous plane over the cartilages, avoid intradermal blanching pressure; upper lip filler should respect the superior labial artery depth to protect this branch.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.

vertebral-artery.name: Vertebral artery
vertebral-artery.summary: Major artery of the posterior circulation, ascending through the cervical transverse foramina to the skull; not a facial vessel but essential neck anatomy.
vertebral-artery.course: Arises from the first part of the subclavian artery; ascends through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1 (prevertebral part first, deep to the scalenes and longus colli), winds behind the lateral mass of the atlas, pierces the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and dura, and joins its fellow to form the basilar artery.
vertebral-artery.branches: Cervical muscular and spinal branches; intracranially: posterior inferior cerebellar, anterior spinal and meningeal branches.
vertebral-artery.relations: Anterior to the cervical nerve roots as they exit; sympathetic plexus surrounds it; the vertebral vein(s) accompany it; at C1 it grooves the posterior arch medial to the rectus capitis lateralis.

injector_notes.relevance: No direct role in facial aesthetics; included for completeness of neck vasculature and to define the deep limits of posterior neck injections.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep posterior triangle or suboccipital injections could theoretically injure it with catastrophic consequences; no aesthetic procedure should approach its course.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Keep all posterior neck injections superficial (subcutaneous over trapezius); suboccipital nerve blocks should follow established landmarks and stay superficial to the suboccipital muscles.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

internal-jugular-vein.name: Internal jugular vein
internal-jugular-vein.summary: Principal venous channel of the head and neck, draining the brain, face and neck into the brachiocephalic vein; main collecting vessel for facial venous blood.
internal-jugular-vein.course: Continuation of the sigmoid sinus from the jugular foramen; descends within the carotid sheath, lateral to the internal then common carotid artery with the vagus nerve posterior between them, deep to sternocleidomastoid, from the skull base to behind the medial clavicle where it joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
internal-jugular-vein.drains: Inferior petrosal sinus, pharyngeal veins, common facial vein (facial vein), lingual, superior and middle thyroid veins, and sometimes the occipital vein.
internal-jugular-vein.relations: Sternocleidomastoid covers it; crossed by the omohyoid and spinal accessory nerve; ansa cervicalis lies on the sheath; thoracic duct (left) or right lymphatic duct arches near its termination.

injector_notes.relevance: Final common pathway for facial venous drainage; relevant to neck procedures and to understanding valveless facial venous connections.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep lateral neck injections risk venous puncture, haematoma and air embolism; not a structure aesthetic needles should approach.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Keep neck injections subcutaneous over platysma; the vein is deep to SCM and safe from superficial work, but avoid deep injections along the anterior SCM border where the sheath is shallow at the clavicle.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

external-jugular-vein.name: External jugular vein
external-jugular-vein.summary: Superficial vein of the neck draining the scalp and deep facial regions, visible crossing sternocleidomastoid obliquely.
external-jugular-vein.course: Formed near the angle of the mandible within/below the parotid by the union of the posterior division of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein; descends vertically, superficial to sternocleidomastoid and deep to platysma, from the mandibular angle toward the midpoint of the clavicle, pierces the deep fascia above the clavicle, and drains into the subclavian vein.
external-jugular-vein.drains: Posterior division of the retromandibular vein, posterior auricular vein, and receives the posterior external jugular, transverse cervical, suprascapular and anterior jugular veins.
external-jugular-vein.relations: Crossed superficially by the great auricular nerve and platysma; the transverse cervical nerve crosses it at mid-SCM; the spinal accessory nerve lies deep as it crosses the posterior triangle.

injector_notes.relevance: Surface landmark of the lateral neck; relevant for neck and platysma treatments and for locating the great auricular nerve.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Neck injections: puncture causes visible bruising and haematoma in the superficial plane; deep injection near its clavicular course risks entry into the thoracic inlet region.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Platysmal band toxin is intradermal or superficial intramuscular into the platysma, superficial to the vein; avoid fanning deep over the mid-SCM where the vein, great auricular and transverse cervical nerves cross.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

anterior-jugular-vein.name: Anterior jugular vein
anterior-jugular-vein.summary: Superficial vein of the anterior neck draining the submental region down toward the external jugular or subclavian vein.
anterior-jugular-vein.course: Begins near the hyoid from the confluence of superficial submental veins; descends near the midline, superficial to the strap muscles and deep to platysma, then turns laterally deep to sternocleidomastoid just above the sternum to join the external jugular vein; communicates with its fellow via the jugular venous arch in the suprasternal space.
anterior-jugular-vein.drains: Submental and submandibular superficial veins, small laryngeal and thyroid twigs, jugular venous arch.
anterior-jugular-vein.relations: Lies with the transverse cervical nerve branches superiorly; the suprasternal space of Burns contains the jugular venous arch; platysma covers it.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to submental and anterior neck treatments including platysma toxin and skin boosters.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Anterior neck injections can bruise along its course; no embolic significance.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Keep anterior neck injections intradermal or subcutaneous above platysma; avoid deep midline injections toward the suprasternal notch.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

facial-vein.name: Facial vein
facial-vein.summary: Main vein of the face, running a straighter and more posterior course than the facial artery from the medial canthus to the lower border of the mandible; largely valveless.
facial-vein.course: Continuation of the angular vein from the medial canthus; descends obliquely behind the facial artery across the cheek, superficial to buccinator and deep to zygomaticus major and levator labii superioris (but superficial to the artery at the mandibular border), crosses the mandible at the anterior border of masseter deep to platysma, runs superficial to the submandibular gland, and joins the anterior division of the retromandibular vein to form the common facial vein draining into the internal jugular vein.
facial-vein.drains: Angular vein, superior and inferior labial veins, deep facial vein (connecting to the pterygoid plexus), submental vein, external palatine and submandibular tributaries.
facial-vein.relations: Crosses the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve at the mandibular border (nerve superficial); the facial artery is anterior and more tortuous; the deep facial vein connects it to the pterygoid plexus, and the angular vein connects it via the superior ophthalmic vein to the cavernous sinus.

injector_notes.relevance: Its valveless communications with the ophthalmic veins and pterygoid plexus define the classic danger triangle of the face for infection spread; also a major vessel in the midface injection field.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Midface and nasolabial injections: venous puncture causes bruising and haematoma; valveless connections mean facial infections (including infected filler) can spread to the cavernous sinus; rare reports of venous filler embolisation.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Nasolabial and cheek filler: supraperiosteal or subcutaneous placement avoids the vein's deeper course along the buccinator; aspirate before injection in the midface.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

angular-vein.name: Angular vein
angular-vein.summary: Vein at the medial canthus formed by the supratrochlear and supraorbital veins, continuing as the facial vein; the venous link between the face and the orbit.
angular-vein.course: Formed at the medial canthus by union of the supratrochlear and supraorbital veins; descends with the angular artery along the naso-facial junction, superficial to the medial canthal region and orbicularis oculi, continuing as the facial vein at the nasal ala level.
angular-vein.drains: Supratrochlear and supraorbital veins of the forehead; communicates through the orbit with the superior ophthalmic vein and hence the cavernous sinus.
angular-vein.relations: Accompanies the angular artery (vein slightly medial/superficial); lies over the medial canthal tendon region; connected to the superior ophthalmic vein by the nasofrontal tributary.

injector_notes.relevance: Defines the venous arm of the medial canthal danger zone; relevant to tear trough and naso-facial injections.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Medial canthus and naso-facial groove: venous puncture causes marked bruising; the valveless communication with the cavernous sinus makes perinasal infections dangerous; arterial embolism via the adjacent angular artery is the blindness mechanism here.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Tear trough and naso-facial filler: supraperiosteal or sub-orbicularis placement below the rim with a cannula, avoiding the superficial vein at the canthus; small volumes.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

supratrochlear-vein.name: Supratrochlear vein
supratrochlear-vein.summary: Paramedian forehead vein descending to the medial canthus to help form the angular vein.
supratrochlear-vein.course: Ascends the paramedian forehead in the subcutaneous plane with the supratrochlear artery, pierces the frontalis/corrugator region near the medial brow, and converges with the supraorbital vein at the medial canthus to form the angular vein; communicates with the superior ophthalmic vein through the superomedial orbit.
supratrochlear-vein.drains: Medial forehead and glabellar skin toward the angular vein; tributary communication to the superior ophthalmic vein.
supratrochlear-vein.relations: Runs with the supratrochlear artery and nerve; superficial on the glabella and medial forehead.

injector_notes.relevance: Part of the glabellar-medial canthal vascular field; venous anatomy mirrors the arterial danger zone.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Glabellar injections: venous puncture causes bruising; the valveless orbital communication matters for infection spread; blindness risk here is arterial via the companion supratrochlear artery.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Glabellar filler (expert use): deep supraperiosteal midline placement, tiny aliquots; avoid the superficial paramedian plane where the vein and artery ascend.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

supraorbital-vein.name: Supraorbital vein
supraorbital-vein.summary: Forehead vein descending from the supraorbital region to the medial canthus, joining the supratrochlear vein to form the angular vein.
supraorbital-vein.course: Begins on the forehead near the supraorbital notch with the supraorbital artery; descends across the brow, superficial to frontalis and orbicularis oculi, to the medial canthus where it unites with the supratrochlear vein; communicates with the superior ophthalmic vein through the supraorbital notch.
supraorbital-vein.drains: Lateral forehead and brow toward the angular vein; orbital communication with the superior ophthalmic vein.
supraorbital-vein.relations: Runs with the supraorbital artery and nerve at the notch; crosses the corrugator and orbicularis oculi superficially.

injector_notes.relevance: Part of the forehead-brow vascular field for filler and toxin work.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Brow and forehead injections: bruising along its course; orbital communication relevant to infection; blindness risk in this zone is arterial via the companion supraorbital artery.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Forehead filler: subcutaneous plane between frontalis and skin or supraperiosteal midline; avoid direct passes at the supraorbital notch zone.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

superior-ophthalmic-vein.name: Superior ophthalmic vein
superior-ophthalmic-vein.summary: Principal orbital vein draining the eyeball and orbit into the cavernous sinus, receiving the angular vein tributaries at the medial canthus.
superior-ophthalmic-vein.course: Formed in the superomedial orbit from the nasofrontal tributary (communicating with the angular vein) and the superior vorticose/ethmoidal veins; passes posterolaterally with the ophthalmic artery above the optic nerve through the annulus of Zinn and superior orbital fissure into the cavernous sinus.
superior-ophthalmic-vein.drains: Angular (nasofrontal) vein, ethmoidal, lacrimal, ciliary and vorticose veins, central retinal vein (often), inferior ophthalmic vein; drains to the cavernous sinus.
superior-ophthalmic-vein.relations: Crosses above the optic nerve with the ophthalmic artery; lies within the muscle cone; valveless, so flow can reverse with pressure changes.

injector_notes.relevance: The venous conduit linking the facial danger triangle to the cavernous sinus; understanding it explains infection spread and orbital congestion after periorbital trauma.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Perinasal and periorbital infections (including infected injection sites) can spread retrograde to cause cavernous sinus thrombosis; blindness from filler is arterial, not venous, but orbital haematoma and congestion complicate deep periorbital work.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Aesthetic injections never enter the orbit; periorbital filler stays preseptal (subcutaneous or sub-orbicularis in the tear trough/lid-cheek junction), never through the orbital septum.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Beleznay K et al. Avoiding and Treating Blindness From Fillers: A Review of the World Literature. Dermatol Surg 2015;41(10):1097-1117.

superficial-temporal-vein.name: Superficial temporal vein
superficial-temporal-vein.summary: Vein of the temple and lateral scalp descending in front of the ear to help form the retromandibular vein.
superficial-temporal-vein.course: Formed by confluence of temporal and parietal scalp veins; descends within the subcutaneous tissue/temporoparietal fascia, anterior to the ear, crossing the zygomatic arch root with the superficial temporal artery, enters the parotid and unites with the maxillary vein to form the retromandibular vein.
superficial-temporal-vein.drains: Temporal and parietal scalp, temple skin, receives the middle temporal (sentinel) vein, transverse facial vein and anterior auricular veins.
superficial-temporal-vein.relations: Runs with the superficial temporal artery (vein often anterior); the auriculotemporal nerve is posterior; receives the sentinel vein in the upper temporal fossa.

injector_notes.relevance: Temple filler safety: the temple contains large-calibre veins whose injury causes haematoma and whose intravascular injection carries embolic risk to the retromandibular/internal jugular system.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Temporal fossa: intravenous injection of filler can cause local occlusion and rarely pulmonary embolism of product; vein injury causes expanding haematoma in the loose temporal planes.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Temple filler: supraperiosteal on bone (below the venous plexus) or superficial subcutaneous; avoid the intermediate fascia plane; aspirate and use small aliquots.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Cotofana S et al. Injection-anatomy literature on the temporal fossa vasculature.

middle-temporal-vein-sentinel-vein.name: Middle temporal vein (sentinel vein)
middle-temporal-vein-sentinel-vein.summary: Large-calibre perforating vein of the temporal fossa, also called the sentinel vein; the key surgical landmark of the temporal danger zone marking the nearby temporal branch of the facial nerve.
middle-temporal-vein-sentinel-vein.course: Drains the temporalis region; pierces the deep temporal fascia near the lateral orbital rim and zygomaticofrontal suture area (roughly at or just behind the orbital rim, about 1.5-3 cm lateral to the lateral canthus), traverses the superficial temporal fat pad, and joins the superficial temporal vein in the upper temple.
middle-temporal-vein-sentinel-vein.drains: Temporalis muscle and deep temporal tissues toward the superficial temporal vein; receives tributaries from the lateral orbital and zygomatic region.
middle-temporal-vein-sentinel-vein.relations: Lies close to the temporal branch of the facial nerve as the nerve crosses the zygomatic arch and temple (the nerve runs in the temporoparietal fascia just above the vein's emergence); accompanies the middle temporal artery; the zygomaticotemporal nerve foramen is nearby deeper.

injector_notes.relevance: The sentinel vein is the single most useful landmark for the temporal danger zone: its visible position warns of the adjacent temporal branch of the facial nerve and the deep temporal vascular planes.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Temporal fossa (Scheuer danger zone): injuring the vein during supraperiosteal temple filler causes profuse, hard-to-control bleeding and haematoma; intravenous injection risks embolisation; the adjacent temporal branch of the facial nerve can be injured by deep dissection or aggressive cannula trauma causing frontalis paralysis (brow ptosis).
injector_notes.depth_tips: Temple filler: place supraperiosteal boluses on bone above the mid-fossa (the one-up-one-over zone) away from the orbital rim where the vein pierces, or stay superficial subcutaneous; avoid the plane of the vein at the temporal fusion line; blunt cannula and slow injection.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.
Cotofana S et al. Injection-anatomy literature on the temporal fossa and sentinel vein.

retromandibular-vein.name: Retromandibular vein
retromandibular-vein.summary: Vein formed within the parotid gland behind the mandibular ramus, dividing to contribute to both the external jugular and the common facial veins.
retromandibular-vein.course: Formed within the parotid by union of the superficial temporal and maxillary veins; descends through the parotid, posterior to the mandibular ramus and superficial to the external carotid artery, emerging at the lower pole of the gland where it divides into an anterior division (joining the facial vein to form the common facial vein) and a posterior division (joining the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein).
retromandibular-vein.drains: Superficial temporal and maxillary veins; receives parotid, transverse facial and middle temporal tributaries.
retromandibular-vein.relations: The external carotid artery lies deep to it within the parotid; the facial nerve branches lie superficial to it as they cross from the stylomastoid foramen into the face; the great auricular nerve crosses the gland superficially.

injector_notes.relevance: Key relationship in parotid-region anatomy; the facial nerve branches crossing superficial to it explain nerve risk in preauricular procedures.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Preauricular and jaw-angle injections: deep injection into the parotid risks vessel puncture, haematoma, sialocele and facial nerve branch injury.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Keep preauricular and masseter-region injections within the planned target (intramuscular masseter, subcutaneous jawline); never inject deep into the parotid bed behind the ramus.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

common-facial-vein.name: Common facial vein
common-facial-vein.summary: Short trunk formed by the facial vein and the anterior division of the retromandibular vein, draining into the internal jugular vein.
common-facial-vein.course: Formed near the lower pole of the parotid/submandibular region by union of the facial vein and the anterior division of the retromandibular vein; crosses the submandibular triangle superficial to the submandibular gland and the external carotid region, deep to platysma, to enter the internal jugular vein near the level of the hyoid.
common-facial-vein.drains: Facial vein and anterior division of the retromandibular vein.
common-facial-vein.relations: Lies superficial to the submandibular gland and the loop of the hypoglossal nerve region; crosses the external carotid artery superficially; deep to platysma and the deep cervical fascia.

injector_notes.relevance: Convergence point of facial venous drainage; relevant to submandibular-region procedures.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep submandibular injections risk haematoma; no specific embolic concern for typical aesthetic work.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Submandibular and jawline injections should remain subcutaneous or supraperiosteal along the mandible, not deep into the submandibular triangle.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

deep-facial-vein.name: Deep facial vein
deep-facial-vein.summary: Valveless connecting channel between the facial vein and the pterygoid venous plexus, passing deep to the ramus and buccinator region.
deep-facial-vein.course: Passes backward and downward from the facial vein (near the level of the nasal ala/cheek), deep to the zygomaticus muscles and masseter, across the buccinator/buccal fat pad region, to join the pterygoid plexus in the infratemporal fossa.
deep-facial-vein.drains: Facial vein territory toward the pterygoid plexus (which communicates with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins and with the inferior ophthalmic vein).
deep-facial-vein.relations: Crosses the buccal fat pad region; near the buccal nerve and artery on buccinator; the pterygoid plexus surrounds the lateral pterygoid.

injector_notes.relevance: Completes the map of valveless communications between the superficial face and the deep venous system of the skull base.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep cheek injections and infected midface sites can theoretically seed the pterygoid plexus and cavernous sinus; clinically, cheek filler infections warrant aggressive treatment.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Cheek filler: supraperiosteal on bone or subcutaneous; avoid deep buccal space injection which also risks this channel and the buccal fat pad.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

submental-vein.name: Submental vein
submental-vein.summary: Vein accompanying the submental artery under the chin, draining to the facial vein.
submental-vein.course: Runs with the submental artery on the superficial surface of the mylohyoid, from the chin backward below the mandible to join the facial vein as it crosses the submandibular region.
submental-vein.drains: Submental skin, chin and anterior floor-of-mouth region toward the facial vein; contributes to anterior jugular tributaries.
submental-vein.relations: With the submental artery between the mandible and mylohyoid; platysma and anterior belly of digastric are superficial.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to submental contouring (deoxycholic acid, skin tightening) and chin filler.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Submental injections: bruising and haematoma if the plane is too deep; keep within the pre-platysmal fat.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Submental deoxycholic acid and filler should be placed in the subcutaneous pre-platysmal fat, superficial to platysma, with a grid technique avoiding the mandibular border zone of the marginal mandibular nerve.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

occipital-vein.name: Occipital vein
occipital-vein.summary: Vein of the occipital scalp draining with the occipital artery toward the suboccipital plexus and deep cervical veins.
occipital-vein.course: Begins in the occipital scalp plexus at the vertex/posterior scalp; descends with the occipital artery, pierces the deep fascia at the superior nuchal line between the trapezius and SCM attachments, and drains into the suboccipital venous plexus, deep cervical or external jugular vein.
occipital-vein.drains: Occipital scalp; connects the scalp plexus to the suboccipital plexus and vertebral venous system.
occipital-vein.relations: Accompanies the occipital artery and greater occipital nerve at the superior nuchal line; overlies semispinalis capitis and the suboccipital muscles.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to occipital scalp injections and greater occipital nerve blocks.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Occipital injections: bruising; deep suboccipital injection could theoretically reach the vertebral venous system.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Occipital scalp and nerve block injections stay subcutaneous above the galea/fascia at the superior nuchal line.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

posterior-auricular-vein.name: Posterior auricular vein
posterior-auricular-vein.summary: Vein of the postauricular region joining the posterior division of the retromandibular vein to form the external jugular vein.
posterior-auricular-vein.course: Begins on the scalp behind the ear; descends with the posterior auricular artery behind the auricle over the mastoid, to the angle of the mandible where it joins the posterior division of the retromandibular vein.
posterior-auricular-vein.drains: Postauricular scalp and auricle toward the external jugular vein.
posterior-auricular-vein.relations: Runs with the posterior auricular artery in the auriculomastoid groove; the great auricular nerve ascends anterior to it over SCM; the lesser occipital nerve is above.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to periauricular and ear procedures.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Postauricular injections: bruising; no embolic significance.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Keep periauricular injections subcutaneous.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

superior-labial-vein.name: Superior labial vein
superior-labial-vein.summary: Vein draining the upper lip to the facial vein, accompanying the superior labial artery.
superior-labial-vein.course: Runs horizontally in the upper lip with the superior labial artery between orbicularis oris and the mucosa, draining laterally into the facial vein near the oral commissure.
superior-labial-vein.drains: Upper lip toward the facial vein; valveless.
superior-labial-vein.relations: With the superior labial artery deep to orbicularis oris; the infraorbital nerve's superior labial branches cross the region.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to upper lip filler bruising risk.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Upper lip injections: venous puncture causes the common post-lip-filler bruise; valveless drainage links the lip to the facial vein and danger triangle.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Submucosal or subdermal lip filler with small aliquots and lateral-to-medial threading reduces vessel hits; compress after injection.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

inferior-labial-vein.name: Inferior labial vein
inferior-labial-vein.summary: Vein draining the lower lip to the facial vein, accompanying the inferior labial artery.
inferior-labial-vein.course: Runs horizontally in the lower lip with the inferior labial artery between orbicularis oris and mucosa, draining laterally into the facial vein.
inferior-labial-vein.drains: Lower lip toward the facial vein; valveless.
inferior-labial-vein.relations: With the inferior labial artery deep to orbicularis oris and depressor labii inferioris region; mental vessels anastomose medially.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to lower lip filler bruising risk.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Lower lip injections: venous bruising; infected lip sites communicate with the valveless facial system.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Subdermal/submucosal placement, small aliquots, avoid deep plane at the wet-dry junction where the vessels run.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

facial-nerve-trunk.name: Facial nerve (trunk)
facial-nerve-trunk.summary: Motor nerve of the muscles of facial expression (CN VII); exits the stylomastoid foramen, traverses the parotid gland and divides into its five terminal branch groups.
facial-nerve-trunk.course: Exits the stylomastoid foramen (roughly at the midpoint of the anterior border of the mastoid, about 1.5-2 cm deep, near the tragal pointer which points to the trunk about 1 cm deep and anteroinferior to it); gives the posterior auricular nerve and branches to the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid; enters the parotid gland, crosses superficial to the external carotid artery and retromandibular vein, and divides at the pes anserinus into temporofacial and cervicofacial divisions, which form the temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches radiating from the anterior gland border.
facial-nerve-trunk.branches: Within the face: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches (plus posterior auricular, digastric and stylohyoid branches near the trunk).
facial-nerve-trunk.innervates: All muscles of facial expression (frontalis, orbicularis oculi and oris, corrugator, procerus, nasalis, zygomaticus major and minor, levator group, risorius, depressor anguli oris and labii inferioris, mentalis, buccinator, platysma) plus posterior auricular and occipital muscles, stylohyoid and posterior digastric.
facial-nerve-trunk.relations: Within the parotid it lies superficial to the external carotid artery and retromandibular vein (vein between nerve and artery); the trunk lies deep to the parotid fascia, medial to the mastoid tip and external auditory canal cartilage.

injector_notes.relevance: Its branches are the motor substrate of every toxin treatment and the structures at risk in facial danger zones; the trunk itself is deep and protected.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Preauricular and parotid-region deep injections or surgery can injure the trunk causing complete hemifacial paralysis; toxin should never be placed into the parotid bed.
injector_notes.depth_tips: All facial toxin injections target specific superficial mimetic muscles; keep preauricular work subcutaneous; the trunk is roughly 1 cm deep to the tragal pointer and must not be approached.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

temporal-branch-of-facial-nerve.name: Temporal branch of facial nerve
temporal-branch-of-facial-nerve.summary: Branch of the facial nerve crossing the zygomatic arch to supply the frontalis and upper orbicularis oculi; the nerve of the temporal danger zone.
temporal-branch-of-facial-nerve.course: Leaves the upper parotid and crosses the zygomatic arch, roughly along Pitanguy's line (from 0.5 cm below the tragus to 1.5 cm above the lateral brow), running within or just deep to the temporoparietal fascia, over the periosteum of the arch and superficial to the deep temporal fascia, to reach the deep surface of frontalis, corrugator supercilii and the upper orbicularis oculi.
temporal-branch-of-facial-nerve.innervates: Frontalis, upper orbicularis oculi, corrugator supercilii, anterior and superior auricular muscles.
temporal-branch-of-facial-nerve.relations: Runs in the temporoparietal fascia plane with the frontal branch of the superficial temporal artery nearby; the sentinel (middle temporal) vein pierces the deep fascia just below its course; the zygomaticotemporal sensory nerve is deep near the arch.

injector_notes.relevance: Injury or toxin diffusion causes frontalis weakness: brow ptosis and forehead asymmetry, the classic complication of temple-region procedures.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Temporal region and zygomatic arch (Scheuer danger zone): deep temple dissection or aggressive cannula work in the temporoparietal fascia can injure it; toxin injected too deep over the arch or diffusing from temporalis treatment can paralyse frontalis causing brow ptosis.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Temple filler: supraperiosteal on bone (deep to the nerve plane) or superficial subcutaneous (above it), never within the temporoparietal fascia; toxin near the lateral brow/arch should be superficial and low-volume.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

zygomatic-branch-of-facial-nerve.name: Zygomatic branch of facial nerve
zygomatic-branch-of-facial-nerve.summary: Branch of the facial nerve crossing the zygomatic bone to the lateral orbit, supplying orbicularis oculi and the zygomaticus muscles.
zygomatic-branch-of-facial-nerve.course: Leaves the anterosuperior parotid, runs forward across the zygomatic arch and zygomatic bone, superficial to the periosteum and deep to the subcutaneous tissue/SMAS, toward the lateral canthus, dividing into branches entering the deep surface of orbicularis oculi.
zygomatic-branch-of-facial-nerve.innervates: Orbicularis oculi (lower and lateral parts), zygomaticus major and minor (partly), and contributes to the midface plexus with buccal branches.
zygomatic-branch-of-facial-nerve.relations: Crosses the zygomatic bone near the zygomaticofacial nerve foramen (sensory); the transverse facial vessels run below the arch; the zygomaticus major origin is deep to its distal course.

injector_notes.relevance: Explains lateral periorbital toxin effects and risks; injury causes lower lid weakness (ectropion risk) and asymmetric blink.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Lateral canthus and zygomatic region: deep toxin diffusion from crow's feet injection can weaken lower orbicularis causing lid laxity appearance or worsen festoons; cheek filler dissection planes are below the nerve.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Crow's feet toxin: intradermal or superficial subcutaneous, lateral to the orbital rim, never deep on the zygomatic bone; cheek filler: supraperiosteal placement is below the nerve plane and safe from it.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

buccal-branch-of-facial-nerve.name: Buccal branch of facial nerve
buccal-branch-of-facial-nerve.summary: Motor branch of the facial nerve to the mid-cheek muscles, running with the parotid duct across the masseter; distinct from the sensory buccal nerve of V3.
buccal-branch-of-facial-nerve.course: Leaves the anterior parotid border, runs horizontally forward across the masseter, roughly parallel to and above/below the parotid duct and transverse facial artery, deep to the SMAS, forming a plexus over buccinator and entering the deep surfaces of the midface muscles.
buccal-branch-of-facial-nerve.innervates: Buccinator, zygomaticus major and minor, levator labii superioris and alaeque nasi, upper orbicularis oris, nasalis and procerus (via plexus).
buccal-branch-of-facial-nerve.relations: Runs with the parotid duct and transverse facial artery on masseter; the buccal nerve (V3 sensory) and buccal artery lie deeper on buccinator; the facial vein crosses posteriorly.

injector_notes.relevance: Explains smile asymmetry after masseter-region toxin diffusion; its duct-level course is the landmark to avoid.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Masseter toxin placed too high, too anterior or too superficial can diffuse to zygomaticus major/risorius or this branch, causing asymmetric smile; parotid duct region injections risk the same plus sialocele.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Masseter toxin: inject into the lower third, posterior bulk of the masseter, staying deep within muscle and below the parotid duct line (line from tragus to chelion); avoid anterior border fanning.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

marginal-mandibular-branch-of-facial-ner.name: Marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve
marginal-mandibular-branch-of-facial-ner.summary: Branch of the facial nerve running along the lower border of the mandible to the lower lip depressors; the most clinically vulnerable motor branch in lower face procedures.
marginal-mandibular-branch-of-facial-ner.course: Leaves the lower parotid, descends to run along the mandibular body, in a significant proportion of cases 1-2 cm below the lower border in the upper neck, curving up across the border at the antegonial notch region, deep to platysma and superficial to the facial vein and artery as it crosses them, then continuing to the deep surfaces of depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, mentalis and lower orbicularis oris.
marginal-mandibular-branch-of-facial-ner.innervates: Depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, mentalis, lower orbicularis oris, and contributes to risorius.
marginal-mandibular-branch-of-facial-ner.relations: Superficial to the facial artery and vein at the mandibular border (a key surgical relationship); deep to platysma; the cervical branch communicates with it below.

injector_notes.relevance: The nerve behind asymmetric smile after lower face procedures: depressor labii inferioris weakness produces the characteristic lower lip asymmetry.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Mandibular border and submandibular region (Scheuer danger zone): deep jawline filler dissection, submental procedures or platysma toxin diffusion can injure or weaken it; deoxycholic acid injected too close to the mandibular border is a recognised cause of temporary marginal mandibular paresis.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Jawline filler: stay supraperiosteal along the mandible or subcutaneous, avoiding the deep plane at the antegonial notch where the nerve crosses the facial vessels; platysma toxin: intradermal/superficial; keep submental fat-dissolving injections at least 1-1.5 cm below the mandibular border in the pre-platysmal fat.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

cervical-branch-of-facial-nerve.name: Cervical branch of facial nerve
cervical-branch-of-facial-nerve.summary: Lowest branch of the facial nerve, descending to supply the platysma and communicating with the transverse cervical nerve.
cervical-branch-of-facial-nerve.course: Leaves the lower parotid pole, descends behind the mandibular angle into the neck, deep to platysma, running forward on the submandibular region to enter the deep surface of the platysma; communicates with the transverse cervical nerve (cutaneous, C2-C3).
cervical-branch-of-facial-nerve.relations: Runs deep to platysma over the submandibular gland and external jugular vein region; the marginal mandibular branch runs parallel above it; communicates with the transverse cervical nerve on the SCM.

injector_notes.relevance: Platysma is the target of neck toxin treatments (platysmal bands, Nefertiti lift), so this nerve's muscle is intentionally treated; its communication with the transverse cervical nerve matters for neck sensation.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Overly deep neck toxin can diffuse beyond platysma to the marginal mandibular branch (asymmetric smile) or deeper structures; inadvertent injury is rare in injection work.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Platysmal band toxin: grasp the band and inject directly into the superficial muscle belly intramuscularly; Nefertiti technique: intradermal/superficial injections along the jawline and upper neck, never deep to platysma.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

supraorbital-nerve.name: Supraorbital nerve
supraorbital-nerve.summary: Larger terminal branch of the frontal nerve (V1) supplying the forehead and anterior scalp as far back as the vertex.
supraorbital-nerve.course: Arises from the frontal nerve in the orbit; exits through the supraorbital notch or foramen (about 25-30 mm from midline, at the medial-to-middle brow junction, roughly the medial limbus line) with the supraorbital artery, and divides into a superficial branch that pierces frontalis to supply forehead skin, and a deep branch that ascends between the galea and pericranium toward the superior temporal line and vertex.
supraorbital-nerve.innervates: Skin of the forehead and anterior scalp to the lambdoid region, upper eyelid (part), conjunctiva and frontal sinus mucosa.
supraorbital-nerve.relations: Exits with the supraorbital artery; the supratrochlear nerve is about 1 cm medial; the deep branch runs supraperiosteal just medial to the superior temporal line where it can be compressed in brow procedures.

injector_notes.relevance: Target of forehead nerve blocks and relevant to forehead filler placement planes.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Forehead injections at the brow can injure the nerve causing dysaesthesia; deep branch injury causes scalp numbness; companion artery creates the embolic risk.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Forehead nerve block: inject 1-2 ml local anaesthetic just above the brow on the medial limbus line; forehead filler: avoid deep passes directly over the notch; the supraperiosteal deep branch plane near the temporal line should be respected in temporal-forehead transitions.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

supratrochlear-nerve.name: Supratrochlear nerve
supratrochlear-nerve.summary: Smaller medial terminal branch of the frontal nerve (V1) supplying the medial forehead, glabella and upper nose root.
supratrochlear-nerve.course: Arises from the frontal nerve in the superomedial orbit; exits the orbit between the trochlea and the supraorbital foramen (about 1.5-2 cm from midline), pierces corrugator supercilii and frontalis, and ascends the paramedian forehead with the supratrochlear artery.
supratrochlear-nerve.innervates: Skin of the medial forehead, glabella, nasal root and medial upper eyelid; conjunctiva.
supratrochlear-nerve.relations: Runs with the supratrochlear artery through corrugator; the infratrochlear nerve is below it at the medial orbit; about 1 cm medial to the supraorbital nerve.

injector_notes.relevance: Target of glabellar nerve blocks; its passage through corrugator explains brow-region sensitivity.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Glabellar injections: nerve irritation causes transient dysaesthesia; the companion artery dominates the risk profile (blindness).
injector_notes.depth_tips: Glabellar toxin targets corrugator/procerus intramuscularly, through which the nerve passes - transient numbness can occur; keep injections into muscle, not deep onto the orbital rim.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

infratrochlear-nerve.name: Infratrochlear nerve
infratrochlear-nerve.summary: Terminal branch of the nasociliary nerve (V1) exiting the medial orbit to supply the medial eyelids, lacrimal sac and nasal root.
infratrochlear-nerve.course: Arises from the nasociliary nerve in the orbit; passes forward below the trochlea, exits the orbit above the medial canthal tendon with the dorsal nasal artery, and ramifies over the medial canthus and nasal root, deep to orbicularis oculi.
infratrochlear-nerve.innervates: Skin of the medial upper and lower eyelids, side of the nasal root, conjunctiva, lacrimal sac and caruncle.
infratrochlear-nerve.relations: Exits with the dorsal nasal artery above the medial canthal tendon; the angular vessels cross superficially below; the supratrochlear nerve exits above.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to medial canthal and nasal root injections and to nasociliary anaesthesia for nasal procedures.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Medial canthus injections risk nerve irritation and, more importantly, the adjacent dorsal nasal/angular arteries (blindness route).
injector_notes.depth_tips: Naso-facial and tear trough injections: cannula, supraperiosteal below the medial canthus; avoid deep boluses at the orbital rim exit point.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

external-nasal-nerve.name: External nasal nerve
external-nasal-nerve.summary: Cutaneous terminal of the anterior ethmoidal nerve (V1) supplying the nasal dorsum, tip and ala.
external-nasal-nerve.course: The anterior ethmoidal nerve travels through the anterior ethmoidal canal into the nasal cavity, then its terminal external nasal branch emerges onto the face between the nasal bone and the upper lateral cartilage, runs down under nasalis and the superficial fascia of the nasal dorsum to the tip.
external-nasal-nerve.innervates: Skin of the distal nasal dorsum, tip, columella (part) and ala.
external-nasal-nerve.relations: Emerges at the osseocartilaginous junction of the nasal dorsum, deep to nasalis and the nasal SMAS; the dorsal nasal artery and lateral nasal branches run with it in the subcutaneous plane.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to non-surgical rhinoplasty and nasal blocks; explains tip sensitivity.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Nasal dorsum filler: nerve compression or injury causes nasal dysaesthesia; the greater risk is the companion vasculature (necrosis, blindness route).
injector_notes.depth_tips: Nasal filler: midline supraperiosteal/supraperichondrial plane; anaesthesia of the nose can be achieved with infratrochlear plus external nasal region infiltration at the nasal root and dorsum.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

infraorbital-nerve.name: Infraorbital nerve
infraorbital-nerve.summary: Terminal branch of the maxillary nerve (V2) supplying the lower eyelid, cheek, nasal sidewall and upper lip; the key sensory nerve of the midface.
infraorbital-nerve.course: Continuation of the maxillary nerve through the inferior orbital fissure into the infraorbital groove and canal in the orbital floor; emerges through the infraorbital foramen (about 6-10 mm below the infraorbital rim on the mid-pupillary line), deep to levator labii superioris, and divides into inferior palpebral, external and internal nasal, and superior labial branches.
infraorbital-nerve.innervates: Skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, lateral nose and upper lip; mucosa of the upper lip and cheek; anterior maxillary teeth via the anterior superior alveolar branch.
