infraorbital-nerve.relations: Emerges with the infraorbital artery (artery usually superomedial) and vein; levator labii superioris overlies it, and levator anguli oris is medial; the zygomaticofacial nerve foramen is lateral and superior on the zygoma.

injector_notes.relevance: Target of the infraorbital nerve block (essential for pain-free lip and midface filler) and a structure to avoid in tear trough and cheek injections.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Infraorbital region (Scheuer danger zone): direct needle injury at the foramen causes prolonged paraesthesia; intravascular injection into the companion artery risks cheek necrosis and embolism toward the ophthalmic system.
injector_notes.depth_tips: For blocks, palpate the foramen ~1 cm below the rim on the pupil line and inject beside, not into, the foramen; for tear trough and cheek filler, approach from lateral or below with a cannula in the supraperiosteal or subcutaneous plane, avoiding the foramen zone.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

zygomaticofacial-nerve.name: Zygomaticofacial nerve
zygomaticofacial-nerve.summary: Small branch of the zygomatic nerve (V2) supplying the skin over the malar prominence.
zygomaticofacial-nerve.course: Arises from the zygomatic nerve in the orbit; traverses the zygomaticofacial canal and emerges through the zygomaticofacial foramen on the lateral face of the zygomatic bone (roughly at or below the orbital rim junction, on the malar eminence), piercing orbicularis oculi to reach the skin.
zygomaticofacial-nerve.innervates: Skin over the cheek prominence (malar eminence).
zygomaticofacial-nerve.relations: Emerges near the zygomatic branch of the facial nerve (motor) crossing the bone; the zygomatico-orbital artery and zygomaticotemporal nerve are lateral/superior.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to malar/cheek filler: foramen location marks a spot where needles can cause sharp pain and dysaesthesia.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Malar filler: direct needle hits at the foramen cause neuropraxia; companion small vessels bruise.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Cheek filler: supraperiosteal placement slightly above or medial to the foramen zone, or subcutaneous; aspirate and avoid direct foramen injection.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

zygomaticotemporal-nerve.name: Zygomaticotemporal nerve
zygomaticotemporal-nerve.summary: Small branch of the zygomatic nerve (V2) supplying the skin of the anterior temple; a recognised migraine trigger point.
zygomaticotemporal-nerve.course: Arises from the zygomatic nerve in the orbit; traverses the zygomaticotemporal canal to emerge through the zygomaticotemporal foramen on the temporal (posterior) surface of the zygomatic bone; ascends in the temporal fossa between bone and temporalis, piercing the deep temporal fascia about 2 cm above the zygomatic arch (roughly behind the zygomaticofrontal suture line) to reach the temporal skin.
zygomaticotemporal-nerve.innervates: Skin of the anterior temple; carries parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland en route.
zygomaticotemporal-nerve.relations: Its fascial exit point lies near the sentinel vein emergence and the temporal branch of the facial nerve plane; the zygomatico-orbital artery is inferior.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to temple filler (nerve injury causes temporal dysaesthesia) and to migraine trigger deactivation surgery.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Temporal fossa injections: deep needle passes at its fascia-piercing point (posterior to the orbital rim, above the arch) can injure it; bleeding from adjacent sentinel vein.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Temple filler: supraperiosteal placement should stay above the mid-fossa safe zone and avoid the rim-adjacent exit zone; superficial subcutaneous placement stays above the deep fascia it pierces.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

auriculotemporal-nerve.name: Auriculotemporal nerve
auriculotemporal-nerve.summary: Branch of the mandibular nerve (V3) supplying the temple, upper auricle, external auditory meatus and TMJ, and carrying secretomotor fibres to the parotid.
auriculotemporal-nerve.course: Arises in the infratemporal fossa by two roots that encircle the middle meningeal artery; runs backward behind the TMJ capsule and the neck of the mandible, deep to the parotid, then ascends over the posterior root of the zygomatic arch with the superficial temporal vessels (nerve posterior to the artery) into the temporal scalp.
auriculotemporal-nerve.innervates: Skin of the upper two-thirds of the auricle (lateral surface), external acoustic meatus, tympanic membrane (outer), TMJ and temporal scalp; conveys postganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland.
auriculotemporal-nerve.relations: Superficial temporal artery runs anterior to it over the arch root; within the parotid it is near the facial nerve; its auricular branches cross the great auricular nerve territory.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to temple and preauricular injections and to TMJ-region treatments; aberrant regeneration after parotid surgery causes Frey syndrome (gustatory sweating), sometimes treated with toxin.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Preauricular and TMJ-region injections: nerve irritation causes temple/ear dysaesthesia; intravascular injection of the adjacent superficial temporal artery is the greater danger.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Temple and preauricular injections: superficial subcutaneous or supraperiosteal planes; for Frey syndrome toxin, inject intradermally over the affected cheek skin mapped by starch-iodine test.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

buccal-nerve-v3.name: Buccal nerve (V3)
buccal-nerve-v3.summary: Sensory branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) supplying the cheek skin and buccal mucosa; not to be confused with the motor buccal branch of the facial nerve.
buccal-nerve-v3.course: Arises from the anterior division of V3 in the infratemporal fossa; passes forward between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid, descends on the lower head and the temporalis tendon, deep to the mandibular ramus and masseter, emerging onto the lateral surface of buccinator with the buccal artery, piercing the buccopharyngeal fascia to reach the cheek.
buccal-nerve-v3.innervates: Skin over buccinator (cheek), buccal mucosa and the buccal gingiva of the mandibular molars; carries no motor fibres to facial muscles (motor fibres to buccinator come from the facial nerve).
buccal-nerve-v3.relations: Runs with the buccal artery on buccinator; the buccal branch of the facial nerve (motor) crosses the cheek more superficially over the masseter with the parotid duct; the deep facial vein is nearby.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to intraoral injections, buccal fat procedures and deep cheek filler; anaesthetised in buccal nerve blocks for dental work.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep cheek and intraoral buccal injections: nerve injury causes cheek numbness; the deeper concern is the buccal artery and pterygoid plexus connections.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Cheek augmentation stays supraperiosteal or subcutaneous; avoid deep injection through buccinator into the buccal space where the nerve, artery and fat pad lie.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

mental-nerve.name: Mental nerve
mental-nerve.summary: Terminal sensory branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3) exiting the mental foramen to supply the chin and lower lip.
mental-nerve.course: Continuation of the inferior alveolar nerve within the mandibular canal; emerges through the mental foramen (typically below the second premolar apex, about midway between the alveolar crest and lower border) with the mental artery, and divides under depressor anguli oris into mental (chin), inferior labial and gingival branches.
mental-nerve.innervates: Skin of the chin, skin and mucosa of the lower lip, and the labial gingiva of the mandibular anterior teeth.
mental-nerve.relations: Emerges with the mental artery; depressor anguli oris overlies the foramen; the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve crosses the region more laterally at the mandibular border.

injector_notes.relevance: Target of the mental nerve block for lower lip and chin procedures; must be respected in chin and jawline augmentation.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Chin and jawline filler: direct needle passes over the foramen cause lower lip/chin numbness and neuropraxia; intravascular injection of the mental artery risks chin necrosis; aggressive deep fanning at the premolar line is the typical error.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Chin filler: midline supraperiosteal or subcutaneous; for jawline, fan from entries away from the foramen; mental block: inject adjacent to the foramen (palpable below the second premolar), not into it.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.
Scheuer JF et al. Anatomy of the Facial Danger Zones: Maximizing Safety during Soft-Tissue Filler Injections. Plast Reconstr Surg 2017;139(1):50e-58e.

inferior-alveolar-nerve.name: Inferior alveolar nerve
inferior-alveolar-nerve.summary: Branch of the mandibular nerve (V3) running through the mandibular canal to supply the lower teeth, terminating as the mental nerve.
inferior-alveolar-nerve.course: Arises from the posterior division of V3; descends between the sphenomandibular ligament and the ramus, lateral to the medial pterygoid and posterior to the lingual nerve, enters the mandibular foramen on the medial ramus (giving the mylohyoid nerve just before entry), and travels within the mandibular canal with the inferior alveolar vessels, supplying the molar and premolar teeth before terminating at the mental foramen.
inferior-alveolar-nerve.innervates: Mandibular teeth, buccal gingiva (posterior part, via buccal overlap), chin and lower lip via the mental nerve; the mylohyoid nerve supplies mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric.
inferior-alveolar-nerve.relations: Lingual nerve runs anterior and medial to it above the foramen; the maxillary artery origin and the sphenomandibular ligament lie nearby; within bone it is flanked by the inferior alveolar artery.

injector_notes.relevance: Mostly dental relevance, but defines the deep limit for jawline filler: in older or resorbed mandibles the canal lies closer to the surface.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep supraperiosteal jawline filler over a resorbed mandible can theoretically compress or injure canal contents causing prolonged numbness; intraoral deep injections risk the foramen on the medial ramus.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Jawline filler: supraperiosteal placement on the lateral mandible with small boluses; avoid deep pressure injection in atrophic mandibles; stay subcutaneous over the body where possible.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

lingual-nerve.name: Lingual nerve
lingual-nerve.summary: Branch of the mandibular nerve (V3) supplying general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, floor of mouth and lingual gingiva.
lingual-nerve.course: Arises from the posterior division of V3; descends between the medial pterygoid and the mandible, anterior to the inferior alveolar nerve, joined by the chorda tympani (taste and parasympathetic fibres); passes below the superior constrictor attachment, runs forward on hyoglossus and genioglossus in the floor of mouth, looping under the submandibular duct, to enter the tongue.
lingual-nerve.innervates: General sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, floor of mouth mucosa and lingual gingiva; carries chorda tympani taste fibres and parasympathetic fibres to the submandibular ganglion (submandibular and sublingual glands).
lingual-nerve.relations: Lies above the deep part of the submandibular gland; the submandibular duct crosses under it (duct loops beneath the nerve); the lingual artery is deeper on hyoglossus; the hypoglossal nerve runs below.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to submandibular and floor-of-mouth anatomy and to submandibular gland toxin treatment (sialorrhoea).
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep submandibular or intraoral floor-of-mouth injections can injure the nerve (tongue numbness, taste disturbance) or cause floor-of-mouth haematoma.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Submandibular gland toxin is placed into the gland parenchyma under guidance or careful palpation, staying superficial to the mylohyoid/hyoglossus plane; never inject deep toward the floor of mouth.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

great-auricular-nerve.name: Great auricular nerve
great-auricular-nerve.summary: Largest ascending branch of the cervical plexus (C2-C3), supplying the skin over the parotid, angle of mandible, earlobe and lower auricle; the most commonly injured sensory nerve in facelift and parotid surgery.
great-auricular-nerve.course: Emerges at Erb's point (posterior border of sternocleidomastoid at its midpoint) and ascends almost vertically across the SCM, deep to platysma and with the external jugular vein, toward the earlobe and parotid, dividing into anterior branches (skin over the parotid and angle of mandible) and posterior branches (mastoid region and lower auricle/earlobe).
great-auricular-nerve.innervates: Skin over the parotid gland and angle of the mandible, the earlobe, lower auricle (both surfaces) and the mastoid region.
great-auricular-nerve.relations: Runs with the external jugular vein on the SCM surface (nerve typically posterior to the vein); the lesser occipital nerve runs parallel above, and the transverse cervical nerve crosses below; platysma overlies it.

injector_notes.relevance: Surface landmark of the lateral neck; its course matters for neck and jawline injections, and its injury causes earlobe and jaw-angle numbness.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep injections over the mid-SCM and parotid tail (jawline, neck) risk neuropraxia; platysma toxin or deep neck filler fanned across the SCM can reach it.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Lateral neck injections: intradermal or subcutaneous above platysma; jawline filler supraperiosteal along the mandible anterior to the masseter; avoid deep injection over the SCM midline vertical course (roughly tragus-to-mid-clavicle line).

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

lesser-occipital-nerve.name: Lesser occipital nerve
lesser-occipital-nerve.summary: Branch of the cervical plexus (C2, sometimes C3) ascending along the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid to supply the upper lateral neck and scalp behind the ear.
lesser-occipital-nerve.course: Emerges at Erb's point on the posterior border of the SCM; ascends along the posterior border of the SCM, superficial to the deep fascia and deep to platysma, toward the scalp behind the auricle, where it pierces the deep fascia near the cranium and ramifies.
lesser-occipital-nerve.innervates: Skin of the upper lateral neck and the scalp posterior/superior to the auricle.
lesser-occipital-nerve.relations: Runs parallel and superior to the great auricular nerve along the SCM posterior border; the spinal accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle deep and medial to it; the occipital artery territory is posterior.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to upper lateral neck and postauricular procedures; injury causes occipito-auricular numbness or neuralgia.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep injections along the SCM posterior border (upper neck, occipital hairline) risk nerve irritation.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Keep upper lateral neck injections subcutaneous; occipital and mastoid-region work stays superficial to the deep fascia.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

transverse-cervical-nerve.name: Transverse cervical nerve
transverse-cervical-nerve.summary: Branch of the cervical plexus (C2-C3) crossing sternocleidomastoid horizontally to supply the anterior neck skin, communicating with the cervical branch of the facial nerve.
transverse-cervical-nerve.course: Emerges at Erb's point (mid-posterior border of SCM), hooks around the border and runs transversely forward across the SCM, deep to platysma and the external jugular vein, dividing into ascending and descending branches that pierce the deep fascia to supply the anterior neck skin as far as the chin; its ascending branch communicates with the cervical branch of the facial nerve beneath platysma.
transverse-cervical-nerve.innervates: Skin of the anterior triangle of the neck from the mandible to the sternum (with the supraclavicular nerves below).
transverse-cervical-nerve.relations: Crosses the external jugular vein at mid-SCM; deep to platysma (which it pierces); communicates with the cervical branch of CN VII; the great auricular nerve ascends parallel above.

injector_notes.relevance: Explains anterior neck skin sensation and the territory treated in platysma and neck skin procedures.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep neck injections across the mid-SCM can cause transient anterior neck numbness; platysma toxin is intentionally superficial and safe from it.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Platysmal band toxin: inject into the grasped band (superficial intramuscular); skin boosters: intradermal; both planes are superficial to this nerve.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

supraclavicular-nerves.name: Supraclavicular nerves
supraclavicular-nerves.summary: Terminal branches of the cervical plexus (C3-C4) descending over the clavicle to supply the lower neck, shoulder and upper chest skin.
supraclavicular-nerves.course: Emerge as a common trunk at Erb's point (posterior border of SCM), then divide into medial, intermediate and lateral supraclavicular nerves that fan downward, deep to platysma, crossing the clavicle (medial over the sternoclavicular region, intermediate over the mid-clavicle, lateral over the acromion) to reach the skin of the lower neck, shoulder and upper chest to the second rib/deltoid.
supraclavicular-nerves.innervates: Skin of the lower posterior neck, supraclavicular fossa, shoulder and upper anterior chest.
supraclavicular-nerves.relations: Cross the clavicle and the external jugular vein region deep to platysma; the spinal accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle medial/superior; cephalic vein is anterior at the deltopectoral groove.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to lower neck and decolletage procedures (skin boosters, toxin, energy devices).
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep supraclavicular injections risk nerve irritation and, deeper still, the subclavian vessels and lung apex; aesthetic work stays superficial.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Decolletage and lower neck treatments: intradermal or subcutaneous only; never inject deep in the supraclavicular fossa.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

greater-occipital-nerve.name: Greater occipital nerve
greater-occipital-nerve.summary: Medial branch of the dorsal ramus of C2; the principal sensory nerve of the occipital scalp, and the target of occipital neuralgia blocks.
greater-occipital-nerve.course: Emerges between the atlas and axis, curves around the inferior border of obliquus capitis inferior, ascends through semispinalis capitis, pierces semispinalis and then trapezius near their attachments at the superior nuchal line (roughly 2 cm lateral and 2 cm inferior to the external occipital protuberance/inion, just medial to the occipital artery), and runs with the occipital artery in the scalp to the vertex.
greater-occipital-nerve.innervates: Skin of the occipital scalp as far forward as the vertex; supplies semispinalis capitis en route.
greater-occipital-nerve.relations: Emerges medial to the occipital artery at the superior nuchal line; the lesser occipital nerve is lateral; the third occipital nerve is medial; lies superficial to semispinalis capitis and the suboccipital triangle contents (vertebral artery is deep within the triangle).

injector_notes.relevance: Target of greater occipital nerve blocks used for cervicogenic headache, occipital neuralgia and some migraine protocols; also relevant to occipital scalp injections.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Blocks placed too deep in the suboccipital region risk the vertebral artery and epidural space; correct technique stays superficial at the nuchal line; companion occipital artery puncture causes haematoma.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Inject subcutaneously at the superior nuchal line just medial to the palpable occipital artery (~2 cm lateral to the inion); aspirate; never inject deep toward the lamina or into the suboccipital triangle.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

spinal-accessory-nerve.name: Spinal accessory nerve
spinal-accessory-nerve.summary: Motor nerve (CN XI) to sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, crossing the posterior triangle of the neck superficially, where it is notoriously vulnerable to injury.
spinal-accessory-nerve.course: Emerges from the jugular foramen, passes posteroinferiorly (usually through or deep to the SCM, supplying it), exits at the posterior border of the SCM around the junction of its upper and middle thirds (roughly 1-2 cm above Erb's point), crosses the posterior triangle superficially on levator scapulae under the investing fascia, and enters the deep surface of trapezius about 2 cm above the clavicle at its anterior border.
spinal-accessory-nerve.innervates: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (with proprioceptive contributions from C2-C4).
spinal-accessory-nerve.relations: Crosses the posterior triangle superficial to the prevertebral fascia over levator scapulae; Erb's point (cervical plexus emergence) is just below its SCM exit; the transverse cervical vessels cross below; lymph nodes lie along its course.

injector_notes.relevance: Critical for trapezius slimming toxin (off-label) and for understanding neck contour; injury causes shoulder drop, winging and chronic pain.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Trapezius toxin injections placed in the upper medial trapezius near its anterior border can affect the nerve causing shoulder weakness; deep posterior triangle injections risk direct injury.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Trapezius slimming: inject into the bulk of the upper trapezius muscle belly away from its anterior border near the posterior triangle; keep all posterior triangle injections strictly subcutaneous.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

hypoglossal-nerve.name: Hypoglossal nerve
hypoglossal-nerve.summary: Motor nerve (CN XII) to the tongue muscles, looping forward above the hyoid in the submandibular region.
hypoglossal-nerve.course: Exits the hypoglossal canal, descends between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein, curves forward (crossing the occipital artery loop), crosses the external and internal carotid arteries superficially about 2-3 cm above the carotid bifurcation, passes deep to the posterior belly of digastric tendon, runs forward on the hyoglossus above the greater horn of the hyoid, deep to mylohyoid, and breaks into branches entering the tongue.
hypoglossal-nerve.innervates: All intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus; the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid are supplied by C1 fibres carried with it.
hypoglossal-nerve.relations: Crossed by the occipital artery; runs above the hyoid greater horn with the lingual artery deep (on hyoglossus) and the submandibular duct and lingual nerve above; the deep part of the submandibular gland lies lateral.

injector_notes.relevance: Relevant to deep submandibular anatomy; tongue deviation on protrusion signals injury.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep submandibular or submental injections through mylohyoid could theoretically injure it causing tongue weakness; far beyond normal aesthetic planes.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Submental and submandibular aesthetic injections stay superficial to platysma/mylohyoid; no aesthetic technique should reach the hyoglossus plane.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

vagus-nerve-cervical.name: Vagus nerve (cervical)
vagus-nerve-cervical.summary: Cranial nerve X descending within the carotid sheath, giving laryngeal branches in the neck before continuing to the thorax and abdomen.
vagus-nerve-cervical.course: Exits the jugular foramen and descends vertically within the carotid sheath, posterior between the internal jugular vein (lateral) and the internal then common carotid artery (medial), from the skull base to the root of the neck, passing posterior to the subclavian vessels into the thorax (right crosses the subclavian artery, giving the recurrent laryngeal which hooks under it; left descends to the aortic arch).
vagus-nerve-cervical.innervates: In the neck: pharyngeal branches (pharyngeal plexus, soft palate and pharynx muscles), superior laryngeal nerve (external laryngeal to cricothyroid; internal laryngeal sensory to the larynx above the cords) and superior cardiac branches.
vagus-nerve-cervical.relations: Within the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein and carotid artery; the cervical sympathetic trunk lies posterior on the prevertebral fascia; the ansa cervicalis lies on the anterior sheath.

injector_notes.relevance: No direct aesthetic role; part of deep neck anatomy marking the limits of any neck injection.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep anterior/lateral neck injections could theoretically cause vagal irritation (bradycardia) or recurrent laryngeal involvement (hoarseness); such depths are never appropriate in aesthetic practice.
injector_notes.depth_tips: All aesthetic neck injections remain superficial to platysma; the carotid sheath is a hard boundary identified by the carotid pulse.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

phrenic-nerve.name: Phrenic nerve
phrenic-nerve.summary: Motor nerve to the diaphragm (C3-C5), descending on the anterior scalene muscle under the prevertebral fascia.
phrenic-nerve.course: Formed at the lateral border of the anterior scalene from C3-C5 (mainly C4); descends vertically on the anterior surface of the anterior scalene, deep to the prevertebral fascia, passing behind the subclavian vein and in front of the subclavian artery (lateral to the internal jugular vein at the root of the neck), crossing in front of the internal thoracic artery into the thorax to the diaphragm.
phrenic-nerve.innervates: Diaphragm (motor) and sensory to the pericardium, mediastinal pleura, diaphragmatic pleura and peritoneum.
phrenic-nerve.relations: On anterior scalene under prevertebral fascia; the transverse cervical and suprascapular vessels cross superficial to it; the internal jugular vein is anteromedial; the thoracic duct is near on the left.

injector_notes.relevance: No aesthetic role; included for complete neck nerve mapping and as a caution for any deep lower neck procedure.
injector_notes.danger_zones: Deep supraclavicular or scalene-region injections (never aesthetic) risk phrenic palsy with hemidiaphragm paralysis; this anchors the rule that lower neck aesthetic work stays superficial.
injector_notes.depth_tips: Keep all supraclavicular and lower neck injections intradermal/subcutaneous; never inject deep to the deep cervical fascia in the lower neck.

refs: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 42nd ed. Elsevier, 2020.

glabellar-complex.name: Glabellar Complex (Frown Lines)
glabellar-complex.summary: Treat the corrugator at its insertion over the medial brow and along its superolateral course toward brow_mid; treat procerus at the glabella midline. Stay at or above the orbital rim and lateral to the supratrochlear notch to avoid the supratrochlear and supraorbital neurovascular bundles. Keep the lateral corrugator point above mid-pupil and not too close to the levator palpebrae to reduce eyelid ptosis risk. Identify the supraorbital notch by palpation before injecting. No doses are given; dosing is per product label and instructor guidance.
glabellar-complex.plane: Deep intramuscular into corrugator belly (below the brow, posterolateral to supratrochlear notch) and superficial intramuscular into procerus at the midline
glabellar-complex.targets: Corrugator supercilii muscle, Procerus muscle, Orbital part of orbicularis oculi
glabellar-complex.danger: Supratrochlear artery, Supraorbital artery, Supratrochlear nerve, Supraorbital nerve
glabellar-complex.common_complications: Eyelid ptosis from toxin spread to levator palpebrae superioris; brow ptosis if frontalis is overtreated inferiorly; bruising at supratrochlear vessels; headache; asymmetric brow elevation (Mr Spock sign) if lateral frontalis is left unbalanced

frontalis-forehead-lines.name: Frontalis / Forehead Horizontal Lines
frontalis-forehead-lines.summary: Frontalis is the only brow elevator, so treat the upper two-thirds of the forehead and preserve the lower 1-2 cm above the brow to retain lift and avoid brow ptosis and heaviness. Keep injection points at least 1.5-2 cm above the superior orbital rim; respect the supraorbital and supratrochlear notches medially. Balance lateral frontalis near the temporal fusion line to avoid quizzical brow. Frontalis is thin and closely applied to periosteum inferiorly, so injections are superficial intramuscular, not supraperiosteal. No doses given.
frontalis-forehead-lines.plane: Superficial intramuscular into frontalis, injected in a horizontal row pattern well above the brow
frontalis-forehead-lines.danger: Supraorbital artery, Supratrochlear artery, Supraorbital nerve
frontalis-forehead-lines.common_complications: Brow ptosis and brow heaviness; forehead heaviness with masked appearance; asymmetric or quizzical (Mr Spock) brows; compensatory lateral brow elevation; bruising

lateral-canthal-lines.name: Lateral Canthal Lines (Crow's Feet)
lateral-canthal-lines.summary: Inject in a fan of two to four points lateral to the orbital rim, keeping all points at least 1 cm outside the bony rim to protect intraorbital structures. Injections are superficial because the orbicularis is thin here and skin is delicate; stay subcutaneous to avoid bruising of superficial temporal and periorbital vessels. Keep the lowest point above the zygomatic arch to avoid spread into zygomaticus major, which would drop the lip corner. No doses given.
lateral-canthal-lines.plane: Subcutaneous, just deep to dermis within the thin lateral orbicularis oculi
lateral-canthal-lines.danger: Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery, Superficial temporal vein, Zygomaticotemporal nerve, Zygomaticofacial nerve
lateral-canthal-lines.common_complications: Bruising (superficial temporal and periorbital vessels); lower lid droop or ectropion in patients with poor lid snap-back; lip asymmetry from spread to zygomaticus major if injected too low and medial; dry-eye sensation

bunny-lines-nasalis.name: Bunny Lines (Nasalis)
bunny-lines-nasalis.summary: Treat the transverse nasalis with a small point on each upper nasal sidewall, roughly midway between rhinion and the medial canthus. Stay high on the nasal sidewall and lateral enough to avoid the angular artery ascending toward the medial canthus, and medial enough to avoid spread to levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, which would drop the upper lip. Compress the sidewall with the non-injecting hand to limit diffusion. No doses given.

bunny-lines-nasalis.danger: Angular artery, Lateral nasal artery, External nasal nerve
bunny-lines-nasalis.common_complications: Upper lip drop or elongation from spread to levator labii superioris alaeque nasi; smile asymmetry; bruising along angular artery territory; incomplete correction if levator contribution to the lines is not assessed

brow-lift-lateral-orbicularis.name: Chemical Brow Lift (Lateral Orbicularis Oculi)
brow-lift-lateral-orbicularis.summary: Weaken the lateral orbicularis (the lateral brow depressor) with one or two superficial points at the brow tail just lateral to the lateral canthus, allowing unopposed lateral frontalis to elevate the brow. Combine logically with balanced frontalis treatment; weakening lower frontalis instead would drop the brow. Keep points superficial and lateral to the orbital rim, and avoid the superficial temporal vessels in the temporal hairline. No doses given.

brow-lift-lateral-orbicularis.danger: Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery, Superficial temporal vein
brow-lift-lateral-orbicularis.common_complications: Brow asymmetry if one side is undertreated; eyelid ptosis if injected too medial or deep near the levator; accentuated upper-lid hooding if frontalis support was already marginal; bruising

masseter-hypertrophy.name: Masseter Hypertrophy / Lower Face Slimming
masseter-hypertrophy.summary: Ask the patient to clench and palpate the masseter borders; inject the bulky lower third of the muscle between gonion and the antegonial notch, keeping points posterior and inferior. Stay behind a vertical line from tragus to avoid the parotid duct and buccal branches of the facial nerve crossing the anterior muscle, and stay below the zygomatic arch to avoid the transverse facial artery. The facial artery crosses the mandible at the antegonial notch - inject away from the notch and keep the needle within muscle belly, not into submucosa. No doses given.

masseter-hypertrophy.targets: Superficial part of masseter, Deep part of masseter
masseter-hypertrophy.danger: Facial artery, Transverse facial artery, Buccal branch of facial nerve, Marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve
masseter-hypertrophy.common_complications: Smile asymmetry or weakness from spread to risorius or zygomaticus major; paradoxical bulging of untreated superficial fibers; masticatory fatigue; sunken appearance over the anterior cheek if overdone; bruising at facial artery crossing

mentalis-chin-dimpling.name: Mentalis / Chin Dimpling (Peau d'Orange)
mentalis-chin-dimpling.summary: Treat chin dimpling with one or two paramedian points in the mentalis near its origin low on the anterior mandible, above menton. Keep points low and paramedian: points placed too high or too lateral can weaken depressor labii inferioris or orbicularis oris, causing lower lip asymmetry and incompetence. The mental nerve and vessels exit at the mental foramen, roughly below the second premolar on a line from the pupil - avoid injecting lateral and deep at that level. No doses given.

mentalis-chin-dimpling.danger: Mental artery, Mental nerve, Inferior labial artery
mentalis-chin-dimpling.common_complications: Lower lip asymmetry or weakness; mouth incompetence with drooling or speech change; chin descent (witch's chin appearance) if overtreated in a chin that needs projection; bruising

platysmal-bands-nefertiti.name: Platysmal Bands / Nefertiti Lift
platysmal-bands-nefertiti.summary: For bands, have the patient grimace to activate platysma, pinch the band between thumb and finger, and inject a series of small points along it from the jawline toward the clavicle, lifting the band off deeper structures to avoid spread to laryngeal and strap muscles (dysphagia, dysphonia). For the Nefertiti lift, inject a row of points along the mandibular border to weaken platysmal downward pull on the jawline. Stay superficial: the external and anterior jugular veins lie just deep to platysma, and the marginal mandibular and cervical branches of the facial nerve run near the jawline. No doses given.
platysmal-bands-nefertiti.plane: Intramuscular into the platysma band, grasped and lifted away from the neck before injection
platysmal-bands-nefertiti.danger: External jugular vein, Anterior jugular vein, Cervical branch of facial nerve, Great auricular nerve
platysmal-bands-nefertiti.common_complications: Dysphagia or dysphonia from deep spread to laryngeal or strap muscles; neck weakness and difficulty flexing the neck; bruising over jugular veins; asymmetric jawline

lip-flip-orbicularis-oris.name: Lip Flip (Upper Orbicularis Oris)
lip-flip-orbicularis-oris.summary: A small amount of toxin into the upper orbicularis oris at the vermilion border relaxes the purse-string action and everts the upper lip slightly, simulating more vermilion show without filler. Place one to two points per side at or just above the vermilion border, medial to the philtral columns, very superficially and in minimal quantity. The superior labial artery runs in the submucosa posterior to the muscle at about the level of the wet-dry border - stay anterior and superficial. Conservative placement is essential: orbicularis weakness impairs puckering, drinking through a straw, and speech. No doses given.

lip-flip-orbicularis-oris.danger: Superior labial artery, Superior labial vein
lip-flip-orbicularis-oris.common_complications: Difficulty puckering, whistling, or using a straw; mild speech change; lip asymmetry; perioral incompetence if overtreated

gummy-smile-llsan.name: Gummy Smile (Levator Labii Superioris Alaeque Nasi)
gummy-smile-llsan.summary: Gummy smile from hyperactive lip elevators is treated with a point in LLSAN just lateral to the alar base at the medial nasolabial fold; the levator labii superioris and zygomaticus minor may also contribute, so assess the smile pattern first. Stay superficial and inferior to the infraorbital foramen region and respect the angular artery ascending in the nasolabial groove and the facial artery as it winds toward the nose. Overweakening elongates the upper lip and flattens the nasolabial fold. No doses given.

gummy-smile-llsan.targets: Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi muscle, Levator labii superioris muscle

gummy-smile-llsan.common_complications: Upper lip elongation or drop; flattened nasolabial fold; smile asymmetry; difficulty elevating the lip on smiling or speaking

perioral-lines.name: Perioral Lines (Smoker's Lines)
perioral-lines.summary: Fine radial perioral rhytids respond to very small, superficial toxin points at the vermilion border, one to two per lip quadrant, combined as needed with light resurfacing or superficial filler. Doses must be minimal and symmetric because orbicularis oris controls speech, eating, and expression; test lip function afterward. The superior and inferior labial arteries run in the submucosa near the wet-dry junction - keep injections anterior and superficial to the muscle. No doses given.

perioral-lines.danger: Superior labial artery, Inferior labial artery, Superior labial vein, Inferior labial vein
perioral-lines.common_complications: Lip weakness affecting speech, whistling, or drinking through a straw; asymmetric smile; perioral flattening; bruising of labial vessels

temple.name: Temple
temple.summary: Target is the temporal fossa: restore volume either as a deep supraperiosteal bolus high in the fossa near the superior temporal line (one finger up from the zygomatic arch, one over from the lateral orbital rim) or as superficial subcutaneous injection above the superficial temporal fascia. The superficial temporal artery and vein run in the superficial layer, the frontal branch of the facial nerve crosses the zygomatic arch at Pitanguy's line, and the middle temporal vein (sentinel vein) pierces the deep temporal fascia - inject slowly, low pressure, small aliquots, and consider aspiration at the deep supraperiosteal site. Avoid the temporal crest fusion zone where vessels concentrate.

temple.danger: Middle temporal artery, Superficial temporal artery, Frontal branch of superficial temporal artery, Middle temporal vein (sentinel vein), Superficial temporal vein, Temporal branch of facial nerve
temple.common_complications: Vascular occlusion (branches anastomose with orbital circulation - blindness risk); bruising of middle temporal or superficial temporal vessels; visible irregularity or Tyndall effect if placed too superficial in thin skin; temporal headache

forehead-glabella.name: Forehead / Glabella
forehead-glabella.summary: Target is the superficial forehead and glabellar subcutaneous plane to smooth horizontal hollowing and glabellar furrows. This is one of the highest-risk zones for vascular occlusion with blindness: the supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries exit at the notches and anastomose freely with the ophthalmic system. Stay superficial in the subcutaneous plane, midline or paramedian, away from the notches; use small aliquots, low pressure, slow retrograde injection, and consider a cannula from a lateral entry point. Never bolus deeply against periosteum near the supraorbital rim. Know the occlusion reversal protocol before treating.

forehead-glabella.common_complications: Vascular occlusion with skin necrosis and risk of blindness (supratrochlear and supraorbital to ophthalmic anastomoses); contour irregularity and visible lumps in thin forehead skin; bruising; persistent edema

nasal-dorsum-tip.name: Nasal Dorsum and Tip (Non-Surgical Rhinoplasty)
nasal-dorsum-tip.summary: Target is the deep midline avascular plane of the nasal dorsum (radix to rhinion to tip) and the columellar base at subnasale for tip projection. The nose is a supreme danger zone: dorsal nasal, lateral nasal, columellar, and angular arteries anastomose with the ophthalmic system, and nasal skin is unforgiving of occlusion. Inject strictly midline, deep on cartilage or bone, with tiny aliquots, minimal volume, low pressure, and constant awareness of skin blanching or pain; many injectors aspirate and pinch the dorsum to compress lateral vessels. Avoid lateral nasal sidewall injections. Stop immediately and begin the occlusion protocol for any blanch, livedo, or visual symptom.

nasal-dorsum-tip.common_complications: Vascular occlusion with skin necrosis of tip or ala; blindness via dorsal nasal to ophthalmic anastomosis; telangiectasia; overcorrection and dorsal widening; product visibility in thin skin

tear-trough-infraorbital.name: Tear Trough / Infraorbital Hollow
tear-trough-infraorbital.summary: Target is the supraperiosteal plane along the tear trough ligament and orbital rim to blend the lid-cheek junction. Palpate the infraorbital foramen (about 1 cm below the rim on the mid-pupillary line) and stay lateral or well medial of it to avoid the infraorbital neurovascular bundle; the angular artery and vein pass medially near the medial canthus. Use a cannula from a lateral entry in many protocols, deposit small amounts deep to the muscle, and avoid any superficial placement, which causes Tyndall discoloration and prolonged malar edema from lymphatic compression. Undertreat rather than overfill.

midface-malar-zygomatic.name: Midface / Malar and Zygomatic
midface-malar-zygomatic.summary: Targets are the deep medial cheek fat and the supraperiosteal plane over the zygomatic eminence and arch to restore midface projection and support. Deep bolus injection over the malar eminence and along the zygomatic arch is generally safe if truly supraperiosteal and away from the infraorbital foramen (mid-pupillary line, about 1 cm below the rim) and the zygomaticofacial foramen. The transverse facial artery runs about 1 cm below the zygomatic arch, and the facial artery ascends medially - map these mentally, inject slowly with small aliquots, and aspirate where a needle is used. Lateral-to-medial sequencing avoids pushing the face wider than intended.

nasolabial-fold.name: Nasolabial Fold
nasolabial-fold.summary: Target is the subcutaneous plane along the nasolabial fold, usually placed medial to the fold so the cheek does not appear heavier, with optional deep support at the piriform fossa for a deep superior fold. The facial artery courses through the nasolabial region and continues as the angular artery toward the medial canthus - it can be superficial here, so favor small aliquots, slow retrograde technique, blunt cannula from an inferior entry, and aspiration if using a needle deep at the piriform rim. Treat the cause (midface volume loss) before the fold itself for natural results.

lips.name: Lips
lips.summary: Targets are the vermilion body, vermilion border, and philtral columns. The superior and inferior labial arteries run between orbicularis oris and the mucosa near the wet-dry border, more superficial than often taught, so inject in the anterior two-thirds of the lip, keep depth superficial to the muscle toward the dry vermilion, use small aliquots with slow low-pressure delivery, and consider aspiration or a cannula from the modiolus entry for the body of the lip. Respect the philtral columns for definition and avoid overfilling the upper lip relative to the lower. Watch for blanching or disproportionate pain as occlusion warning signs.
lips.plane: Submucosal and intramuscular-submucosal plane of the vermilion and lip body; subdermal at the vermilion border
lips.danger: Superior labial artery, Inferior labial artery, Superior labial vein, Inferior labial vein
lips.common_complications: Vascular occlusion of labial arteries with mucosal or skin necrosis; lumps, asymmetry, and product migration; prolonged swelling and bruising; overfilled, unnatural projection

marionette-lines.name: Marionette Lines
marionette-lines.summary: Target is the subcutaneous plane along the marionette fold and the pre-jowl transition to lift the downturned corner. Inject lateral to the fold with a fanning technique from a single entry, supporting the commissure from below rather than filling the crease alone. The facial artery gives off the inferior labial artery in this region and the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve crosses the mandibular border nearby - keep injections superficial, slow, and in small aliquots, and avoid deep boluses at the mandibular border. Combine with DAO neuromodulator when depressor overactivity drives the downturn.
marionette-lines.plane: Subcutaneous fanning from a point lateral to the fold, layered inferior to the mouth corner to support the oral commissure
marionette-lines.danger: Inferior labial artery, Facial artery, Marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve
marionette-lines.common_complications: Bruising from facial or inferior labial vessels; asymmetry; product visibility or lumping in thin perioral skin; worsening of jowl appearance if volume is placed too lateral and inferior

chin.name: Chin
chin.summary: Targets are the supraperiosteal plane at pogonion for projection, paramedian points for width, and subcutaneous blending at the mentolabial sulcus and chin-jowl transition. Palpate the mental foramen (below the second premolar, mid-pupillary line) and keep deep injections midline and paramedian, staying medial and inferior to the foramen to avoid the mental neurovascular bundle. Aspirate for deep boluses, inject slowly in small aliquots, and respect the mentalis origin. Assess occlusion, profile, and lower facial height before deciding projection versus vertical lengthening.
chin.plane: Supraperiosteal midline and paramedian boluses for projection, plus subcutaneous layering for shape and mentolabial blending
chin.danger: Mental artery, Mental nerve, Inferior labial artery, Submental artery
chin.common_complications: Mental nerve irritation or transient numbness; bruising of mental or submental branches; asymmetry or lumpiness; vascular occlusion (less common than perioral but reported); overprojection and witch's chin deformity

jawline-prejowl.name: Jawline and Prejowl Sulcus
jawline-prejowl.summary: Targets are the prejowl sulcus (the hollow between chin and jowl) and the mandibular border to straighten and define the jawline. The facial artery crosses the mandible at the antegonial notch, anterior to the masseter, and the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve runs at or just below the border - keep injections subcutaneous or truly supraperiosteal, avoid deep injection at the notch, use slow small-aliquot retrograde delivery, and aspirate before deep boluses. Fill the prejowl first to camouflage the jowl, then extend posteriorly toward the angle for continuity.
jawline-prejowl.plane: Subcutaneous along the mandibular border and prejowl sulcus, with optional supraperiosteal bolstering at gonion
jawline-prejowl.danger: Facial artery, Marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve, Mental artery, Submental artery
jawline-prejowl.common_complications: Vascular occlusion of facial artery branches; transient marginal mandibular nerve irritation with lip depressor weakness; bruising; visible ridging along the border if placed too superficially; widened heavy jawline from overfilling

preauricular-lateral-cheek.name: Preauricular / Lateral Cheek
preauricular-lateral-cheek.summary: Target is the superficial fat of the lateral cheek and preauricular hollow to smooth the concavity in front of the ear and blend the zygomatic and jawline contours. This zone overlies the parotid gland and the facial nerve trunk and its branches, which lie deep within and superficial to the parotid - so stay strictly subcutaneous, never inject into the parotid, and favor a blunt cannula. The transverse facial artery runs about 1 cm below the zygomatic arch and the superficial temporal vessels ascend anterior to the tragus; keep the superior and posterior extent conservative. Small aliquots, low pressure, slow delivery.
preauricular-lateral-cheek.plane: Subcutaneous, in the superficial lateral cheek fat anterior to the parotid, layered with a cannula from a lateral entry
preauricular-lateral-cheek.danger: Transverse facial artery, Superficial temporal artery, Superficial temporal vein, Facial nerve (trunk), Buccal branch of facial nerve
preauricular-lateral-cheek.common_complications: Parotid injury, swelling, or fistula from deep injection; facial nerve branch irritation; bruising of transverse facial or superficial temporal vessels; contour irregularity; vascular occlusion
